An exposition of the prayer of the prophet Habakkuk, in Greek. A book On Adoration and Worship in the Spirit of Truth, and that the shadow is a type of life in Christ according to the Gospel, addressed to Palladius in dialogue form, with one interpreting and one responding, in Greek, in Italy. Seven orations, in Greek. Certain Greek homilies on the sacred creed. A counsel on concord between Greeks and Latins, in Greek. Two letters of the same man to Successus, bishop of Diocaesarea in Isauria. One letter to Augustine on the miracles of Saint Jerome. A Practica collected by the same man before the third synod. A book entitled Ta glaphyra. A Greek vocabulary, and a little work on words which change their meaning by accent, with a Greek-Latin lexicon. All these are preserved in Italy.

Besides these he composed several letters, homilies, and sermons, and other diverse treatises, which have not come to my knowledge.

He flourished, presiding at the Council of Ephesus, under the emperor Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 432, in the fifteenth indiction.

Theodore of Ancyra, bishop of Galatia, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and very learned in secular letters, especially strong in dialectic, eloquent in speech and a keen disputant, being quite distinguished in the Council of Ephesus, wrote there, in dialectical fashion and very obscurely:

Against Nestorius, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished under the prince Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 430.

Sozomen, Greek by nation, an excellent cultivator of secular letters and sufficiently learned in the divine Scriptures, is said to have written some little works for the edification of the Church. Of these there is extant a distinguished work addressed to the prince Theodosius the Younger, from the third consulship of the Caesars Crispus and Constantine down to the seventeenth consulship of the same Theodosius:

Ecclesiastical History, nine books. “The thought once came to me...”

The other things which he composed have not come to my knowledge.

He flourished under the aforesaid emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 450.

On Ecclesiastical Writers

A certain Socrates, Greek by nation, a learned and eloquent man, a distinguished historiographer, renowned for experience of great affairs, wrote, from the time of the first Constantine, the great emperor, down to the reign of Theodosius the Younger, a volume of Ecclesiastical History, one book.

He is also said to have written several other things, but they have not come into our hands. And it should be noted that three Greek authors, namely [Theodoret?], bishop of Cyrus, Sozomen, and this Socrates, each wrote histories of ecclesiastical affairs at almost the same time; Epiphanius Scholasticus translated these into Latin as they stood, and from them Cassiodorus Senator, a monk, made one continuous history, which he called the Tripartite.

Vigilius, a deacon and monk, a man studious and learned in the holy Scriptures, a guardian and director of monastic discipline, is reported to have fashioned certain little works for the edification of monks, which distance of places and times has prevented from coming to our knowledge. The priest Gennadius says, however, that he wrote a very useful rule:

On the Conduct of Monks, one book. He says nothing about the rest. He flourished under the princes Honorius and Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 420.

Osius, bishop of Corduba before Isidore, to whom Chalcidius the grammarian is recorded to have translated Plato’s Timaeus, a learned and eloquent man, presiding at the council of Sardica, uttered many excellent opinions, as is contained in the acts of that same synod. In his old age, however, greatly terrified by Constantius, the Arian prince, and fearing lest, as an old and wealthy man, he should suffer either exile or loss of property, he soon consented to Arian impiety. But not long afterward his life, as he deserved, was ended by a cruel death. For after his impious betrayal, when Saint Gregory, bishop of Eliberis, had come to Corduba by imperial decree and refused to communicate with Osius, the latter, moved with anger, asked Clementinus, Constantius’s prefect and vicar, to drive Gregory into exile. The vicar said to him: “I do not dare send a bishop into exile unless you first depose him from the episcopate.” Osius, tolerating no delay, mounted the chair as judge and summoned Gregory by royal edict. When Gregory appeared before the multitude, and Osius, proud in his arrogance, tried to pronounce the sentence of deposition, Gregory appealed with all his strength to Christ, that he should not allow so unjust a presumption of his to go unpunished. And behold, as the impious Osius sat there and wished to pronounce the sentence, his mouth twisted, and at the same time his neck was distorted; falling to the ground, he suddenly expired. Fear then seized everyone; thereafter no one dared touch Gregory. Osius, while still a Catholic, wrote:

To His Sister, On the Praise of Virginity, one book.

In the aforesaid council, eighteen opinions, one book.

And several letters. He flourished under Constantius as a very old man, by whom also he was deceived, and he died around the year of the Lord 590.

Ithacius, bishop of the city of [Lemica?] in Spain, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, renowned for his manner of speaking, who, together with Bishop [Ursacius?], because of the killing of Priscillian, whom he had accused at Trier, was separated from communion with the Church and driven into exile, and died there. He wrote works not to be despised, among which these are reported:

Against Priscillian, one book.

Chronicles from the Time of Theodosius, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished under the venerable emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 400.

Leporius, priest and monk, studious in the divine Scriptures, but presuming too much on the purity of his life, taught as doctrine that he lived religiously by his own judgment and effort, not by the grace of God, defending the Pelagian error. But after being admonished by the Gallic doctors and corrected in Africa by Saint Augustine, he abandoned his error; the heresy which he had formerly preached he afterward vigorously attacked. Therefore, giving thanks for his correction, he wrote:

A Corrective against Heresy, one book.

And certain other things.

He flourished under the prince Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 450.

Sedulius, priest, a Scot by nation, from early youth a disciple of Hildebert, archbishop of the Scots, a man practiced in the divine Scriptures and very learned in secular letters, excellent in verse and prose, leaving Scotland out of love of learning, came into France, then traversed Italy and Asia; finally, departing from the borders of Achaia, he shone forth in the city of Rome, renowned for wondrous learning. He wrote many works in meter and in prose; of these I have found only the following: To Abbot Macedonius, a distinguished work according to the sequence of the whole Gospel, which he entitled Paschal Song, in meter, four books. “All you who [unclear] paschal [unclear].” On all the Epistles of Paul, in prose, fourteen books. “Before the apostolic words...” On

70 On Ecclesiastical Writers

On the miracles of Christ, one book, “From the quarter of the rising sun.” To the emperor Theodosius, one book, “Leader of the Romulidae [unclear].” On the larger volume of Priscian, one book, “Let us sing, companions, to the Lord.” On the second edition of Donatus, one book, “Sedulius the Scotigene.” An exhortation to the faithful, one book; book 2. Several letters to various persons, one book, “Sedulius the Scotigene.” On the miracles of Christ in prose, two books. He also published a number of other things, which have not come to my knowledge. At length, as Sigebert writes, he was ordained bishop, but he does not state the church or city where. He flourished under Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 430.

Victorinus of Marseilles, rhetorician, a man most learned in secular letters and very devoted to the holy Scriptures, attempted to expound the holy Scriptures; but, being occupied with secular literature and having entered the field of the divine utterances without a teacher, he did not accomplish what he wished. Hence the little works that he wrote are indeed distinguished by Christian feeling and pious zeal, but are shaped with a lighter weight of opinions. He published, addressed to the person of his son Ethernius, commentaries from the beginning down to the death of the patriarch Abraham:

On Genesis, four books.

And certain other things which are hidden from us. He flourished under Theodosius and Valentinian, in the year of the Lord 430.

Philippus, monk and priest, once a hearer and disciple of blessed Jerome, a studious and learned man, an outstanding lover of voluntary poverty, who by word and example instructed many in piety, after the death of his master published certain commentaries on the divine Scriptures, among which there survives, as they say, an excellent work:

On Job, one book. A collection of letters, one book.

He flourished under the princes Theodosius and Valentinian, in the year of the Lord 430. And he died under Marcian.

Vincentius, monk and priest of the monastery of the island of Lerins, a Gaul by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, distinguished in life and character. There survives an outstanding work of his, which he composed under the name Peregrinus, very famous among the ancient doctors and worthy of praise, on avoiding the errors and gatherings of heretics:

Against all heretics, two books.

It is also read that he wrote a number of other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the reign of Theodosius and Valentinian, in the year of the Lord 429.

Abbot of Spanheim

Paulus, priest, a Pannonian by nation, which is now called Hungary, a man devoted to sacred letters and sufficiently learned, venerable no less for the cultivation of religion than for knowledge of the Scriptures, a zealous defender of the Christian faith, is said to have written not a few volumes, the reading of which is considered quite suitable for confounding heretics. There survive his works addressed to Constantia, a virgin dedicated to Christ:

On virginity and contempt of the world, two books.

Concerning other works I have so far found nothing. He flourished under Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 430.

Isaac, formerly a monk, priest of the church of Antioch, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, of very celebrated reputation for delivering homilies to the people, beloved by God in life and conduct, venerable to men, wrote in the Syriac tongue, in imitation of Saint Ephrem, several devout little works, the reading of which is judged very useful for religious men. Among these I have found the following among our materials:

Against the Nestorians and Eutyches, two books. An exhortation to the spiritual life, one book. On the struggle against vices, one book. On access to God, one book. On the difficulty of the virtues, one book. A dialogue on spiritual progress, one book. On the order of the monastic life, one book. On violent operation, one book. On humility, one book. On the three orders of those making progress, one book. On the solitude of monks, one book. On various temptations, one book. On the instruction of novices, one book. On penitence, one book. A poem on the devastation of Antioch, one book.

He delivered several homilies to the people, but they have by no means come into our hands. He flourished under Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 440.

Eucherius, bishop of Lyons in Gaul, a learned man, imbued from youth with monastic discipline, ready in talent, composed in speech, pleasing to God and men in life and conduct, since indeed he turned many away from iniquity by word and example, wrote several excellent volumes, but so far few have come to my knowledge. For I have found only these:

On contempt of the world, one book.

Ex-

On Ecclesiastical Writers

Expositions of the divine names, 1 book. Formulas of spiritual [unclear], To the sons Solon and Uranus, 1 book. An epitome of Cassian, 4 books. Certain letters to various persons, 1 book. To Bishop Hilary, On the praise of the desert, 1 book. The beginning of the commentaries on Genesis. Instructions, 2 books. He flourished under Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 440.

Hilary, bishop of Arles, to whom Eucherius, bishop of Lyon, when he was seeking the wastes of the desert, published a book On the Praise of the Desert, was a man learned in the divine scriptures and sufficiently eloquent in speech. His merits of holiness the catholic Church proclaims. He showed such compassion toward the poor that, after all his possessions had been cheerfully distributed for their use, he was thereafter called, and was, the father of poverty. Among other things he wrote, in quite distinguished style, the Life of his predecessor, St. Honoratus the bishop, 1 book; almost countless homilies; and certain other works. He flourished under Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 440. He died, however, under the emperors Valentinian and Marcian.

Zosimus, pope, a Greek by nationality, sat in the pontificate after St. Innocent for one year and eight months. He was a learned, holy man, beloved by God, who by word and example governed the Church entrusted to him [unclear], and for whose edification he elegantly enacted many provisions, as is contained in his acts. He wrote for the ecclesiastical estate to various persons: Letters, 1 book. From the report of our brother [unclear]; On Easter, to Hilary, 1 book; On the priesthood, to Esychius, 1 book: “Your affection demands before...” He died under the emperors Honorius and Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 419, in the second indiction, on the seventh day before the Kalends of January.

Boniface, the first pope of that name, succeeding blessed Zosimus, presided over the Church for three years and four months. He was a man of great learning and quite fit for the governance of souls, who enacted many provisions for ecclesiastical utility, which are found scattered in the canons of the holy fathers. He wrote, for the edification of the faithful, as they say, some little works; of these I have found only: Decretal letters, 1 book: “To the Roman Church, which...” He died under the emperors Honorius and Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 422, in the fifth indiction, on the eighth day before the Kalends of November.

Proba, a most elegant woman, wife of Adelphius, Roman proconsul, a woman most learned in secular literature and not ignorant of the divine scriptures, burning with marvelous zeal, surpassed her sex by her learning. Perfectly instructed in Greek and Latin letters, and excelling both in meter and prose, since she held Virgil word for word in her mind, she conceived the idea of describing the New and Old Testament from his verses and of showing, by his own poems, that he had thought in this way. And so, courageously undertaking the work laid up in her mind, carefully going through all the books of Virgil, taking now this verse, now that one, sometimes half a verse, and sometimes smaller particles of verses, with marvelous industry, preserving everywhere the measure of the feet, she described the catholic volumes in the poet’s verses. This work, composed in almost seven hundred verses, she entitled with a Greek word, A Virgilian cento, 1 book: “Long since to have profaned...” If she wrote anything further, I do not know.

Nevertheless this work is counted among the apocrypha, since, although a devout woman undertook a pious study, Virgil nevertheless never intended that his little verses be referred to the honor of Christ or to our faith. For the interpretation of this matter is not proper but fictive, assumed by Proba. She flourished, however, as some think, under Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 430.

Eudoxia, wife of Theodosius the Younger, a woman most devout in the Christian religion and most learned both in the divine scriptures and in secular letters, returning from Jerusalem, brought with her the relics of the most holy protomartyr Stephen and placed them honorably in the basilica of the blessed martyr Lawrence. Since she was very learned and excellent in prose and verse, she is said, in imitation of Proba, wife of Adelphius, to have bent Homer’s poems back toward the Christian faith, likewise placing before the little work she published the following title: Homeric centos, 1 book. She also wrote certain other works. Since Saint Jerome, in a certain letter, declares that he had read Homeric centos and Virgilian centos, they must necessarily have been composed before his death. She flourished with her husband Theodosius, who took up the empire in the year of the Lord 423.

Primasius, an African bishop, as some will have it once a disciple of blessed Augustine, a man indeed learned in the holy scriptures, gloriously imbued with the disciplines of secular letters, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, is said to have composed many little works, which among the ancients were held at a great price. Of these I have found only: Against heresies, to Bishop Fortunatus, 1 book. [unclear] In

74 On Ecclesiastical Writers

On the Apocalypse of John, to Castorius, five books. But the book Apocalyptica which he composed has not yet come to my knowledge.

He flourished under the emperor Theodosius II, in the year of the Lord 440.

Vtilius, bishop of a certain city in Africa, though I have not been able to discover the name of the city, was certainly a man very learned in the sacred Scriptures and, in my judgment, sufficiently instructed in secular disciplines, profound in understanding, sweet and adorned in speech. He is said to have written many little works, but I have seen one notable work, which he wrote to the above-mentioned bishop Primasius, entitled:

On the Parts of the Divine Law, one book. “To the holy and most blessed bishop ...”

Of the rest I have seen none.

He flourished at the same time as Primasius, in the year of the Lord 440.

Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, a man most learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, a distinguished theologian and computist: in the times of Leo Augustus, the successors of the heretic Dioscorus, after a sedition had been raised by Timothy, cruelly slew him on his journey, and set up that same Timothy in his place as an idol for the Alexandrian bishopric. He wrote, among other things, to Saint Leo the pope:

On the Celebration of Easter, three letters.

To Hilary, on the same matter, four letters. “Since your holiness ...”

Several letters to various persons. And certain other things.

He flourished under the emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 460.

Paschasinus, Sicilian bishop, learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular letters, reverend no less for his way of life than for his knowledge, is said to have presided in place of blessed Pope Leo the Great at the Council of Chalcedon, in which, together with the holy fathers to the number of two hundred, he condemned the heretics Eutyches and Dioscorus. Eutyches was a priest and abbot of a very celebrated monastery of Constantinople; he asserted that Christ the Lord was only God and not man, and wrote various things in support of his error, all of which were condemned together with their author. Paschasinus, however, wrote to Pope Leo:

On the Question of Easter, two letters. “The writings of your apostolate ...”

To the same, On the Miracle of the Font, one letter. “Not one day alone ...”

The acts of the Council of Chalcedon, [unclear] book[s]. “The rules of the saints ...”

He flourished under Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 450.

Leo, the first pope of that name, a Tuscan by nation, after Sixtus III sat in the chair of Peter for twenty-one years. He was a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and so celebrated and eloquent in declaiming homilies to the people that he had no superior in the Roman Church, as his most famous sermons will testify. He was the Cicero of ecclesiastical diction, the Homer of sacred theology, the Aristotle of the arguments of faith, the Peter of apostolic authority, the Paul in the Gallican pulpit. His sermons pierce the heart, clothe the soul, and confirm the catholic faith in sweet, brief speech. Nor is it any wonder: bearing the fire of divine love kindled in his breast, what else would he speak but burning words? He wrote many little works; of these I have found only the following, namely:

Against Eutyches the priest, two books.

On the Nicene Creed, one book.

Testimonies to Leo Augustus, one book.

To the questions of Bishop Januarius, one book.

On the Passion of the Lord, twenty-four homilies, one book.

Many homilies to the people, one book.

To Bishop Flavian against Eutyches, one book.

To Leo Augustus against Eutyches, one book.

To Bishop Turibius against the Priscillianists, one book.

To Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, one book.

Many letters to various persons, one book.

Of the rest I have found nothing.

He died at last, after many labors for the benefit of the Church, under Leo Augustus, in the year of the Lord 461, in the fourteenth indiction, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July.

The Abbot of Spanheim

Peter, bishop of Ravenna, a learned and most holy man, shining in life with many miracles, was of excellent talent in declaiming homilies to the people, and by word as well as example converted many to the path of truth. He wrote many things for the edification of the faithful, among which are reported:

Several sermons or homilies, one book.

Two copies of these sermons exist in the library of Eberbach.

To Eutyches the priest, one letter. “Sad, I read your sad letter ...”

He also wrote several other letters.

He flourished under Marcian Augustus, in the year of the Lord 450.

Pope Leo wrote many letters. He was indeed a learned man, an outstanding lover of catholic unity, who deposed and excommunicated Eutyches the priest and archimandrite, who held impious views concerning Christ’s humanity, as in a certain letter to the aforesaid Pa

On Ecclesiastical Writers

...sent to Pope Leo testifies, he accomplished and endured many things for the extirpation of heresies. He wrote in the Greek language certain little works not to be despised; of these there are cited:

Acts with Eutyches the Presbyter, one book. Against the Errors of the Same, one book. To Pope Leo on the Same Matter, one letter. “No diabolical thing...” A Book of Letters to Various Persons, one book. And some other things which we do not know. He flourished under Theodosius the Younger and Marcian, in the year of the Lord 454.

Hilarius the pope, a Sardinian by birth, after Leo the Great sat in the pontificate for six years and as many months. He was a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and distinguished by the adornment of many virtues; constantly intent on alms and holy works, he shone with a great reputation for holiness [unclear]. At Rome, when a synod of fifty bishops had been held, he made a number of decrees for ecclesiastical propriety. He wrote certain necessary little works; of these I have found only:

A Synodal Decree, one book. “Since a religious [unclear]...” To the Bishops of the Province of Tarragona, one letter. “After the letters of your...” To Ascanius, Bishop of Tarragona, one letter. “Of divine grace toward us...” On the Council of Nicaea, one letter. On the Council of Ephesus, one letter. On the Council of Chalcedon, one letter. A Book of Letters to Various Persons, one book. He died under Leo Augustus, in the year of the Lord 468, in the sixth indiction, on the ninth day before the Kalends of March; Simplicius succeeded him.

Eusebius, bishop of Milan, very learned in the holy Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, both familiar and dear to the most blessed pontiff Leo, fighting and writing bravely for the holy Catholic faith against the heretics, is said to have published some little works for the edification of the faithful. Among the things he is said to have written in matters of faith is:

To Saint Leo the Pope, one letter. “Having returned [unclear]...” He flourished under the emperor Marcian, in the year of the Lord 450.

Asclepius the African, bishop of the territory of Vaga, a studious and learned man, an outstanding declaimer of homilies to the people, and a most vigorous assailant of heretics, wrote many volumes for the edification of the people. By their publication he was named glorious in every land, since he showed himself a useful teacher not only in words but also in works. For many most learned men made his age famous. Of his writings there are cited:

Against the Donatists, one book. Against the Arians, one book. Countless Homilies to the People, one book. And many other things unknown to us. He flourished under Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 440.

The Abbot of Spanheim

Prosper, bishop of Reggio after Faventius, an Aquitanian by birth, was a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular letters, excellent in verse and prose, eloquent in speech, profound in sense, subtle in intellect, vigorous in assertion, and most holy in life and conduct. He was once notary of the blessed Pope Leo the Great, and composed many letters in his person. He also wrote from his own vein many splendid little works; of these I have found only the following: from the Sentences of the blessed bishop Augustine, in hexameter and pentameter verses, mixed with prose, a most beautiful work, which he wished to entitle:

Epigrams, one book. “When it pleases to direct the mind to sacred things...” On the Contemplative Life, three books. “The contemplative life in...” On Free Will, one book. “To the lord and most beloved brother Ru...” Responses to the Chapters of the Gauls, one book. “The doctrine which the holy...” To the Objections of the Vincentians, one book. “Certain Christian...” To the Extracts of the Genoese, one book. “In the books of blessed memory...” A Great Sum of 350 Propositions, one book. “True knowledge is that which...” Against Cassian on Free Will, one book. A Chronicle of Histories, one book. A Book of Letters to Various Persons, one book. On Illustrious Men, one book. On the Captivity of Rome, one book. He says that he wrote some other things besides, but they have not come into our hands. He flourished in the times of the great emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 460. His feast is celebrated on the seventh day before the Kalends of July.

Victor, bishop of Cartenna, a city of Mauretania, learned in the holy Scriptures and an outstanding declaimer of sermons, a notable persecutor of heretics, is said to have written many volumes, in which he both instructed the devout people and powerfully crushed those who erred concerning the faith. Of these the following are cited:

Against the Arians, one book. Against the Donatists, one book. Consolatory Address to Basilius, one book. On Penitence Also, one book. Homilies to the People, two books. He published not a few other things as well, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Marcian Augustus, in the year of the Lord 450.

Vi-

On Ecclesiastical Writers

[unclear]

Victorinus, an Aquitanian by nation, a man very devoted to the divine Scriptures and most learned in secular letters, is said to have left certain little works of his own genius, which have not yet at all come to my knowledge. At the command of Pope Hilarius he wrote, for finding the date of Easter, The Great Cycle of 532 years, in four books.

This is called the great cycle of 532 years; when these have run their course, all the computations of the heavenly bodies return to the same point. Dionysius the abbot afterwards corrected it, and down to this our own age it has endured, although in some matters it has failed. This Victorinus also wrote certain letters.

He flourished under the emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 460, and wrote his cycle under Pope Hilarius, in the third year of his pontificate.

[unclear]

Peter, priest of the church of Edessa, learned and practiced in the holy Scriptures, endowed with an outstanding power and talent for declaiming homilies to the people, so that in his own times he had no equal, wrote in the Syriac language many very distinguished volumes, of which only very few have come to my knowledge:

Commentaries on the Psalms, four books.

He also played in meter on the Psalms, five books.

He dictated, and delivered, almost countless homilies to the people, which are found among us rarely. But neither is the number of his treatises certain to us.

He flourished under the emperor Marcian, in the year of the Lord 300.

S[unclear], learned in [unclear] and sufficiently trained in secular letters, subtle and keen in intellect, often fought against the force of heretics, both by writing and by disputing. Hence, at the request of a certain Secunda, a virgin dedicated to Christ, he wrote a distinguished and memorable volume:

Against Marcion and Valentinus, one book.

Against Eunomius and Aetius, six books.

He published some other things as well, but they have not yet come to my knowledge.

He flourished under Theodosius the Younger, around the year of the Lord 440.

V[unclear]rsinus, a monk, learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of humane letters, subtle in intellect and cautious in speech, is said to have composed many treatises for the benefit of the faithful, but I do not remember that any of them has ever come into our hands. There is, however, circulated a distinguished work of his against those who rebaptize persons once duly baptized, whose title is:

The Abbot of Spanheim.

On not rebaptizing heretics, one book. He flourished, as I have found, under Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 490.

Julianus, bishop of the church of Toledo in Spain, a Moor by nation, to whom Saint Prosper is said to have written three books On Contemplation, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in secular studies, scholastic in speech, clear in understanding, wrote many notable volumes, of which the following are reported:

On holy virginity, one book. On the nature of the soul, [8] books. On the resolution of questions, one book. On contempt of the world, one book. Prognosticon of the future age, three books. The faith of the nascent Church [unclear]. Letters to various persons, one book. On vices and virtues, two books. Letters to various women, one book.

He is said to have composed some other works as well, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperor Marcian, in the year of the Lord 450.

Victorianus Buconius, bishop of the city of Castelliana in Mauretania, a man trained by constant study in the divine writings and by no means moderately learned in the disciplines of secular letters, a most powerful hammer of heretics and an outstanding teacher of the faithful peoples, is said to have written many little works in defense of the Catholic faith, of which the principal ones are reported as follows:

Against the Jews, one book. Against the Arians, one book. Against all heretics, two books. On the sacraments also, one book.

He flourished under the emperor Marcian, in the year of the Lord 460.

Museus, priest of the church of Marseille, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and polished by very subtle exercise in their meanings, scholastic and elegant in language, at the urging of Saint Venerius the bishop excerpted from the holy Scriptures lessons and responsories suited to the several festive days of the whole year, and arranged psalms suitable for singing in the church at the several times. He also wrote to Bishop Eustasius an excellent work:

On the sacraments, seven books. Several homilies to the people. And certain other things.

He flourished under the rulers Marcian and Leo, in the year of the Lord 440.

Vincentius, a priest, a Gaul by nation, much practiced in the divine writings, having a tongue polished by practice in speaking and by greater reading, and not ignorant of secular letters either, wrote, as our Gennadius reports, an excellent work, to be very greatly embraced by devout men:

Commentaries on the Psalms, one book. And certain other things. He flourished under the emperor Marcian, in the year of the Lord 450.

80 On Ecclesiastical Writers.

Cyrus, Alexandrian by birth, a physician by art, having from a philosopher become a monk for the love of Christ, a man very learned in secular letters, remarkable in skill of speaking, in his writings using syllogisms more than the authorities of the divine readings: while he inveighs too much against Nestorius, he is alleged to support the Timothean doctrine, and being uncertain of himself, he suspends his mind from agreement with the Council of Chalcedon, nor does he think one should assent that the Son of God after the incarnation is confessed in two natures. Of his writings, however, the following is reported:

Against [unclear], one book. Against heretics, one book.

He flourished under Leo Augustus, in the year of the Lord 460.

Salvianus, priest of the church of Marseille, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in secular letters, teacher of the bishops of his time, wrote in scholastic and clear speech many varied little works, of which the following are reported. To Claudius, bishop of Vienne, he wrote several letters, seasoned with the salt of wisdom. To Marcellus the priest:

On the good of virginity, three books. Against avarice, four books. To Claudius, bishop of Vienne, one book. On the beginning of Genesis, the Hexameron, one book. On the final part of Ecclesiastes, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. Homilies made to bishops, one book. On the sacraments also, one book.

He also published many other works, which have by no means come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperor Zeno, in the year of the Lord 480.

Samuel, priest of the church of Edessa, learned in the divine Scriptures by constant exercise, an outstanding declaimer of homilies to the people, skilled in the Greek and Syriac language, first flourished at Edessa; later, coming to Constantinople, and there held in high esteem, he closed his final day. He wrote, both in Greek and in Syriac, almost countless little works, of which very few have come to my knowledge. For I found only:

Against the Nestorians, one book. Against the Eutychians, one book.

He flourished under Zeno Augustus, in the year of the Lord 480.

Gennadius, bishop of the city of Constantinople, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote in the Greek language

The Abbot of Spanheim.

some little works on the sacred volumes, but they have by no means come into our hands. For he was an outstanding preacher of homilies, and no less distinguished in life than in knowledge of the Scriptures. Among other things, a work of his commentaries is said to have been prepared: On Daniel the Prophet, one book; many homilies to the people, one book. He died under Emperor Leo I, who ruled in the year of the Lord 460.

Claudius (others call him Claudianus), bishop of Vienne, to whom Salvianus the presbyter composed one book, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and most highly trained in secular letters, famous no less for holiness than for learning, shone in his times. Because of frequent earthquakes he was the first to institute litanies, which the Roman Church thereafter undertook to continue. He wrote On the State of the Soul, three books; also letters, and certain other things. He flourished under Emperor Zeno, in the year of the Lord 480. And lest the name Claudius trouble anyone, [unclear], let him know that the same man is called Mamertus.

Sidonius, bishop of the Arverni, learned in the divine Scriptures and, in the disciplines of secular letters, in the opinion of all men of his time most erudite, excellent in verse and prose, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote many distinguished little works both in meter and in prose. Of these I have been able to find only those which I set down below, namely: Panegyric to Anthemius Augustus, one book: ‘With auspice and number’; Panegyric to Julius Valerius, one book: ‘Conceive the former things, Phoebus, having traversed [unclear]’; Panegyric to his father-in-law, one book: ‘Speak, speak what I ask, [unclear]’; To Felix, one book: ‘Among the dark-blue [unclear]’; Epithalamium for Ruricius and Hiberia, one book: ‘By chance, stormy [unclear]’; Epithalamium for Polemius, one book: ‘Phoebus and the thrice three’; Eucharisticon to Faustus, one book: ‘Four days before’; also Epigrams, one book: ‘The stable of the Bistonian king’; To Pontius Leontius Burg[unclear], one book: ‘Hail, mighty Narbo’; Praise of the city of Narbonne, one book: ‘Long do you command, lord [unclear]’; Letters to various persons, nine books.

He also wrote many other works, short indeed, but sufficiently learned, whose titles I have passed over for love of brevity. He flourished in the times of Zeno Augustus, in the year of the Lord 480.

Pope Simplicius, a Tiburtine by nation, after St. Hilarius presided over the Roman and universal Church for fifteen years. He was a learned and holy man, who appeared not only simple according to his name, but also upright, departing from evil and fearing God; many churches

82 On Ecclesiastical Writers

he restored what had collapsed from excessive age, issued statutes necessary for the Christian commonwealth, and wrote some works for the edification of the faithful, of which I have read only:

To John, bishop of Ravenna, one letter. “If anyone, being intent upon the church…” To Florentius and Egistius, bishops, one letter. “Your report [unclear]…” To Severus, bishop, one letter.

But he also wrote many other very useful letters, which I have not yet seen. He died under the emperor Zeno, in the year of the Lord 485, in the sixth indiction, on 6 Nones of March, and was enrolled among the saints.

Servus Dei, bishop of a certain church, whose city’s name I have not been able to find, a man learned through continual exercise in the divine Scriptures and rich in reading the ancients, subtle in intellect and clear in speech, is said to have fashioned some little works. Of these there survives a volume furnished with sacred Scriptures, against those who say that Christ, while living in this life, did not see the Father with his bodily eyes. The title of this work is:

That the Son Saw the Father, one book.

In this work he shows that the Son of God, even from the hour of his conception in the womb of the Virgin Mary by the Holy Spirit, always saw God the Father with his bodily eyes, and thereafter, and now, clothed in human flesh.

He also wrote certain other things.

He is said to have flourished under the emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 480.

Victor, bishop of Capua, learned in the holy Scriptures and sufficiently trained in secular letters, an excellent theologian and computist, sharp in intellect and renowned for eloquence; but very few of his works have come to my knowledge. He refuted the error of Victor of Aquitaine, who, at the order of Pope Hilary, while writing paschal cycles, taught that Easter was to be celebrated on 15 Kalends of May in the year of the Lord 455, although it should more correctly have been celebrated in that year on 7 Kalends of May. Therefore, when this occasion arose, he wrote:

On Easter, one book. One Gospel from the Four, one book.

He flourished under the emperor Zeno, in the year of the Lord 480.

Cerealis, an African bishop, a man very skilled in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular disciplines, was asked by Maximinus, bishop of the Arians, whether he could establish, with a few testimonies of divine Scripture and without, at least, the assertion of disputation, the consubstantiality of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. He replied not with a few, as the other had mockingly asked, but with many testimonies of both Testaments, composing a distinguished work:

Against the Arians, four books.

He also wrote other things.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 460.

The Abbot of Spanheim

John, priest of the church of Antioch, rich in reading the ancients in the holy Scriptures, after he had taught grammar at Antioch for some years, began to wish to profess himself a cleric. Made a priest by legitimate succession, he devoted himself to the divine readings; made more learned by these, he became so powerful in delivering homilies that he had no equal in his time. He wrote a sufficiently well-instructed volume:

Against the Timotheans, one book. Several Homilies to the People, one book.

And many other things.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Zeno, in the year of the Lord 480.

Theodolus, priest, Italian by birth, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular letters, coming from Italy into Coele-Syria, is recorded as having been ordained there as priest and finally as bishop; and by writing and composing many things he transmitted his name to posterity. Of his little works I have found only a metrical work on the miracles of the Old Testament and the fables of the poets, to which he gave the title:

Eclogues, one book. “The lands of the Ethiopians…” On the Harmony of the Scriptures, one book.

Concerning the rest I have found nothing.

He flourished in the year of the Lord 480, under the emperor Zeno, under whom he also died.

Eugenius, bishop of Carthage in Africa, a learned and holy man, a public confessor of the undivided Trinity, suffered many injuries at the hands of the Arians while they were persecuting the Christians in Africa. For with many other bishops, their tongues cut out, he was sent into exile. He wrote some little works full of faith and learning, of which the following are reported:

Exposition of the Catholic Faith, one book. Apology for the Faith, one book. Disputation Held with the Arians, one book. To His Church, when he was going into exile, one letter.

He is nevertheless said to have written other things, but they have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of the emperor Zeno, in the year of the Lord 480.

Felix, the third pope, Roman by birth, after the holy pontiff Simplicius sat in the chair of Peter for eight years, a good, learned, and holy man, who, inflamed with zeal for the faith, Peter and Acacius

84 On Ecclesiastical Writers

He condemned the Eutychian bishops, banishing them into exile. For this reason, holding a synod at Rome, he established many things for the benefit of the Church, and wrote:

A synodal decree, one book. To Flavius Boethius [unclear]. Several decretal letters, one book.

He died under the emperor Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 495, indiction 1.

Gennadius, priest of the church of Marseille, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, fully trained in both Greek and Latin eloquence, wrote many little works, and translated not a few volumes of the ancient fathers from Greek into Latin speech. Of his own writings he himself, at the end of Illustrious Men, listed the following:

On his faith, to Pope Gelasius, one book. Against Nestorius, six books. Against Eutyches, nine books. Against Pelagius, three books. Against all heresies, eight books. On illustrious men, one book. James, surnamed [unclear]. On the heresy of the thousand years, one book.

He wrote these and certain other works which have not yet come to me. He flourished under the emperor Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 490.

Gelasius, the first pope of that name, an African by birth, sat after Felix in the pontificate for four [unclear], a holy man and most learned in the divine Scriptures. As soon as he entered upon the pontifical office, he sent into exile the Manichaeans whom he found in the city, and publicly burned their books at the basilica of Saint Mary Major. He established many things for the benefit of the Church, and wrote very many works against heretics. Of his little works the following are reported:

A synodal decree, one book. The necessity of things [unclear]. Against the Arians, two books. Hymns in the manner of Ambrose, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. Several weighty prayers.

And certain other things. He arranged Graduals, Alleluias, and Tracts, with prefaces appropriate for the Mass, and separated the authentic books of the holy fathers from the apocryphal, as is found in distinction 15, Sancta Romana.

He died while Anastasius Augustus was emperor, in the year of the Lord 426.

Faustus, formerly abbot of the monastery of Lerins, bishop of Riez in Gaul, was indeed a learned and eloquent man, but stained by the Pelagian error; hence also his little works are counted among the apocrypha, just as

The Abbot of Spanheim.

as is clear in distinction 15, Sancta Romana. At length, corrected and amended by blessed Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, he abandoned his error and returned to the truth of the catholic faith. As proof of this, he published an excellent volume against his former errors, which he entitled On the Grace of God. Of his little works there are reported:

The same volume, On the Grace of God, 1 book. Against the Arians, 1 book. Against the Anthropomorphites, 1 book. On the Holy Spirit, 1 book. “The catholic faith in one...” To Gratus the Deacon, Against Nesto[rius], 1 book. To Felix the Prefect, 1 book. Several homilies to the people.

He flourished under the emperor Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 490.

Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe in Africa, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular letters, subtle in intellect, deep in understanding, sweet, eloquent, and polished in speech, ready in teaching, sharp in argument, fit and very gentle in persuasion, shone out most brightly no less for the holiness of his life than for his knowledge of the Scriptures. He wrote many distinguished volumes, of which the following are reported:

On the Grace of God and Free Will, 7 books. On the Holy Trinity, 1 book. On the Truth of Predestination, 2 books. On the Remission of Sins, 2 books. Disputation with King Thrasamund, 1 book. Rule of the True Life, 1 book. On Predestination, to Monimus, 3 books. “Your letters, dearest son...” To Ferrandus the Deacon, 1 book. “Your letter, holy brother and [unclear]...” On Conjugal Continence, 1 book. “Your letter, holy [unclear]...” On Virginity, to Proba, 1 book. “With spiritual desire and...” On Prayer, to the Same, 1 book. “The Lord in Christ [unclear]...” On Charity, to Eugippius the Abbot, 1 book. “Would that, holy brother, such...” On the Sacrament of the Incarnation, 1 book. “As the true light in no way...” Of many sermons, 1 book. “Adam without a, Abel without b,” etc., 1 book. Of various questions, 1 book. “Although an ineffectual [unclear]...” Mythologies, to Catus the Presbyter, 3 books. “Lest concerning your commands...” On Obscure Discourses, 1 book. “Vir-” [unclear] ii I [unclear] N [unclear] [unclear] S [unclear] [unclear] R [unclear] [unclear] T [unclear] [unclear] V [unclear] [unclear] X [unclear] [unclear] Y [unclear] [unclear] Z

86 On Ecclesiastical Writers.

On the Moralized Meaning of Virgil, one book. Incipit: “Indeed he was seeking [unclear].” On the Immensity of the Son of God, one book. On the Passion of the Lord, one book.

He is said also to have written many other things, which have not come to my knowledge. For he was trained in both Greek and Latin speech. It should be noted that the title of the book On Adam without a is The Book without Letters, namely On Adam without a, On Abel without b, On Cain without c, and so with the rest according to the sequence of the letters. But in the book whose title is Exposition of the Virgilian Content, according to the Moral Philosophers, with marvelous industry he sought, and found, gold in the mud, so to speak, while he inclined the work of the poet toward physical reasoning. He wrote this work to a certain deacon. Another work, the Mythologies, he wrote to Catus, a priest of Carthage, and On the Obscure Expressions of the Ancients to Chalcidius the grammarian, already an old man, when he himself was still young and a teacher and rector in the school of humane letters. He flourished in the times of Thrasamund, king of the Vandals, persecutor of the Catholic churches, under Emperor Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 500.

Ferrandus, deacon of the church of Carthage, to whom some little works of the above-mentioned Saint Fulgentius are extant, a man both devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and no less venerable for holiness of conduct than for doctrine, is said to have composed certain volumes of lively talent. Of these, only the following have come to my knowledge:

To Count Reginus:

On the Seven Rules of Innocence, one book. Incipit: “For the labor of social life.” This book is extant among the [Ebirbacenses?].

To Saint Fulgentius, one letter. Letters to Various Persons, one book.

He flourished with Fulgentius under Emperor Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 500.

Anastasius II, pope, a Roman by birth, sat after the pontiff Saint Gelasius for one year and ten months. He was indeed an erudite man, but, seduced by Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, not long afterward paid the due penalties for his error. For when he wished to obey the necessity of nature, struck by God, the wretched man poured out his intestines with his feces, as is clear in Distinction 19, Anastasius. And this was the second infamous pope. He wrote to Emperor Anastasius:

On the Peace of the Church, one letter. Incipit: “The beginning of the pontificate.”

He is said to have written other letters too, but they have not come into our hands. He died, struck by divine judgment, when he had secretly wished to recall from exile Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, condemned and cast out by the Church, under Anastasius Augustus, in the year of the Lord 498.

Ana-

The Abbot of Sponheim.

The decretals of Pope [Anastasius?], and one letter, which is found in the second volume of the works of Saint Jerome.

Paschasius, deacon of the Roman church, a learned and holy man, father of the poor, wholly intent on the distribution of alms, was of such virtue and holiness that Pope Gregory writes, in the fourth book of the Dialogues, that after his death a demoniac was cured by the touch of his dalmatic. Saint Germanus, bishop of Capua, saw his soul in the pains of purgatory, tormented for no other reason than that, in the election of Pope Symmachus, he had preferred Laurentius, and had persisted in this opinion, though peacefully, until death. He wrote, as Gregory attests, a notable volume against the errors of the Greeks:

On the Holy Spirit, 3 books. And certain other things.

He flourished under the emperor Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 500.

Symmachus, pope, a Sardinian by birth, a learned and holy man, obtained the pontificate after Anastasius, not without discord among the factions of Laurentius, and held it for fifteen years and six months. A man merciful and generous toward the poor, he loved the clergy, enriched the churches, and drove heretics out of the city. After holding a synod at Rome of one hundred and twenty bishops, he canonically cleared himself of the charges brought against him, and drove Peter, bishop of Ravenna, with his accomplices into exile. He wrote certain letters, works not to be despised, of which I have found:

Decree of the first synod, 1 book. It begins: “Because frequent...”

Decree of the Roman synod, 1 book. It begins: “When in one place at blessed...”

Acts of another Roman synod, 1 book. It begins: “The fourth synod held...”

On the transgressions of clerics, 1 book. It begins: “Indeed well, brotherly...”

Letters to various persons, 1 book.

He died under the emperor Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 515, in the eighth indiction, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August; Pope Hormisdas succeeded him.

Symmachus the patrician, senator and Roman consul, father-in-law of Boethius, a distinguished philosopher and rhetorician, and a magnificent worshipper of the Christian faith, was banished into exile at Pavia together with Boethius by Theoderic, king of Italy, on suspicion of having aimed at liberty; and not long afterward he had him cruelly slain. Since he was a learned and most eloquent man, he composed several works, of which I have been able to find only a certain short but elegant volume:

Letters to various persons, 1 book. It begins: “Surely you laugh because...”

Of the rest I have seen nothing. He died in the reign of Anastasius, killed by Theoderic, king of Italy, at Ravenna, in the year of the Lord 524, in the eleventh indiction.

Aui-

[page] 83. ON ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS.

Avitus, bishop of Vienne, a man erudite in the divine Scriptures and most learned in secular letters, a theologian, rhetorician, and most renowned poet, who in his time was held in esteem no less for the sanctity of [his] life than for the erudition of the Scriptures, wrote, both in verse and in loose prose, not a few little works; but very few have come to my knowledge. Of these, the following, composed in heroic and elegant meter, are reported: On the origin of the world: 1 book. On original sin: 1 book. On the sentence of God: 1 book. On the flood of the world: 1 book. On the passage of the Red Sea: 1 book. On virginity, to his sister Fuscina: 1 book. Of letters to various [persons]: 9 books. Of many homilies: 1 book. And many others. He flourished under the princes Zeno and Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 500.

Godelbert, presbyter, learned by continual exercise in the divine Scriptures and rich in old reading, and moreover most erudite in secular letters, a profound theologian, renowned orator, and distinguished poet, subtle in talent and adorned in eloquence, wrote in heroic meter a most renowned work, running most elegantly through histories and allegories from the beginning of the world up to the childbirth of the Virgin; the title of which work is: Allegories of the Scriptures: 1 book. But he wrote also several others. He flourished, as they report, in the times of Anastasius Augustus, in the year of the Lord 500.

Eugypius, presbyter and abbot, erudite in the holy Scriptures, and singularly devoted to the reading of the books of Saint Augustine, and sufficiently instructed in the letters of the secular arts, illustrious also in life and in the conversation of monastic institution—to whom several letters of Saint Fulgentius of Ruspe are reported [addressed]—wrote certain necessary little works, of which I have found only the following. He culled a great volume, having three hundred chapters, from the books of blessed Augustine the bishop, [dedicated] to Proba; which begins thus: The Prologue (letter 1): "To the lady deservedly venerable…" But the book thus (book 1): "What I wrote to you…" The Life of Saint Severinus the monk: 1 book. He flourished under the emperor Anastasius, according to Honorius the presbyter; but according to Sigebert, he flourished then under Tiberius Constantine, in the times of Pope Pelagius II, in the year of the Lord 580.

The Abbot of Sponheim.

Benedict, the first abbot and founder of Monte Cassino, by country a man of Nursia, the foremost founder of the monks of the West, a man of most holy conduct, illuminated with a prophetic spirit, from whose order many very learned and most holy men thereafter shone forth, converted countless peoples from iniquity to Christ by word and example. From his order the Roman see has had eighteen pontiffs, more than two hundred cardinals, sixteen hundred archbishops in various churches, and almost four thousand bishops. Distinguished abbots who were famous for learning, writings, or life: fifteen thousand seven hundred. Those canonized or entered in the catalogue of saints, as we learn from ancient records: fifteen thousand six hundred, apart from those whose names in all these categories have not come down to us. And concerning these illustrious men of our order we have already written four special books, in which we have recorded the names of some, if not of all.

Saint Benedict wrote, in a clear style and with excellent discretion:

The Rule of Monks, 1 book.

It has seventy-three chapters.

Under this rule twenty orders serve, which we have set out one by one in the first book On the Illustrious Men of Our Order, of which some are rare among us. He flourished under Justin the Elder, in the year of the Lord 530. And he died, as some hold, in the year of the Lord 542, in the fifth indiction, on the twenty-first day of the month of March, when he was sixty-two years old, on the Saturday of Holy Easter. But Marianus Scotus, an excellent computist, writes otherwise, speaking thus: If the holy father Benedict the abbot, as some write, died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, on the Saturday of Holy Easter, he is seen to have died in the year of the Lord 601. For unless [unclear] in the ninety-sixth year before that year, his death has no [unclear]; for if he was born then, he was very small. Therefore Saint Father Benedict died, according to this reckoning of Marianus, in the last year of the emperor Maurice, namely in the year of the Lord 601, at about the ninetieth year of his age, in the fourth indiction, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April.

Boethius, an orator and distinguished poet, learned in the divine Scriptures, in secular letters the most learned of all in his time, was the son-in-law of the patrician Symmachus; a man most abundantly imbued with Greek and Latin eloquence, since he translated many volumes, both of Aristotle and of other philosophers, from the Attic tongue into Latin; subtle in talent, ready in understanding, and Catholic, in speech not inferior even to Tully. It is certain that he had the friendship of Saint Benedict, and that on Monte Cassino he ate at his table with Tertullus, the senator father of the monk Placidus. He wrote many excellent volumes, of which I have found the following. To Symmachus, his father-in-law, patrician of the city of Rome:

On the Holy Trinity, 1 book. Long investigated.

1 book. I ask whether the Father, Son.

Indeed anxiously and long.

I have known the Christian faith.

Unity is that by which one.

In the winter season of this year.

This second [unclear].

When these matters have been dispatched, which belong to.

The great things indeed of the book.

Alexander in the commentaries.

How great things for the studious.

Of speaking and disputing.

1 book. Many ancient philosophers.

At your exhortation, father.

Every method of making distinctions.

Many ancient Greeks.

When all the philosophers.

You ask that from the hebdomads.

Among all the authors of antiquity.

Indeed the perception of all.

Songs which certain.

But since, my patrician.

Your [unclear] knows the intention.

On the Predication of Power, 2 books.

Letters to Various Persons, 1 book.

Besides these, the common Latin translation into two books of Aristotle’s Prior Analytics is believed to be by Boethius.

He is also said to have written some other works, but they have not come to my knowledge. He died in the same year as the patrician Symmachus and Pope John, under the emperor Anastasius, by order of King Theoderic at Ravenna, after a long exile, slain in prison, in the year of the Lord 524, in the second indiction. And under the name of Severinus he is said to have been entered in the catalogue of saints. Hor-

The Abbot of Sponheim.

Pope Hormisdas, a Campanian by birth, after Symmachus presided over the Church as pontiff for nine years, a good, learned, and vigorous man. When a synod had been assembled at Rome, he condemned the Eutychian heresy; and the Manichaeans, springing up again, he banished into exile after their books had been burned. Among the other little works of his talent he wrote:

A synodal decree, one book.

To the Emperor Justin, letter 1. Among those things which pertain to unity

To the clerics of Second Syria, letter 2. Having read the letters of your affection

Several letters to various persons, two books.

He died under the elder Emperor Justin, in the year of the Lord 521, in the fourteenth indiction, on the eighth day before the Ides of August; John succeeded him.

And certain other things.

On the Catholic Faith, one book.

Evodius, bishop of Ticinum, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, of singular eloquence both in Greek and in Latin, was sent by Pope Hormisdas to Constantinople in matters of the faith to the heretical emperor Anastasius. After receiving many wrongs, he was driven from the city together with his companions, Anastasius saying: “Why do you deliver mandates to us, when we are under no one’s rule? The Roman pontiff ought to obey us, not also to command.” Evodius wrote to Pope Symmachus.

He flourished under the emperor Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 510.

And certain other things.

Jordanes, from a monk bishop of the Goths, a man zealous in the divine Scriptures and suitably learned in secular letters, gentle in disposition and clear in speech, an investigator of times and an unworthy writer of deeds done, is said to have composed certain distinguished volumes, of which very few have come to my knowledge. For I have found only:

[unclear]

In the first of these he reviewed the deeds of the Romans, but in the second the origin and deeds of the Goths, down to the end of their kingdom.

He flourished under the emperor Justinian, in the year of the Lord 530.

Faustus, a monk and disciple of our most holy father Benedict, an Italian by nationality, a man venerable in [unclear] and morals, when he was seven years old was offered by his parents to the divine father Benedict. By him, at length, after the perfect instruction of the regular profession, he was sent with blessed Maurus into Gaul to build a monastery; there, having lived among many in great holiness, after Saint Maurus had died he returned to Monte Cassino. At the request of the brothers, however, he wrote in a very clear [unclear]

92 On Ecclesiastical Writers

[unclear] in eloquence, to Boniface, the second pontiff of the city of Rome,

The Life of Saint Maurus the Abbot, one book.

He flourished under the emperor Phocas, in the year of the Lord 600.

Justinian the Great, emperor, nephew through his sister of the elder Justin, who reigned afterward for 38 years, a man of great and excellent talent, deservedly gained a place among the ecclesiastical writers. He both published a most distinguished volume against the heretics and, through the hands of John the patrician and the consuls Theophilus and Dorotheus, with marvelous brevity corrected the Roman laws, which lay in more than two thousand books. For, reducing to twelve books all the constitutions of the emperors that were contained in many volumes, he called it the Code. Again, reducing the laws of the individual magistrates and judges, which had extended to nearly two thousand books, as we have said, to the number of fifty books in three volumes:

The Code of the Digests, or Pandects, 50 books.

The Institutes, 4 books. “The imperial majesty...”

Epitome of the Laws, one book. “O...”

On the Incarnation of the Lord, against Eutyches, 3 books.

Against the African Bishops, one book. “These things which necessarily...”

Who would doubt that he also wrote other works, especially many elegant letters, which have not come into our hands? At last, in his old age, having become mad and foolish, he died in the year of the Lord 565, in the thirteenth indiction. Justin the Younger succeeded him.

Dionysius, a Roman abbot, surnamed, as is said, Exiguus, a man certainly great and very renowned in talent and knowledge, learned in the holy Scriptures, and nobly instructed in the discipline of secular letters, distinguished in Greek and Latin eloquence, an outstanding computist and calculator of times, wrote some little works in the Latin tongue. Of these I have found only the following:

The Great Paschal Cycle of 532 Years, one book. “O...”

On the Reckoning of the Paschal Feast, one book. “The reckoning of the Paschal feast...”

I have found nothing about the rest. He translated from Greek into Latin the life of Saint Pachomius the abbot, also the book of Gregory of Emesa on the condition of man, the writings of Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, to Pope Leo, and certain other things. He began his cycle in the year of the Lord 532, which was the last year of the great paschal cycle; once completed, it always returns to the same point.

The Abbot of Sponheim.

He therefore flourished under Justinian the Great, emperor, in the year of the Lord 540.

Facundus, bishop of Hermiane, sufficiently learned in the holy Scriptures, is said to have written some volumes for the edification of readers. Of these there has come down to us only a great and excellent work, composed in an elegant style and furnished with great authorities of the ancients:

In Defense of the Three Chapters, 12 books.

He flourished under the emperor Justinian, in the year of the Lord 540.

Justinian, bishop of Valencia, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of human letters, had from one mother three brothers who were bishops, namely Justus, Nebridius, and Elpidius, learned and erudite men who wrote various little works, which nevertheless have by no means come into our hands. He himself, among other things, composed for a certain man named Rusticus:

On Five Questions, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished in Spain under the emperor Justinian, in the year of the Lord 540.

Justus, bishop of the church of Urgell, brother of the aforesaid bishop Justinian, himself also a man practiced and learned in the holy Scriptures, of excellent talent in expounding the divine and canonical volumes, wrote a sufficiently elegant and commendable volume in a scholastic style:

On the Song of Songs, one book. And many other things.

He flourished with his brother under the emperor Justin, in the year of the Lord 530.

Apringius, bishop of the church of Pax in Spain, learned in the divine Scriptures and most erudite in secular letters, subtle in talent and eloquent in speech, expounded the sacred Scriptures so gloriously and profoundly that, in comparison with him, the ancient writers seemed not to have expounded them. Of his little works there exists a notable volume, with subtle meaning and illustrious style:

On the Apocalypse of John, one book.

On the Song of Songs, one book.

He also published many other works, which have not come into our hands.

He flourished in the times of Theodotus, king of the Goths, under Justinian the Great, emperor, in the year of the Lord 530. Cassio-

94 On Ecclesiastical Writers

[unclear]

Cassiodorus, monk and abbot of a monastery near the city of Ravenna, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and, in secular letters, easily the most erudite of all in his time, shone forth most illustriously no less in holiness than in knowledge. He was first chancellor of Theoderic, king of Italy, and a senator of Ravenna, and later consul of the city of Rome; afterward, despising the vain honors of the world for the love of God, he became a monk. From then on, applying the study of humane letters to the exposition of the holy Scriptures, he composed many very elegant treatises. Of his works the following are reported: In the person both of himself and of King Theoderic, he wrote

Letters to Various Persons, 28 books.

[unclear]

On the Nature of the Soul, 1 book. “When now the undertaking [unclear]” 1 book.

On the Whole Psalter, 1 book. “Blessed is the man,” etc. “Exceedingly”

An Introduction to Divine Readings, 2 books. “When the pursuits of secular studies”

On the Song of Songs, 1 book. “Solomon, inspired”

An Introduction to Secular Letters, 9 books. “Our purpose is”

He compiled the Tripartite History, 12 books. “Very usefully at the beginning”

A Catalogue of the Roman Consuls, 1 book.

On Etymologies, 1 book.

The Priest Previously Noted, 1 book.

On Figures and Tropes, 1 book.

A Memorial of the Scriptures, 1 book.

On Orthography, 1 book.

A Summary on the Apocalypse, 1 book.

On the Canonical Epistles, 7 books.

[unclear]

He also composed many other works which have not come to the knowledge of our reading. He flourished in the times of Justin the Elder down almost to the end of the reign of Justin the Younger, being more than 58 years of age, in the year of the Lord 575.

Arator, subdeacon of the sacrosanct Roman Church, a man practiced in the divine Scriptures and nobly learned in the letters of secular disciplines, powerful in verse and prose, subtle in intellect, clear and polished in speech, wrote a very notable volume, composed in meter, to a certain abbot Florianus:

On the Acts of the Apostles, 1 book. “That Judea of its crime”

To Abbot Florianus, 1 epistle. “They who flourish in merits”

To Pope Vigilius, 1 epistle. “With wave-beaten walls”

And certain other things which I have not seen.

This Arator, a very illustrious poet and notable theologian, offered to Pope Vigilius, before the confession of Saint Peter on the seventh day before the Ides of April, in the presence of many bishops and learned men, the codex on the Acts of the Apostles which he had composed in elegant meter; and, at the pontiff’s command, [unclear] in great part

The Abbot of Sponheim.

He recited it publicly before everyone. As the hour was passing, Pope Vigilius handed the volume to the venerable Surgentius, the primicerius, to be placed in the archive, so that he might read it through at a time of leisure. All the learned men earnestly begged His Holiness to order the book to be read before them in its entirety. When he had ordered this to be done in the church of Saint Peter in Chains, a great crowd of religious men and noble laymen assembled; and, as Arator himself recited in clear words, both books were heard four times, since on one day only half a book was read, because of the continual repetitions which the listeners requested with manifold favor. Where now, in these times, is such zeal for letters? Where is love of saving knowledge? Our religious and nobles, clerics also and pontiffs, heap up not books but revenues; not letters, but avarice do they cultivate. Now Antimachus reads many poems, and, as individuals withdraw, scarcely a single Plato is found and remains. But of these matters we are now speaking out of season. Arator flourished under the emperor Justinian, in the year of the Lord 540.

Victor, bishop of the Cummenian church in Africa, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular letters, was banished into exile in Egypt by the emperor Justinian and Eutychius, bishop of the city of Constantinople, for his defense of the Three Chapters. Summoned back again from there to Constantinople, when he resisted the emperor and the bishop, detractors of the same Chapters, he was sent to be guarded in a monastery of the same city; and, remaining under the same condemnation, as they say, he died. Among the other little works of his talent he wrote, from the beginning of the world down to the first year of Justin the Younger, a very useful history concerning deeds and ecclesiastical wars: History, one book. For the Defense of the Three Chapters, and certain other works. He flourished under the emperor Justinian, in the year of the Lord 540.

Gregory, the first pope from the monks of the order of Saint Benedict, a Roman by nation, sat after Pope Pelagius in the chair of Peter for thirteen years and six months. He was a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and indeed most highly instructed in secular letters, prince of theologians, splendor of philosophers, and light of rhetoricians, whole and most holy in life and conduct. When he was explaining the divine Scriptures, the Holy Spirit several times appeared to him in visible form, and in visible teaching revealed to him the secrets of their mysteries. He, at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, held a synod of twenty-four bishops,

On Ecclesiastical Writers

he established many things for the benefit of the Church, and promulgated the decree concerning the immunity of monasteries. He wrote, moreover, several necessary volumes, of which the following are reported:

To Leander, bishop of Seville:

Moralia on the Book of Job, 35 books. “Among many often...”

On Pastoral Care, 2 books. “Pastoral care me...”

Dialogues on the miracles of the saints, 4 books. “One day, when too much...”

On the Song of Songs, 4 books. “After from paradise...”

On the prophet Ezekiel, 2 books. “Of almighty God...”

Brief homilies on the Gospels, 2 books. “The Lord and our Redeemer...”

A brief explanation of the four Gospels, 4 books. “Matthew, as in order...”

On the seven penitential psalms, 1 book. “If enticed...”

Letters to various persons, 10 books. “Gregory, bishop, servant...” or “Very necessary...”

Rationale of Divine Offices, 1 book.

Preface to the New and Old Testament, 1 book.

On the Sacraments, 1 book.

There is extant among the Eberbach books a brief and learned disputation of Gregory against the Arians, which begins: “For love of the Catholic faith.”

When he was still a levite, in the person of Pope Pelagius he composed a very distinguished letter to Elias, bishop of Aquileia, who refused to accept the Three Chapters of the Council of Chalcedon; this letter is not found among his letters. It is reported also that he composed many other works, namely on the prophets, on the Books of Kings, also on the books of Moses, and on other holy scriptures. After his death, before these had yet been multiplied, his most wicked rivals, envying his glory and sanctity, burned them with fire, as John the Deacon complains in the book of his life. The most blessed Pope Gregory died in the second year of the emperor Phocas, which was the year of the Lord 605, in the eighth indiction, on the fourth day before the Ides of March, shining with many miracles.

Leander, bishop of Seville, formerly a monk, by country from the province of Carthagena in Spain, born of his father Severianus, was a man most devoted to study and nobly learned both in the divine scriptures and in secular letters, pleasing in speech, most excellent in talent, and also holy in life and conduct and beloved of God. By his preaching and industry Hermenegild, son of Leuvigild, the Arian king of the Goths, was brought back to the confession of the orthodox faith and, on the vigil of Easter, was killed by his heretical father and received the crown of martyrdom. His brother [Richardus?], as soon as he received the kingdom after his father’s death, at Leander’s urging and preaching renounced heresy and converted the whole people of the Visigoths subject to him to the Catholic faith. To this Leander blessed Gregory dedicated the volumes of his commentaries on Job. Leander himself wrote several little works, of which the following are reported. When, on account of the Catholic faith, he had been banished into exile by the Arians, he wrote:

Against Heretics, 2 books.

Against the institutions of the Arians, 1 book.

On Virginity, to Florentina, 1 book.

Prayers in a double edition on the Psalms, 1 book.

On Contempt of Death, to his brother, 1 book.

On the praise of sacrifices, 1 book.

Letters to various persons, 1 book.

But he published some other works which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the year of the Lord 590, under the emperor Maurice. He died under [Richardus?], the most devout prince of the Goths, renowned for miracles.

Priscian the grammarian, by country from Caesarea, a man most learned in secular letters, skilled in Greek and Latin eloquence, held in great esteem at the court of Chosroes, king of the Persians, wrote certain distinguished volumes in the grammatical art, which among the ancients were held in great authority. Of these the following are reported. To Julian the patrician:

On the Parts of Speech, 2 books.

On Construction, 1 book.

On Accents, 1 book.

On Cosmography, 1 book.

On Natural Questions, to Chosroes, 1 book.

He is said to have written some other works also, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished, as some hold, in the times of Chosroes, king of the Persians, and of the emperor Heraclius, in the year of the Lord 610.

Marcus, a monk, disciple of the holy father Benedict and very dearly beloved by him, a man learned in the divine scriptures, most pious in secular letters, a distinguished orator and poet, eminent in morals and conduct, wrote after blessed Pope Gregory, adding certain things in a most elegant flowing heroic verse:

The Life of Saint Benedict, 1 book. And certain other things.

He was illustrious down to the reign of the emperor Heraclius Augustus, in the year of the Lord 610.

Fortunatus, bishop of Poitiers, an Italian by nation, a man [unclear], subtle in talent, polished and eloquent in speech, excellent in verse and prose, shone forth among all the teachers of his age no less clearly for the holiness of his conduct than for the knowledge of his learning. He, by the power of Saint Mar-

On Ecclesiastical Writers

...freed by [Martin?] from pain in his eyes, he came to Tours to his tomb to give thanks; and, proceeding to Poitiers, he was ordained there first priest and then bishop, and was distinguished for great learning and religion. He also wrote many useful and devout little works in elegant verse, of which I have seen only the following:

To Saint Radegund, daughter of the last king of the Thuringians, captive of the king of the Franks, later abbess of the monastery of Poitiers, in hexameter verse: The Destruction of the Kingdom of the Thuringians, one book.

To [Iuininius?] on Radegund, one book.

To Justin the Younger, one book.

To Sophia Augusta, one book.

In the Person of Radegund, one book.

In Praise of Bishop Martin, one book.

On Leontius, the Venerable Bishop, one book.

In Praise of the Same, one book.

Hymns, seventy-seven, one book.

On the Miracles of Saint Martin, four books.

The Life of Saint Hilary of Poitiers, [unclear] book.

To Oporicus, on His Life, one book.

The Life of Saint Maurilius, Bishop, one book.

Letters to Various Persons, one book.

Poems to Friends, one book. Incipit: “Rex regionis apex.”

He composed many other works also, but since they are brief, I did not wish to record them under the name of books. For he wrote many epitaphs and short verses, which I have seen. He flourished under Justin the Younger Augustus, in the year of the Lord 570.

Gregory, bishop of Tours, formerly a monk, once a disciple of Saint Avitus, bishop of Clermont, a learned and noble man, also gentle and humble, was of such sanctity and purity that even in life he shone with miracles. Visiting the thresholds of the apostles Peter and Paul, he was received by the blessed Pope Gregory with the greatest reverence and charity, as truly a saint, and was loved by him as a singular and unique friend. He wrote several volumes in a simple and open style, of which there are extant:

On the Praise of the Holy Martyrs, one book. Incipit: “Hieronymus presbyter Statueram illa tantum scrib[ere?]”

On the Miracles of Saint Julian the Martyr, one book. Incipit: “Magnum in nobis quo Omnibus sanctis in Chri[sto?]”

On the Miracles of Saint Martin, one book.

[unclear]

Abbot of Sponheim.
