The responsory “Cornelius centurio,” while the supreme pontiff was celebrating Mass at Rome, he offered with great devotion to St. Peter on the altar at the time of the offertory. The ministers of the altar, hurrying up, thought that the wealthy king had offered gold of great weight; but, finding a little sheet written and noted, they were amazed, praising the prince’s talent and devotion. Hence the Pope decreed, in memory of the most holy king, at the request of the clerics, that this responsory should thereafter be sung in honor of St. Peter.

He flourished under the emperor Otto II, in the year of the Lord 980.

Ammonius, a monk of the monastery of Fleury, of the Order of St. Benedict, a Gaul by birth, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in the disciplines of secular letters, is said to have composed some small works both in meter and in prose, but they have by no means come into our hands. After the monk Adrevaldus he wrote one volume:

On the miracles of St. Benedict, book 1.

On the affairs of the Franks, or on the origin and deeds of the Franks, book 1.

He flourished under the emperor Otto III, in the year of the Lord 990.

Heriger, abbot of the monastery of Lobbes, of the Order of St. Benedict, very learned in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters

132 On Ecclesiastical Writers

[unclear] learned, excellent in verse and in prose; Berno, abbot of Reichenau, mentions him in a certain book addressed to Aribo, archbishop of Mainz. He wrote a notable dialogue under the person of himself and of Adelbold, a clerk and monk then living at Rome, afterwards bishop of Utrecht, about whom we must speak immediately, entitled On the Discordance of the Church, one book; The Life of St. Ursmar, in verse, one book; To Hugo, on Questions, one book; On the Divine Offices, one book; The Deeds of the Bishops of Lobbes, one book; On the Body and Blood of the Lord, one book; and many other works. He flourished under the emperor Otto III, in the year of the Lord 990.

Flavaldus, a monk of Reims, of the Order of St. Benedict, learned in the divine scriptures and exceptionally instructed in secular letters, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote little works not unworthy of reading; by his zeal he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. Among these there is said to be a distinguished work, from the founding of the city of Reims, which they relate was built and so named in memory of their lord by the soldiers of Remus, who had fled after Remus was killed by his brother Romulus, down to his own times; in it, inserting many things about the holy martyrs and other matters and deeds, he wished to give the volume this title: The Deeds of the Bishops of Reims, one book. Also Lives of Many Saints, one book. He is said besides to have written many other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

Albertus, a monk of Lobbes and afterwards abbot of the monastery of Gembloux, teacher of Burchard, bishop of Worms, a man learned in the divine scriptures and very well instructed in secular letters: while he was still a monk, he kept the public school of the monks at Lobbes, in which he instructed Burchard, together with others, in both kinds of literature. Among other works of his talent he wrote Lives of Several Saints, one book; Chants in Honor of the Saints; and certain other things. He flourished in great religious devotion and discipline in the times of the emperor Otto II, in the year of the Lord 980.

Aribo, archbishop of Mainz, [unclear] after St. Boniface the martyr, to whom Berno, abbot of the monastery of Reichenau, wrote a treatise on the coming of the Lord, was a man devoted to and learned in the divine scriptures. Having held a synod at Seligenstadt with Burchard, bishop of Worms, and his other bishops and abbots, in the year 1023, indiction 6, he established many useful things, which are contained in authentic writings. He also wrote On the Fifteen Gradual Psalms, one book; To Abbot Berno, one letter; and

The Abbot of Spanheim.

And certain letters to others. He died under Emperor Conrad the Younger, in the year of the Lord 1031.

Burchardus, formerly a monk of the monastery of Lobbes of the Order of St Benedict, bishop of Worms in Germany, once a hearer and disciple of Albert of Gembloux, abbot at Lobbes, of whom mention is made in the canon, distinction 73, In nomine domini, a man most devoted to divine Scripture and very learned, wrote from the opinions of the holy fathers, of general councils, and of the supreme pontiffs a great and distinguished work after Isidore, namely the Decrees, which he divided into twenty books: 'In the New Testament after'. Letters to various persons, one book.

He flourished under the holy Emperor Henry, in the year of the Lord 1020.

Berno, abbot of the monastery of Reichenau, of the Order of St Benedict, in the diocese of Constance, German by nation, a man learned in divine Scripture and very nobly instructed in secular letters, a musician and poet, second to none in his time, outstanding in life and conduct, wrote certain excellent volumes both in verse and in prose; of these I have found only the following. For Piligrim, otherwise Peregrinus, archbishop of Cologne, he composed an excellent and useful volume: On music or tones, two books: 'Every regular mo[de?]'. On the instruments of music, one book: 'That music is not to be contem[ned?]'. On the coming of the Lord, to Aribo, one book: 'Of highest dignity'. Also on the office of the Mass, one book. On the fast of the Ember Days, one book. On the fast of Saturday, one book. On the measure of the monochord, one book. Letters to various persons, one book.

He also published many other things which have not yet come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of St Henry, the first emperor but the second king, because the first did not receive the crown of the Empire, in the year of the Lord 1026.

Adelboldus, bishop of Utrecht, formerly, as they say, a monk of Lobbes of the Order of St Benedict, under whose persona Abbot Heriger composed the dialogue on the coming of the Lord, a man learned in divine Scripture and nobly instructed in secular letters, held in great esteem at the court of the holy Emperor Henry, overthrew the unbelievers no less by arms than by learning. He wrote: The Life of the holy Emperor Henry, one book. On the praise of the Holy Cross. On the praise of the blessed Mary.

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

But he also published several other works, both in verse and in prose, which have not come to my knowledge. He died under Emperor Conrad the Younger, in the year of the Lord 1027, in the tenth indiction, in the eighteenth year of his episcopate, on the fifth day before the Kalends of December.

Osbertus, monk of Canterbury of the Order of St Benedict, a man learned in divine Scripture and highly skilled in the art of music, subtle in intellect and brilliant in eloquence, published various treatises in both literatures, by which he transmitted the fame of his name to posterity. Among other things he wrote: The Life of St Dunstan, archbishop, one book. Also On music, one book.

He flourished in the times of the holy Emperor Henry, in the year of the Lord 1020.

Odilo, the fourth abbot of Cluny, of the Order of St Benedict, a holy and learned man, presiding over the monastery for fifty-six years, directed the souls of many to Christ by word and example. Peter Damian, bishop and cardinal of Ostia, described his life, full of virtues and miracles, in a lucid discourse. He composed for the edification of his brothers: Elegant sermons, one book.

He died under Emperor Henry II, in the year of the Lord 1048, in the [unclear] indiction, in the eighty-seventh year of his age, on the first day of the month of January.

Fulbertus, bishop of Chartres, most learned in divine Scripture and, in the disciplines of secular letters, the most learned of all the learned men of his time, a famous poet and dialectician, presided for many years over the public school and trained very many most learned hearers. Most holy also in life, he is read to have shone with many miracles. Among other things he is said to have written: Letters to various persons, one book. In praises of St Mary, one book. Various hymns and prayers. And certain other devout works.

He flourished in the times of King Henry I, in the year of the Lord 1010.

Bruno, bishop of Würzburg, cousin of Emperor Conrad II, German by nation, a man devoted to divine Scripture, most holy in life and conduct, who, because of the excellence of his merits, was inscribed in the catalogue of the saints and is held to be the special patron of eastern Francia. From the writings of the ancient fathers, a beautiful exposition: On the whole Psalter, one book: 'Blessed is the man who has not gone' [unclear].

The Abbot of Sponheim.

If he wrote anything else, I do not know. He died under Emperor Henry II, in the year of the Lord 1045, in the thirteenth indiction, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June.

Rupert, abbot of the monastery of Cassino, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and notably learned in secular letters, zealous for regular discipline and a strenuous governor, so that for the sheep entrusted to him, by word and example, [unclear], wrote beautiful and elegant

Sermons, one book.

He published also some other things, which have not yet come to our knowledge.

Guido, monk and abbot of the monastery of the Cross of Saint Leufredus, of the Order of the divine father Benedict, by homeland an Aretine, a man practiced in the divine writings and most learned in secular disciplines, a notable dialectician and musician, to be preferred to others also in this, that through his rule on their hand even boys and girls more easily learn unknown chants by themselves than through the voice of a teacher or by the use of some instrument, wrote, among other little works of his talent, against Berengar, cleric of the church of Tours,

On the Body and Blood of the Lord, two books.

Also On Music, [unclear]. And other things which I have not seen.

He flourished under Emperor Conrad the Younger, in the year of the Lord 1030.

Egelnoth, archbishop of Canterbury, learned and not ignorant of secular letters, most holy in life and conduct, a most merciful advocate of the poor, at whose urging Cnut, king of England, made many alms, especially to the church of Chartres, over which at that time the most learned man Fulbert, bishop, presided, of whom we made mention above, is said to have written, in honor of almighty God, a beautiful work,

In Praise of Saint Mary; Letters to Various Persons, one book.

And certain other things.

Clarmannus, a grammarian, from a cleric of Liege made bishop in the times of Emperor Conrad the Younger, in the year of the Lord 1030.

A Brescian, once a hearer of Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, a philosopher and dialectician famous in his time, excellent in verse and prose, wrote in both styles certain commendable little works, of which few have come to the knowledge of our reading. He wrote to Berengar of Tours, formerly his fellow student under Fulbert, then beginning to err and to dogmatize perversely, correcting him at great length in a friendly way,

On the Body and Blood of the Lord, one book. I call it a collection.

Letters to Various Persons, one book.

Moreover he says that he wrote many other things both in verse and in prose, which I have not seen.

He flourished under King Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1040.

Hermann, who was called Contractus, monk of the monastery of Saint Gall, of the Order of the divine father Benedict, a German by nation, son of the count of Veringen in Swabia, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, most universally learned in secular letters, a philosopher, poet, astronomer, rhetorician, and musician, second to none in his time, most skilled in three languages, Greek, Latin, and Arabic, wrote in verse and prose many distinguished volumes, of which I have found only those set down below, namely:

On Music, one book. In considering the single...

On the Monochord, one book. The first is of this world...

On the Composition of the Astrolabe, three books. Therefore in measuring below...

On the Usefulness of the Astrolabe, one book. Whoever of astronomy...

On Eclipses, one book.

On Computation, one book.

On the Squaring of the Circle, one book.

On the Conflict of Rithmomachy, one book. He who is skilled in arithmetic...

On Physiognomy, one book. Of a clear-sighted prudent man...

Lives of Several Saints, one book.

Various hymns and proses.

He also composed, in sweet regular melody, most beautiful chants and proses, among which is that very sweet one concerning the blessed Virgin Mary, Salve regina, and Alma redemptoris mater, and the others of which there is an abundant number. He also translated into Latin not a few volumes of Greek philosophers and Arab astrologers. In his limbs he was, in accordance with his name, contracted, but he always persevered in thanksgiving; whence through the blessed Virgin, Mother of God, he merited to be inwardly wonderfully consoled and illuminated. He flourished in the times of Emperor Henry II, in the year of the Lord 1050.

Guimund, archbishop of Aversa, formerly a monk of the monastery of the Cross of Saint Leufredus, of the Order of the most holy father Benedict, a man very devoted to and skilled in the divine writings, and not ignorant of secular letters also, wrote to Roger, monk,

The Abbot of Spanheim.

against the errors of Berengar of Tours, On the Body and Blood of the Lord, three books. “To the matter in these times...” And certain other works unseen by us. He flourished under Emperor Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1060.

Alphanus, archbishop of Salerno, formerly a monk of the monastery of Cassino, of the order of Saint Benedict, a man nobly learned in the divine Scriptures and perfectly instructed in secular letters, a philosopher and theologian of very celebrated reputation, wrote certain little works of profound meaning, by which, displaying his talent, he also made his name known to posterity. Of these there survive: On the Union of the Word of God and Man, one book. On the Four Humors of the Body, one book. On the Union of the Soul, one book. He also composed other works in every branch of literature, which have by no means come down to us.

Campanus, a Lombard by nation, a philosopher and astronomer, in the opinion of all the most celebrated man of his time, sharp in intellect, scholastic in speech, not ignorant also of the divine Scriptures, an outstanding calculator and computist, published not a few little works of his talent, the reading of which will not be contemptible to rulers of churches. Of these I have read only the following: a great and distinguished work, On the Ecclesiastical Computus, one book. “One of...” On the Construction of the Quadrant, one book. “You ought to know that the circle...” Also a Calendar, one book. He also composed many other works in astronomy, which have not come into our hands. He says that he flourished under King Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1050.

Helpericus, monk of the monastery of St. Gall, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a German by nation, a man much trained in the divine Scriptures and very learned in secular letters, an outstanding philosopher, poet, and astronomer, subtle in intellect and composed in speech, wrote several little works both in meter and in prose; of these I was able to find only the distinguished work, On the Ecclesiastical Computus, one book. “With our brothers ado...” Also On Music, one book. I have seen nothing of the rest. He flourished under Emperor Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1069.

Berthorius, abbot of the monastery of Cassino, of the order of Saint Benedict, a man devoted to and learned in the holy Scriptures, and nobly instructed in the discipline of secular letters, an outstanding philosopher and physician, is said before his conversion to have written many little works in his own field. But afterward, changing his study and being made a physician of souls, he wrote for the edification of his brothers: Elegant Sermons, one book. He also published various other treatises besides, knowledge of which has not reached me.

Rodericus, a monk of the order of Saint Benedict, to whom Guimundus, bishop of Aversa, while still living in the monastery, is said to have written three books against Berengar, a learned man and trained in both divine and secular letters, described in a very lucid style, for the edification of many, The Life of Bruno, Bishop of Cologne, one book. And certain other works. He flourished under Emperor Henry II, in the year of the Lord 1040.

Agerius, from a scholastic a monk of Corbie in Saxony, a German by nation, of the order of Saint Benedict, a man practiced by constant study in the holy Scriptures, rich in ancient reading, and magnificently learned in secular letters, cautious in intellect and sufficiently eloquent in speech, strong in verse and in prose, wrote in a very urbane style a distinguished volume: On the Sacrament of the Altar, three books. On Grace and Free Will, one book. And certain letters. He says, however, that he wrote several other works also, which have not come into our hands.

Libertus, a monk of Metz, of the order of Saint Benedict, French by nation, a man nourished by constant practice in the holy Scriptures and not ignorant of the arts of humanity, which we call liberal, in order to transmit his name to posterity, wrote certain little works of no contemptible reading. Among them there is said to be a brief but useful work, containing a history of the deeds of his own time, which he dedicated To the Bishop of Metz, one book. He flourished in the times of Emperor Conrad the Younger, in the year of the Lord 1030.

Eckbertus, a cleric of the church of Liège, German by nation, elegantly learned in the divine Scriptures and perfectly instructed in the disciplines of secular literature, wrote several little works both in meter and in prose, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of later men. Of these there survives a volume composed in elegant meter, which he entitled On Rustic Riddles, one book. Another larger book On the Same Matter, one book. And certain other works. Cla

The Abbot of Sponheim.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1060.

Leo, the ninth pope, previously bishop of the city of the Leuci, which is called Toul, under the archbishop of Trier, sat in the chair of Peter after Damasus for seven years. He had earlier been called Bruno, a learned and holy man. He wrote several distinguished short works, in which elegance of speech and sublimity of thought are deservedly commended. Among them are these:

To Emperor Constantine Monomachus, On Extirpating Heresies, one book.

To the Patriarch of Constantinople, one book.

Against the Errors of the Greeks, one book.

To the Bishops of Africa and Egypt, one book.

Letters to Various Persons, one book.

He died under King Henry III, the second emperor, in the year of the Lord 1054, in the seventh indiction, shining with many miracles.

Humbert, a monk of Toul, of the order of Saint Benedict, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular letters, distinguished in intellect and eloquence, was brought with him to Rome by Pope Leo IX because of his knowledge of letters, and was ordained cardinal bishop [unclear]. Afterwards, sent by the same pope to Constantinople to refute the heresies of the Greeks, he so refuted and defeated Nicetas, a [unclear] monk, in the presence of Emperor Constantine and Michael the patriarch, that Nicetas anathematized his own book, which he had written against the church of the Latins, and with his own hand threw it into the fire to be burned. And whatever he there said or did in disputation, he wrote up clearly under the name of the Roman and the Constantinopolitan, in the manner of a dialogue, one book. He also wrote certain other works.

He flourished under Emperor Henry II, in the year of the Lord 1059.

Anselm, a monk of Reims, of the order of Saint Benedict, a Gaul by nation, a man whose mind was practiced in the divine Scriptures, wrote certain short works of his study, which have not yet at all come into our hands. And among other things he gathered into one volume the deeds of Pope Leo IX, done throughout Gaul in councils and assemblies, in order to make known with how great authority, when he had come to Reims, he held a synod of other cities; with how great industry and subtlety he examined ecclesiastical cases; with what severity he corrected sinners; and in what way divine power cooperated with him. This was sufficiently evident in one case of the synod of Reims, where, when the bishop of Freising acted contumaciously against apostolic authority, God taking vengeance,

140 On Ecclesiastical Writers

in the sight of all he suddenly fell silent. He wished to give this work the title The Itinerary of Pope Leo, one book.

He flourished under King Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1050.

Lanfranc, archbishop of the church of Canterbury in England, formerly abbot of the monastery of Caen, of the Order of St Benedict, an Italian by nation, from the city of Pavia, a man most learned in divine Scripture and, in secular letters, especially dialectic, in the opinion of all the most learned man of his time, and no less renowned for holiness than for knowledge, left outstanding monuments of his talent. Of these I have found only the following:

A notable work on all the epistles of Paul the Apostle, one book [unclear].

Commentaries on the Psalter, one book.

Against Berengar, a dialogue, Lanfrancus misericor [unclear].

The Deeds of Count William, one book. I have found nothing about the rest.

He flourished under Emperor Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1060.

Peter Damian, formerly a monk of the holy father Benedict, bishop of [Poliziano?], and cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, a man devoted to and learned in divine Scripture, and not ignorant of secular letters, gentle and acute in intellect, calm and orderly in eloquence, and quite capable in persuasion, shone forth no less renowned and distinguished for holiness than for learning. Following the example of the great bishop Gregory, out of love for solitude and quiet he left his bishopric, after he had governed it for some years [unclear], and returned to his monastery; thereafter he spent his life with his brothers in tranquillity of mind. When, however, he was reproved by the supreme pontiff with a charitable rebuke for having, though a useful and suitable man, dismissed the episcopate out of love for his own private salvation, he published apologies addressed to three Roman pontiffs who succeeded one another, Nicholas II, Alexander II, and Gregory VII; in these, humbly excusing his deed by authority, reason, and example, he placated their minds. Of his little works the following are current:

To Leo the Hermit, whether a solitary person, when praying the canonical hours, ought also to say “The Lord be with you,” when there is no one to answer, an instructive little work, which is entitled The Lord Be with You, one book. De mino Leoni amorem [unclear].

Apologies, one book.

On the incontinence of priests, recently [unclear] with several [unclear], Vos alloquor o lepo [unclear], one book.

The Abbot of Spanheim

Rule of Solitaries, one book.

Exhortation to Monks, one book.

Miracles of His Time, one book.

On the Progress of Monks, one book.

Antilogion against the Jews, one book.

On the Avarice of Prelates, one book.

Life of Abbot Odilo, one book.

On the Terror of Death, one book.

On the Meditation of Death, one book.

Against Simoniacal Bishops, one book.

Against a Certain Bishop, one book.

On the Insolence of Malicious Men, one book.

Most Pleasing or Most Approved, one book.

A Rhetorical Declamation, one book.

On the Natures of Certain Animals, one book.

On Flora and Lucilla, one book.

On Cassian the Martyr, one book.

On Saint Boniface, one book.

On Saint Anastasius, one book.

Sermons and Homiliaries, one book.

He flourished under King Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1050.

Bruno, archbishop of the Ruthenians, formerly a monk of the Order of St Benedict, an Italian by nation, a man learned in divine Scripture and an excellent declaimer of homilies to the people, holy indeed and worthy of God, who, preaching the Catholic faith in Prussia, was lawfully crowned with martyrdom by the enemies of Christ. He wrote some distinguished little works of his talent, of which there survive:

Commentaries on Genesis, two books. And certain other works.

He suffered at the hands of the Prussians under St Henry of Bamberg, who was the second king of this name and the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 1008, in the fifth indiction. After they had afflicted him with many tortures and cut off his feet and hands, finally by beheading him they made him a martyr of Christ.

Erhard, a monk of the Order of St Benedict, a man devoted to divine Scripture and learned through continual exercise, subtle in intellect and ready in speech, was of excellent diligence in declaiming homilies to the people. By expounding the divine Scriptures he made his name known, and by frequent examination of them he became an outstanding teacher. He wrote little works of no contemptible reading; of these the following are reported:

[unclear]

“When fervor [unclear] holy [unclear] with the brothers in Gangensis [unclear] to the most beloved Gerard [unclear].”

“To Blanche, once countess, ‘For indeed it must be considered’ [unclear].”

“Hugh, abbot of Cluny [unclear].”

“Admirable and glorious [unclear].”

“Of blessed Boniface [unclear].”

“Glorious [unclear].”

“To the fair [unclear], brothers [unclear].”

And many other things which I have not seen.

“To Lord H. of Ravenna [unclear].”

142. On Ecclesiastical Writers.

Commentaries on Genesis, one book.

On Leviticus, one book.

On Deuteronomy, one book.

He also published some other works, which have not come to my knowledge.

Bernoldus, priest of the church of Constance in the Swabian nation, a German, a devout man, studious and learned in the holy Scriptures, and sufficiently instructed in the discipline of secular letters, brilliant in talent, polished in speech, left for the studies of his own people some little works, which nevertheless have by no means come to the knowledge of our reading. He is said, for the benefit of the ecclesiastical commonwealth, to have composed a volume which he entitled:

The Roman Order, one book.

He flourished in the times of Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1060.

Marbodus, bishop of Rennes, much devoted to the divine Scriptures, learned from reading the ancients, and nobly educated in the disciplines of secular letters, excellent in verse and prose, wrote in both styles not a few volumes, which can please readers no less than profit them. Among these there stands out an outstanding work which he composed in elegant verse with a threefold sense:

On the Song of Songs, one book.

The Passion of the Theban Martyrs, in verse, one book. And certain other works.

He flourished in the times of Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1050.

Marianus, a monk of Fulda, of the order of St. Benedict, a Scot by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, an outstanding historian and computist, leaving his own country, came into Germany as a pilgrim for the love of Christ. First, having become a monk at St. Martin's in Cologne, he was enclosed out of desire for solitude, and remained there for two years. Afterwards, however, he was transferred to Fulda, and remained enclosed there for [unclear] years, until at last, on account of his learning and holiness, by command of the bishop of Mainz and the abbot of Fulda, he moved to Mainz. There, staying enclosed again for seventeen years at St. Martin's, he was held in great honor by all. He wrote, from the beginning of the world down to his own times:

An outstanding Chronicle, one book. We are informed by the divine [unclear]

On the Harmony of the Evangelists, one book. It was in the days of Herod

Also On Computation, one book.

And certain other works.

Abbot of Sponheim.

He died under Henry IV, in the year 1086, in the ninth indiction, in the fifty-eighth year of his age, and was buried at Mainz, at St. Martin's in the greater church, not without a reputation for sanctity.

Wenericus, bishop of Vercelli, formerly a cleric of the church of Trier, a German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in the discipline of secular letters, made his name known to posterity by writing, although his little works have not come to the knowledge of our reading. In that discord which existed between Hildebrand, Pope Gregory VII, and Henry, the third emperor or fourth king, he wrote, in the person of Theoderic, bishop of Verdun, while he was still a cleric at Trier, to that same Pope Gregory a volume instructed by the divine Scriptures, not rebuking him, but beseeching an elder as a father, and, with the friendly feeling of one grieving, suggesting to him all the things which talkative rumor had spread abroad that he had done or said against the right of laws and the propriety of equity. He entitled it:

On the Discord of the Kingdom and the Priesthood, one book.

He flourished under King Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1080.

Theoderic, a monk of the order of St. Benedict, a German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly taught in secular letters, subtle in talent and distinguished in eloquence, is said to have written certain little works of reading not to be despised, of which few have come to my knowledge. Yet I have read, addressed to Richard, abbot of Fulda:

On the Life of Saint Benedict, one book. When [unclear] the heavenly sacrament

On the Translation of the Body of the Same, [unclear]. Since for a long time the Lombard people [unclear]

Letters to Various Persons, one book.

He also composed many other works, both in verse and in prose, which have not come down to us.

Adam, abbot of Perseigne, of the order of the divine father Benedict, learned in the divine Scriptures by continual exercise, rich in reading of the ancients, and sufficiently educated in the knowledge of secular letters, of very celebrated reputation in delivering homilies, transmitted his name with praise to posterity by composing various treatises. There are extant his devout and useful:

Sermons to the Brothers, one book.

On Saints and Various Subjects, one book.

He is also said to have explained certain treatises of sacred Scripture, in which he showed the abundant vein of his talent; but they have not come to my knowledge.

144 On Ecclesiastical Writers

[unclear]

Anselm, bishop of Lucca, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not at all poorly instructed in secular letters, the tireless co-worker of Pope Gregory VII and an outstanding defender against Guibert, set up under him by Henry, so that he defended all his deeds, sayings, or writings against Emperor Henry by the authority of law and of the Scriptures, left very famous monuments of a great intellect, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there are extant:

On Jeremiah the Prophet, 1 book. Also On the Psalter, 1 book. Against Guibert the Antipope, 1 book. And several letters to various persons, 1 book. He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1080.

[unclear]

Willeram, abbot of Mersburg, of the Order of St. Benedict, German by birth, a man learned in the divine writings and not ignorant of secular letters, practiced in verse and prose: after he had for some time devoted himself to literary study at the University of Paris, he returned to his homeland and was made scholasticus of the church of Bamberg. At length, considering that the glory of the world passes away with time, he despised the world and, for love of Christ, put on the monk in the monastery of Fulda; and afterward, as his merits increased, he was consecrated abbot in the monastery of St. Peter near Mersburg, and by writing made his name known to posterity. Of his little works I have read only a volume composed in meter and verse mixed with prose, with beautiful variety, on the marriage of Christ and the Church.

On the Song of Songs, 1 book. “Since the studies of the elders…” Of the rest I have seen nothing. He flourished under Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1070.

[unclear]

Franco, scholasticus of the church of Liège, German by birth, a man splendidly learned in the divine Scriptures and most learned in the discipline of secular letters, a philosopher, astronomer, and distinguished computist, and venerable no less for religion than for knowledge, is said to have composed some treatises on the deeds of writers, which have not yet come to my knowledge. He wrote to Hermann II, archbishop of Cologne, a subtle and excellent work:

On the Squaring of the Circle, 1 book. On the Ecclesiastical Computus, 1 book. And many other things. He flourished under Emperor Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1060.

[unclear]

Bernard, monk of Cluny, of the Order of St. Benedict, a man exercised by constant meditation in the holy Scriptures, and of secular litera-

The Abbot of Sponheim.

not unacquainted with literature, and also conspicuous for religion and uprightness of morals, at the command of the venerable abbot Hugh, gathered all the customs of the monastery of Cluny into one volume in lucid language, giving the work the title:

The Customs of Cluny, one book.

He wrote other things. He flourished under the emperor Henry III, in the year 1050.

Bernard, monk of Corvey in Saxony, of the order of Saint Benedict, German by nation, a man nobly learned in the divine Scriptures, highly skilled in secular letters, excellent in verse and prose, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote to Hartwin, archbishop of Magdeburg, in language indeed lucid but bitter, a volume:

Against Henry IV, one book.

And other things which I have not seen.

He flourished in the times of the same emperor Henry, in the year of the Lord 1070.

Ivo, bishop of Chartres, formerly provost of Saint-Quentin of Beauvais, of the order of regular canons of the divine father Augustine, a man trained in the divine Scriptures, and a most careful interpreter of the canons of the holy fathers and of general councils, revered no less for sanctity than for learning, magnificently reformed his order, which had long fallen into decay. After Burchard, bishop of Worms, he wrote from the canons of the saints a compendious decree, which jurists used before the times of Gratian, which he entitled:

Panormia, [unclear]

Letters to Various Persons, one book. “Ivo of the church of Chartres” [unclear]

And certain other things.

He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1090.

Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, afterwards archbishop of Tours, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, acute in intellect and very eloquent in speech, once a disciple of Berengar of Tours but a persecutor of his error, who endured many persecutions and tribulations for ecclesiastical liberty, even to imprisonment, wrote in both styles, that is, metrical and prose, certain excellent little works, of which as yet only a few have come to the knowledge of our reading. He wrote in elegant meter a very beautiful and useful exposition:

On the Whole Office of the Mass, one book. “I have proposed to write what...”

On His Exile, one book. “Recently I was wealthy...”

On the Misery of This Life, one book. “We are taken from the midst...”

On the Sacrament of the Altar, one book.

Letters to Various Persons, one book.

Hymns and Prayers in Various Meter, one book.

He comprised the epitaph of Berengar, once his teacher, in fifty-two verses.

He wrote many other things, still unknown to us.

He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1090.

Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury in England, formerly abbot of the monastery of Bec in Normandy, of the order of Saint Benedict, once hearer and disciple of Lanfranc, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, second to none in his time in skill in secular letters, whole and most holy in life and conduct, devout in mind, eloquent in speech, vigorous in action, angelic in countenance, mature in gait, exemplary in progress, continual in the study of the Scriptures, was adorned with every notable virtue. He wrote almost countless little works, of which the following are reported among the number:

Against the Gentiles: Why God Became Man, one book. “Often, earnestly, by many...”

On the Incarnation of the Word against the Jews, one book. “Since in all religious...”

On the Holy Spirit against the Greeks, one book. “Come now, little man...”

On the Fall of the Devil, one book. “If anyone [says] one nature...”

On the Diversity of the Sacraments, one book. “It is denied by the Greeks that...”

On Leavened and Unleavened Bread, one book. “That saying of the Apostle, ‘What do you have...’”

Monologion, one book. “To the lord and friend Walram...”

Proslogion, one book. “Anselm, servant of the church...”

On the Will of God, one book. “Human reason, when concerning...”

On the Holy Trinity, one book. “Since free choice is permitted...”

On the Song of Songs, one book. “Concerning those three questions...”

On Peace and Concord, one book. “Since God is truth...”

On Free Choice, one book. “The will in three ways...”

Dialogue on Truth, one book. “Since, at the command of your son...”

On Similitudes, one book. “Lord my God, give a heart...”

On the Measurement of the Cross, one book. “Christian soul, attend...”

Meditations, one book.

Meditations on the Passion of the Lord, one book.

On the Blessed Life, one book.

Abbot of Sponheim.

On blessed sufficiency, one book. On good occupation, one book. On the praises of Saint Mary, one book. The Spur of Love, one book. For the Foolish Man, one book. Against the Foolish Man, one book. On the misery of man, one book. On Antichrist, one book. Dialogue of a Christian and a Gentile, one book. On the eight beatitudes, one book. On the members attributed to God, one book. On the sacraments and divine offices, two books. Proverbs, that is, On the house of conscience, one book. On the Hexameron, one book. To Archbishop Lanfranc, one book. On the Grammarian, one book. On Saint John the Baptist, one book. On the Assumption of Saint Mary, one homily. To William of Hirsau, one letter. Letters to various persons, one book. On original sin, one book. Also some sermons. But he is said to have written many other works, which have come to my knowledge. One homily is extant, which is found with the homilies collected by Alcuin. Likewise clear expositions on all the epistles of St. Paul, which lay hidden for almost 450 years, now in our age rescued from decay and filth by the industry and labor of D. Renatus Casteneus. A dialogue on the Passion of the Lord. He flourished under Emperor Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1080.

William, abbot of the monastery of Hirsau in the diocese of Speyer, of the order of Saint Benedict, a German by nation, to whom the blessed Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, wrote several letters, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, inferior to no one among the Germans of his time in secular letters, a philosopher, an outstanding astronomer and musician, most holy in life and conduct, who, as one reads, shone with many miracles, reformed regular discipline, long since collapsed, in many monasteries of Germany. Therefore, for the preservation of monastic observance, from the statutes of the ancients, he wrote:

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

Constitutions of Monks, twelve books. On music and tones, thirteen books. On the clock, fourteen books. On the correction of the Psalter, fifteen books. To Saint Anselm of Canterbury, one letter. Letters to various persons, seventeen books. He also published some other works, which through the negligence of the ancients have fallen into oblivion. He died under Emperor Henry III, but under the fourth king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1091, in the fourteenth indiction, on the fourth day before the Nones of July, and was buried in the middle of the church of the apostles, with a great reputation for sanctity.

Gelselbert, provost of the monastery of West in England, of the order of Saint Benedict, hearer and disciple of Anselm of Canterbury, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, quick in intellect and cautious in speech, made his name known to posterity by writing, when he composed certain necessary little works. Among these the following are reported: a disputation against the Jews,

To Blessed Anselm the bishop, eighteen books. On the prophet Isaiah, nineteen books. And certain other works. Certain homilies on the Song of Solomon are also circulated under his name, which you will find among the Eberbach monks. He flourished under Henry IV with Anselm, in the year of the Lord 1080.

Gunther, monk of Ellwangen, of the order of Saint Benedict, skilled in the divine Scriptures through constant practice, and nobly learned in the disciplines of secular letters, a distinguished theologian and poet, subtle in intellect and polished in speech, wrote certain excellent volumes both in verse and in prose, of which few have come to my knowledge. His volume in elegant meter is extant:

On the Passion of Saint Cyriacus, twenty books. And certain letters. He flourished in the times of King Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1100.

Theoderic, abbot of the monastery of Saint Trudo in the diocese of Liege, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a German by nation, a man devoted to and learned in the holy Scriptures, and sufficiently instructed in secular letters, excellent in verse and prose, wrote certain excellent little works in both styles, in which he magnificently exercised his talent. Among these the following are reported, written in elegant meter:

Life of Saint Trudo, thirteen books. Life of Saint Bavo, fourteen books. Life of Saint [Remoldus?], fifteen books. And many other works. Cla

The Abbot of Spanheim.

He flourished in the times of Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1100.

Peter Alphonsus, converted from Judaism to the faith, formerly called Moses, whom King Alphonsus, lifting him from the sacred font, distinguished with his own surname, a man learned in the holy Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, as proof of his sincere faith wrote, under the name of Moses the Jew, which he had been, and of Peter the Christian, which he had begun to be, a distinguished dialogue:

Against the Jews, one book. To the one and eternal First... On Knowledge and Philosophy, one book. And certain other works.

He flourished in the times of Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1100.

Honorius, priest and scholasticus of the church of Autun, a man most devoted to the holy Scriptures and very learned, and also nobly instructed in secular sciences, subtle in intellect and clear in eloquence, wrote many excellent little works. Of these he himself, in the book of illustrious men which he entitled On the Lights of the Church, listed the following: a very necessary work on Christ, on the Church, and on the future life, which he entitled

The Elucidarium, three books. On Free Will, one book. The Seal of Saint Mary, one book. The Mirror of the Church, or of Sermons, one book. A Stumbling-Block concerning Priests, one book. A Summary of Histories, one book. The Jewel of the Soul, on the divine offices, six books. On the Image of the World, two books. On the Song of Songs, one book. On the Lights of the Church, one book. On the Body of the Lord, one book. The Ladder of Heaven, on the degrees of visions, one book. The Key of Physics, on the natures of things, one book. On the whole Psalter, one book. On the Pope and the Emperor, one book. A Dialogue from the little works of Augustine, one book. Refreshment of Tables, on feasts, one book. The Food of Life, on the saints, one book.

In addition he published many other works, whose titles I have not yet been able to find. He flourished under Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1120.

[unclear]

You say that you wonder why... The army in the camps of the Eternal... The world therefore is called... At the beginnings of books... Gelasius of the city of Rome... On the Hexaemeron, one book. On the Soul, one book. On the Gospels, one book of homilies. Letters to various persons, one book.

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

[unclear] Sigebert, monk of Gembloux, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a Gaul by nation, a man from his youth most devoted to the divine Scriptures and very learned, and also, in secular letters, second to none in his time in the territory of Liege, practiced in verse and in prose, wrote many volumes in each style, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. He is reproved, however, in that, adhering to the emperor Henry, persecutor of and rebel against the Roman Church, he wrote letters and little works against Hildebrand, Pope Gregory VII, which did not befit his position. What he wrote, indeed, he plainly declared at the end of his Illustrious Men. When he had been placed in the monastery of Saint Vincent at Metz to instruct boys, he wrote in heroic meter:

The Life of Saint Theoderic, bishop, one book. The Passion of Saint Lucy, in verse, one book. On the Translation of the same, one book. The Life of King Sigebert, one book. The Passion of the Theban Martyrs, one book. The Life of Saint Guibert, one book. The Deeds of the Abbots of Gembloux, one book. The Life of Saint Maclou, one book. The Life of Saint Theobald, one book. Against Pope Gregory, one book. An Apology to the Emperor, one book. Marcellus, [unclear], one book. Against the Letter of Pope Paschal, one book. Also Sermons, one book. On Ecclesiastes, in heroic meter, one book. Letters to various persons, one book.

He also published other works after these, which he did not mark together with the little works written above. He flourished in the times of Emperor Henry III, the fourth king, in the year of the Lord 1110. He brought his Chronicle down to the year 1111.

[unclear] Calixtus, the second pope, a Burgundian by nation, brother of the duke of Burgundy, previously archbishop of Vienne, sat in the pontificate after Gelasius for six years; a man learned in the divine writings and not ignorant of secular letters, an especial lover of Saint James the Apostle, in whose honor he raised the church of Compostela to an archiepiscopate. He wrote in composed speech and with the greatest diligence:

On the Miracles of Saint James, one book. Calixtus, bishop, servant... Letters to various persons, one book. And certain other works.

He flourished under Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1120.

The Abbot of Sponheim.

Stephen, also called Herrand, the fourteenth bishop of the church of Halberstadt, formerly abbot of the monastery of Ilsenburg, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote little works not contemptible to read, but few have come into our hands. He wrote, in the person of Count Louis, a most elegant and useful letter to Waltram, bishop of the church of Nienburg, who was defending Henry, a rebel against the Roman Church:

A Defense of the Pope, one book. “As a good man concerning go[od]...” And several letters to various persons, one book. And certain other things.

He died under Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1107, in the fifteenth indiction, and was honorably buried at Reinsburch.

Bernard, first abbot of Clairvaux, of the Cistercian Order, a Burgundian by nation, a noble and holy man, who shone with many miracles in life and after death, learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in intellect, adorned in speech, since indeed in his writings he neglected nothing that could contribute to the adornment of discourse, published many splendid little works, of which the following are reported:

On Consideration, to Eugenius, five books. “It comes into my mind to dictate some...” His Meditations, one book. “Many people know many things...” On Contempt of the World, to clerics, one book. “To hear, as is believed...” On Grace and Free Will, one book. “You asked me, brother Geoffrey...” To the Knights of the Temple, one book. “Recently while I was speaking...” Mirror of the Religious Life, one book. “To Hugh, knight of Christ...” “If any among you [unclear]...” “If I seem to you rather slow...” “When on a certain day bodies...” “Virtue is acquired in peace...” “To the brothers of Mont-Dieu...” “He exhorts indeed the fearful...” “Conscience in which through...” “All dangerous things...”

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

On the Misery of This Life, one book. “The days of man are as a shadow...” On Temptations and Idleness, one book. “The servant of God freely...” On the Will, one book. “All kinds of vices...” An Apology to the Cluniacs, one book. “Until now, if anything me...” On the Degrees of Charity, one book. “To the illustrious man, lord Au[unclear]...” On the Passion of the Lord, one book. On the Magnificat, one book. On Loving God, one book. On the Psalm “He who dwells,” one book. On the Song of Songs, 86 homilies, one book. On “The angel was sent,” one book. To His Sister on the Manner of Living, one book. The Life of Bishop Malachy, one book. Letters to Various Persons, one book. Several Sermons, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished under Emperor Conrad III, in the year of the Lord 1140.

Anselm, scholasticus of Laon, very studious in the divine Scriptures, skilled through long practice, and nobly learned in the disciplines of secular letters, acute in intellect, scholastic in speech, distinguished no less in life than in knowledge, explained the Scriptures of both Testaments in a new kind of exposition, by an interlinear and marginal gloss from the writings of the Fathers. He also wrote certain other little works which have come to me. There is reported:

Commentaries on the Psalter, one book. And certain letters.

He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1110.

Hugh, priest and monk of Saint Victor at Paris, of the Order of the regular canons of Augustine, abbot, as they report, in the same place, a Saxon by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, inferior to none of the ancients in secular philosophy, who, like a second Augustine, was regarded as a most celebrated doctor in his time, subtle in intellect, adorned in speech, and venerable no less for his manner of life than for his learning, wrote almost infinitely many little works, of which few have so far come into our hands:

The Sum of His Sentences, one book. “A difficult thing indeed...” On the Soul of Christ, one book. On the Sacraments, two books. Didascalicon, six books. “Of all things to be sought, the first...” On

Abbot of Spanheim.

153

On the earnest-money of the soul, one book. “I shall speak [unclear] of the soul …” On the manner of praying, one book. “With what zeal and with what [skill?] …” On the praise of charity, one book. “So many now praise …” On the instruction of novices, one book. “Because, brothers, by the granting of [God?] …” On the Rule of Saint Augustine, one book. “These precepts which …” On the mystical ark of Noah, [unclear] books. “When I was sitting once in …” On Ecclesiastes, sixteen homilies, one book. “Those things concerning the book of Solomon …” On the Song of Songs, one book. “At the beginning of the labor …” On the Lamentations of Jeremiah, one book. “How does she sit, etc., how much …” On the Hierarchies of Saint Dionysius, one book. “The Jews seek signs …” On the praise of the fathers, one book. “Man is a microcosm …” On the Magnificat, one book. “Meditation is frequent …” On “You are all fair,” one book. “There were certain men who …” On the love of the bridegroom and the bride, one book. “You ask concerning the soul …” On the medicine of the soul, one book. “O unclean world, etc. …” On meditation, one book. “There are seven petitions …” On the incarnation of the Word, one book. “Alone, solitude, etc. …” On the wisdom of Christ, one book. “Because it has been said to me …” On the vanity of the world, one book. “The reader [unclear] divine writings …” On the substance of love, one book. “The lion, strongest of beasts …” On the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, one book. “Spiritual [unclear], etc. …” On discipline, one book. “You ask concerning the will …” On the five books of Moses, one book. “You ask concerning power …” On the mysteries of the Church, one book. “A spiritual description …” On spirit and soul, one book. [unclear] “of sentences …” On the Lord’s Prayer, one book. [unclear] On confession, one book. [unclear] On the simple nature of God, one book. “An epitome of philosophy …” On the threefold will in Christ, one book. On certain psalms. On the power and will of God, one book. On marriage and concupiscence. On Sacred Scripture, one book. On the nature of animals. On contemplation, one book. “Spiritual [unclear], etc. …” [unclear]

154 On Ecclesiastical Writers

Letters to various persons, one book. He also composed many sermons, and other diverse and varied treatises. He flourished under Emperor Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1130.

Rupert, abbot of the monastery of Deutz near Cologne Agrippina, of the Order of Saint Benedict, German by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures through the Holy Spirit enlightening him by vision, and not ignorant of secular letters, a monk of Saint Lawrence at Liège, on account of his incredible learning was taken from there by Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, and raised to be abbot of the monastery of Deutz. He composed many distinguished little works. Indeed, from the time when he entered the monastery in his youth, he had exercised himself so much in the Holy Scriptures that, even when sleeping, you would have seen that he could not be free from meditating on them, since his tongue and lips moved as if he were reading. Of his little works I have at present found only the following: To Cuno, abbot of Siegburg, afterward bishop of Regensburg:

On the victory of the Word of God, thirteen books. On Genesis, nine books. On the Song of Songs, seven books. On the book of Saint Job, ten books. On the books of Kings, concerning David, fifteen books. On the Holy Trinity in the Old Testament, forty-two books. On the Apocalypse of John, twelve books. On the divine offices, twelve books. Meditations on the burning of Deutz, five books. On the twelve minor prophets, thirty books. On the Gospel of Matthew, eight books. On the Gospel of John, fourteen books. On the Rule of Saint Benedict, one book. An apology for the same work, one book. Letters to various persons, one book.

Finally, he is said to have written many other things, and to have explained the New and Old Testament, for the greater part, in many books; concerning these we have seen nothing up to the present except the things we have marked.

He flourished with great holiness, shining with learning and miracles, under Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1114. He died under Lothair III.

Rupert, abbot of the monastery of Limburg in the diocese of Speyer, of the Order of Saint Benedict, German by nation, a man splendidly learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, in life and conduct

The Abbot of Spanheim.

[unclear] distinguished, so that he deserved to be visited by frequent divine revelations. For many years he devoted himself to secular philosophy in the school of Paris, and became a renowned philosopher. But, considering the philosophy of the present life to be vain, he abandoned the study of vanity; returning to his homeland, he became a monk in the said monastery and [then?] was made abbot. He wrote, moreover, some little works not unworthy of reading, of which I have found only the following:

On the Song of Songs, 4 books. On Contempt of the World, 2 books. On St. John the Baptist, 1 book. Of His Revelations, 1 book.

He wrote certain sermons on the saints whose bodies or patronage they had in the same monastery of Limburg. He flourished under Emperor Henry V, not without a reputation for sanctity, in the year of the Lord 1124.

Rudolf, abbot of Saint-Trond in the diocese of Liege, of the order of the holy father Benedict, a German by nation, a man skilled in the divine Scriptures through constant exercise, not meanly learned in secular letters, strong in verse and prose, an excellent musician, and no less renowned for work than for knowledge, wrote in both styles little works not to be despised, of which there are reported:

Against the Simoniacs, 7 books. Also a Chronicle, 1 book. Many poems.

He also composed several chants in praise of the saints, with sweet and regular melody. He flourished under Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1115.

Franco, second abbot of the monastery of Affligem, of the order of Saint Benedict, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, sufficiently instructed in secular doctrine, strong in talent and renowned for eloquence, wrote certain commendable little works both in meter and in prose, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. When he was still a simple monk in the aforesaid monastery, at the command of his abbot Fulgentius, he began a notable work, which afterward, having been made abbot, he completed, adorned with knowledge and eloquence:

On the Grace of God, 1 book. On the State of Future Glory, in meter, 1 book. Letters to Various Persons, 1 book. Sermons on the Blessed Virgin, 2 books. And certain other things.

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

He was elected abbot of the aforesaid monastery of Affligem under Emperor Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1109, in the thirteenth indiction.

Gilbert, bishop of Poitiers, formerly a Parisian scholastic, surnamed Porreta, a Frenchman by nation, a man much exercised in the divine Scriptures and magnificently learned in secular letters, subtle in talent and confused in speech by the novelty of his terms, was accused of heresy in certain matters by Blessed Bernard, and, convicted in the council of Reims celebrated by Eugenius, is said to have renounced his error. There are those who excuse him, saying that the authorities introduced in his expositions were understood by some in a less sound way. But we, agreeing with the Roman Church, confess that what has once been concluded by it may be infringed by no one. Gilbert wrote many little works, of which the following are reported:

On the Whole Psalter, 1 book. On All the Epistles of Paul, 14 books. On the Gospel of John, 1 book. On Boethius, On the Trinity, 1 book. Books of Questions, etc., 1 book. Several sermons. And certain other things.

He flourished under Conrad III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140.

Lucas, abbot of Mount Saint-Corneille, of the order of the holy father Benedict, learned in the holy Scriptures by continual exercise, and sufficiently instructed in secular letters for his station, having obtained a noble talent in expounding the divine books, transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity by writing various treatises. But I do not recall that any of them has come into our hands. There is reported a notable work of his addressed to Milo, bishop of the church of Therouanne, a man likewise most learned, which I have not yet seen:

On the Song of Songs, 1 book. Several sermons and letters. And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of Lothar, the last emperor, in the year of the Lord 1130.

Wilbert, bishop of Chartres, studious and very skilled in the divine Scriptures, and inferior to none of the learned men of his time in the disciplines of secular letters, acute in talent and sufficiently adorned with eloquence, distinguished in morals and life, and an especial lover and worshipper of the most blessed Mary, Mother of God, wrote a notable little work on this prophecy: “The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah”:

Against the Jews, 1 book. On the Nativity of Saint Mary, 1 sermon. On the Approved Custom,

Abbot of Spanheim.

Various sermons, 2 books.

He is also said to have written several other things, which have not come to my knowledge. I believe he flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1100.

Odo, bishop of Cambrai, a man learned in the Holy Scriptures, nobly educated in humane letters, subtle in intellect and clear in eloquence, notably distinguished, in no slight degree, in composing and delivering homilies to the people after the manner of the ancients, wrote a disputation which he had had with a certain Jew concerning the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, in dialogue form, marked with the first letter of his own name and of the Jew disputing with him:

To Wilbodo the monk, 1 book.

On the Canon of the Mass, 1 book.

On the Unjust Steward, 1 book. “There was a certain rich man.”

Several homilies and letters.

And he composed not a few other things, which have come to my knowledge.

Eadmer, a monk of Canterbury in England, of the Order of St. Benedict, at one time a hearer and disciple of Archbishop Anselm, a man learned through long practice in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, wrote little works not unworthy of reading, by which he both benefited the edification of the faithful and made his name known to posterity. Among these there is a volume on the discord which existed between William, king of the English, and the aforesaid St. Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury:

On Ecclesiastical Liberty, 1 book.

The Life of the same Anselm, 1 book.

And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1120.

Gratian, a monk of Bologna or Classe, of the Order of St. Benedict, by nation, as some will have it, Etruscan, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and burning with wondrous zeal, prompt in intellect and clear in eloquence, also distinguished in life and conduct, after Ivo, bishop of Chartres, wrote a notable volume of decrees, from the statutes, sanctions, and writings of the ancients, which teachers of canon law use in the schools down to the present, approved by Pope Eugene III. Its title is:

The Concord of Discordant Canons, 1 book. “The human race by two.”

He also composed certain other things.

He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1120. [unclear]

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

[unclear]

Hugh, a monk of Corbie, of the Order of St. Benedict, called de Folieto, a man rich and learned in the Holy Scriptures through reading of the ancients, clear in intellect and sweet in eloquence, and no less venerable in conduct than in knowledge, made his name known to posterity by his writings. For he wrote an excellent volume, for all religious and God-fearing people not so much useful as delightful, divided into four little books, headed as follows:

On the Material Cloister, 1 book. “On the ordering of the cloister.”

On the Spiritual Cloister, 1 book. “The cloister of the soul contains.”

On the Cloister of the Soul, 1 book. “In the heavenly Jerusalem.”

On the Cloister of Paradise, 1 book.

And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1120.

[unclear]

Richard, a monk of St. Victor at Paris, of the Order of the Regular Canons of St. Augustine, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, outstanding in intellect, scholastic in eloquence, exceptional in morals and conduct, wrote many and almost innumerable little works, by which he greatly benefited the usefulness of believers and consecrated his name to immortality. Among these the following are reported:

On the Holy Trinity, 6 books. “My just man lives by faith.”

On Contemplation, 5 books. “Arise, Lord, into thy rest.”

On the Twelve Patriarchs, 1 book. “Benjamin a youth.”

On the Mystical Ark, 5 books. “That mystical ark of Moses.”

On the Song of Songs, 1 book. “In the little bed, etc.; the soul which.”

On the Extermination of Evil, 1 book. “What is it to thee, O sea, that.”

On the Advancement of Good, 1 book. “Every head is sick.”

Against the Judaizers, 1 book. “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and.”

On the Tabernacle of the Covenant, 1 book.

On the Forty-Two Stations, 1 book.

On the Four Degrees of Charity, 1 book.

On the Priesthood of Melchizedek, 1 book.

On the Twelve Attendants, 1 book.

On the Pursuit of Wisdom, 1 book.

On the Progress of Monks, 1 book.

On Mental Prayer, 1 book.

On the Threefold Holocaust, 1 book.

On the Authority of Peter, 1 book. “Whatsoever thou shalt bind.” On

The Abbot of Sponheim.

On judicial power, one book. On the difference of sins, [unclear] book(s). On the instruction of novices, one book. On the spirit of blasphemy, one book. On the offices of the Church, one book. On diverse affections, one book. An epitome of the whole Bible, [unclear] book(s). On the Apocalypse of John, one book. On Daniel the prophet, one book. A chronicle from the beginning of the world, one book. On the double Passover, one book. Of divisions or exceptions, twenty-four books. On the vision of Nebuchadnezzar, one book. On the sacrifice of Abraham, one book. On the four winds, one book. On the words of Isaiah, one book. On the Acts of the Apostles, one book. On violent charity, one book. On newness of life, one book. He also composed many other things besides: letters, sermons, and various treatises. He flourished under Conrad III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140.

Guido, fifth prior of the Charterhouse, a man skilled by long study in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, gentle in disposition and distinguished in speech, and venerable no less for his manner of life than for his learning, is said to have composed several little works, by which his name has been endowed with immortality. Of these there is extant an excellent work, written in lucid discourse:

On the life of Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, one book. On the institutions of the Carthusians, one book. And certain other things.

He corrected with diligent study the letters of the most blessed father Jerome, which had been corrupted by the excessive fault of scribes, to the standard of truth, and brought them together into one. He died under Lothair the Younger, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1157, in the fifteenth indiction, on the sixth day before the Kalends of August.

Peter Lombard, bishop of Paris, formerly a scholastic, a man most studious in the divine Scriptures and nobly learned, subtle in intellect and distinguished in speech, transmitted his name to posterity by writing with such great glory that, down to the present day, the school of theologians, wherever it is practiced, names and regards him with singular veneration as the Master. For with discerning study he wrote, from the sayings of the holy fathers, a commendable work:

Four books of Sentences. “Desiring something concerning…” On the whole Psalter, one book. “Since all prophecies…” “Seeking the beginnings of things…” On all the epistles of Paul, four books. “Seeking the beginnings of things…” Various sermons, one book.

He also composed not a few other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Conrad III, emperor, in the year of the Lord [unclear].

Eckardus, first abbot of the monastery of St. Lawrence, which is called Vraugia, in the diocese of Würzburg in the Hercynian Forest, of the order of St. Benedict, a German by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and, in secular letters, inferior to none among the learned Germans of his time, excelling in verse and prose, wrote little works not to be despised in reading, by which he showed the liveliness of his intellect. Of these I know only the excellent work, composed in a double style in imitation of Boethius, very useful and necessary for the instruction and consolation of monks and of all the faithful who fear God, which he entitled:

The Lantern of Monks, one book.

He composed certain elegant sermons and various letters to different persons. He flourished under Conrad III, emperor, in the year of the Lord [unclear]. He was buried in the middle of the church of the aforesaid monastery.

Engelbert, abbot of the monastery of Admont, of the order of St. Benedict, a German by nation, a man very studious and learned in the divine writings, and sufficiently instructed in the disciplines of secular letters, distinguished in intellect and speech, and no less worthy of reverence for his manner of life than for his knowledge, made his name known by writing and expounding various things, and both by word and by example did no slight service to the edification of his brothers. For he wrote:

Elegant sermons, one book. On vices and virtues, one book.

But he also published several other things, which have by no means come to my knowledge.

Peter, priest of the church of Troyes, surnamed Comestor or Manducator, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and excellently trained in secular letters, practiced in verse and prose, wrote in both styles certain distinguished little works, whose authority has long since been approved by the Church through use. He was called Comestor or Manducator for this reason: because [unclear] the authorities of the Scriptures in

The Abbot of Spanheim.

by very frequently citing them in his sermons and little works, as though he had eaten them into the belly of memory. Among the other volumes of his talent he wrote a distinguished work addressed to William, archbishop of Sens, expounding all the historical books of the Bible briefly and usefully, which now by usage is entitled

The Scholastic History, 20 books. Incipit: “Imperatoriae maiestatis.” On the Praises of Saint Mary, 1 book. Sermons on the Season, 1 book. Sermons on the Saints, and very many other things, 1 book.

He flourished under Frederick, the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 1160.

Peter, the Parisian dialectician, called Abelard, a Gaul by birth, a man most learned in secular philosophy, attempting to investigate higher matters, overwhelmed by glory, fell into many errors; through the action of the holy abbot Bernard, he was condemned with his depraved doctrines in the council of Sens. From this time secular philosophy began to defile sacred theology with its useless curiosity. This Peter wrote some little works which, if he had not mixed errors into them, could have benefited posterity. Of these there survives a volume overshadowed by dialectical obscurity, varied with many opinions, which he wished to entitle

His Theology, 1 book. Know Thyself, 1 book. And certain other things.

He flourished under Conrad, the third emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140.

Adelphus, an abbot of the order of Saint Benedict, a man skilled in divine scriptures through long practice, not ignorant of secular letters, an indefatigable cultivator of regular observance, so that by word and example he might show himself a useful shepherd to the sheep of Christ entrusted to him, is said to have forged some little works for their benefit, in which a rich vein of talent commends an adorned eloquence. Of these there survive elegant

Sermons to the Brethren, 1 book. Against the Saracens, 1 book.

The rest which he is said to have composed have not come to my knowledge.

William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, afterward, as he says, a monk of Clairvaux under the divine father Bernard of the Cistercian order, a man studious and learned in divine scriptures, and also distinguished by the holiness of his life and conduct, and for that reason singularly beloved by him, published little works not to be despised in reading; of these few have come to my knowledge. He began to write, but, forestalled by death, did not complete,

The Life of Saint Bernard, Abbot, 1 book. Incipit: “Scripturus vitam servitui.” The Mirror of Faith, 1 book. The Enigma of Faith, 1 book. Sentences of Faith, 1 book. To Theophila, on the Nature of the Soul, 1 book. On Contemplating God, 1 book. On the Nature and Dignity of Love, 1 book. On the Sacrament of the Altar, 1 book. Against Peter Abelard, 1 book. On the Song of Songs, unfinished, 1 book. On Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, 1 book. And certain other things.

There are some who say that this William, while he was still abbot of Saint-Thierry, wrote that well-known letter to the Carthusians whose beginning is “Fratribus de monte Dei orientale lumen,” which is ascribed by many to blessed Bernard. He flourished under Conrad, the third emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140. And he died before Bernard, when he had completed one book on his life; Arnold, abbot of Bonneval, added four other books to it.

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

Conrad, a monk of the monastery of Hirsau on the borders of the Swabians, of the order of Saint Benedict, a German by nation, of the diocese of Speyer, a man most learned in divine scriptures, very skilled in secular letters, an eminent philosopher, rhetorician, musician, and poet, composed many splendid little works under the name Peregrinus. In them the adorned arrangement of the thoughts and the charming cultivation of speech declare their author inferior to none of the ancients. Of these, only the following have come to my knowledge:

A distinguished work of dialogues, under the name of Peregrinus the priest, addressed to Theodora, a virgin consecrated to God, which he entitled The Mirror of Virgins, 1 book. Incipit: “Collaturus tecum, o Theo-.” On the Gospels through the Year, 1 book. Incipit: “Quia in littera veteris te-.” On the Life of the Spirit, the Fruit, and Death, 1 book. Incipit: “Cum omnis divinae paginae.” The Matricularius, 1 book. Incipit: “Cum manifestum sit, mun-.” On the Praises of Saint Benedict, in verse, 1 book. Incipit: “Luce velut solem.” Didascalon, 1 book. Incipit: “Quia te video diu va-.” On Music and the Tones, 1 book. Incipit: “Musica est secundum cui-.”

Of the rest I have seen nothing.

There was another declaimer of the order of Preachers, who according to

Abbot of Spanheim.

...according to the custom of modern writers, he composed sermons to the people under the name of Peregrinus, much inferior to our man in eloquence, and also later in time. Whatever this Conrad wrote, however, echoes Ciceronian eloquence, which the other could not do.

He flourished under the emperor Conrad III, in the year of the Lord 1140.

Arnold, abbot of Bonneval, of the Cistercian order, once the close friend of the blessed abbot Bernard, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and also not ignorant of secular letters, ready in talent and distinguished in eloquence, no less conspicuous in conduct than in doctrine, made his name known to posterity by writing. For after William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, had died, [he wrote] the work on the Life of Saint Bernard, 4 books; The Deeds of Illustrious Men; and certain letters.

He flourished under the emperor Frederick I, in the year of the Lord 1160.

Richard, monk of Cluny, of the order of Saint Benedict, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and in secular letters reputed in his time the most learned of all, subtle in talent and eloquent in speech, by writing and composing various treatises transmitted his name with great glory to the knowledge of posterity. Yet I do not recall that any of them has so far come into our hands. His distinguished and famous work is, however, reported to be:

History and Times, 1 book. Letters to Various Persons, 1 book.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Frederick I, in the year of the Lord 1160.

Ganfred of Auxerre, monk of the Cistercian order, once a hearer and disciple of Peter Abelard, but lest he should also become an imitator of his error, betook himself to the teaching of Saint Bernard of Clairvaux. Under his discipleship he became distinguished in learning and religion, and composed little works of reading not to be despised, by which he made his name known also to posterity.

Against Peter Abelard, 1 book. On the Apocalypse of John, 1 book. Letters to Various Persons, 1 book.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Frederick I, in the year of the Lord 1180.

Peter, cleric of the church of Reims, called de Riga, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and in secular letters the most learned among all the doctors of his time, an outstanding grammarian and philosopher, excellent in verse and prose, wrote not a few volumes in both styles, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these I have seen only the notable metrical work on the Bible, which he entitled Aurora, as follows:

On Genesis, 1 book. It begins: “The beginning of the world, what sort...” 1 book. “These twelve of the fathers...” 1 book. “But the voice of the Lord [to] Moses...” 1 book. “God addresses Moses...” 1 book. “These are the words of God...” 1 book. “After Moses, Joshua...” 1 book. “The Hebrew sins, he says...” 1 book. “To Ruth hastens...” 3 books. “Dwelling on Mount Ephra...” 1 book. “Origen alone, with...” 1 book. “Solomon reigned...” 1 book. “After those subject to him...” 1 book. “You who read the history...” 2 books. “Certain people [assign] the book of Job to Moses...” 1 book. “To Eustochium and Paula...” 1 book. “As far as under the Ethiopians...” 1 book. “Great Alexander...” 1 book. “He shone under Herod...” 1 book. “In the nineteenth year of Tiberius...” 1 book. “These things concerning the new and old law...” 1 book. “[unclear].”

He also published many other things which have not come to my knowledge. In the aforesaid little works he expounded the historical books of the Bible with marvelous brevity, carefully observing the law of meter, and explained each item according to the historical and allegorical sense.

Joachim, abbot of the monastery of Fiore, of the order of Saint Benedict, originally from Calabria, a man zealous and practiced in the divine Scriptures, who, being regarded in his time as a prophet, even attempted to foretell future things. But it seems to me, if I may speak without prejudice to his own opinion or that of his followers, that he spoke more from conjectures drawn from the Scriptures than that he was a prophet. For, to be silent meanwhile about the rest, he dreamed that the emperor Frederick would be an enemy of the Church, whereas we all know that he persevered until death as peaceable, and subject and faithful to the Roman pontiff.

The Abbot of Spanheim.

[unclear]. He wrote, moreover, in plain language several little works, in nearly all of which, as though foreknowing the future, he was accustomed to mix predictions:

On Jeremiah the prophet, one book. On Daniel the prophet, one book. On the Gospel of John, one book. On the Apocalypse of John, eight books. To Henry VI, one book. “You piously ask something from...” “The first time of the synagogue...” On the Seven Seals, one book. The Psalter of Ten Strings, five books. Concords, five books. On the Fifteen Pontiffs, one book. “Go up, baldhead, that...” On Future Times, one book. “Because the general [condition] of the world...” Letters to various persons, one book.

He also published many other things, especially against the Jews and other adversaries of the Catholic faith, which have not come into our hands. But the treatise which he wrote against Peter Lombard, bishop of Paris, was condemned in a general council, as is clear at the beginning of the Decretals, “We condemn.”

He flourished under Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.
