Henry of Kalkar, a German by nation, of the Carthusian order, and prior of the house of St. Barbara in Cologne, a man who had an enlightened mind in the divine Scriptures, and was also not ignorant of secular letters, notable in life and conduct, published little works not to be despised in reading, the use of which is judged very useful for religious and devout brothers. Among them are reported:

The Monastic Exercise, 1 book. Loquagium on rhetoric, 1 book. Cantuagium on music, 1 book. On the origin of my order, 1 book. And certain other works, especially pertaining to the purification of consciences.

He flourished under the emperor Wenceslaus, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Richard Maidstone, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, English by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and remarkably learned in secular philosophy, which they call Aristotelian, distinguished in intellect, scholastic in speech, and an outstanding declaimer, wrote many commendable little works, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among them I have found:

Against the Lollards of Wycliffe, 1 book. Sermons on the season, 1 book. Sermons on the saints, 1 book. The rest are hidden from me.

He flourished in the Oxford school, especially at that time when the heresy of John Wycliffe began to sprout in England, and he wrote various things.

Marsilius of Inghen, English by nation, a man in the divine Scriptures, the first planter of the Heidelberg school, which Rupert, duke of Bavaria and count palatine of the Rhine, established and magnificently endowed, and which Pope Urban VI confirmed on the model of Paris; also, as Wimpheling testifies, canon and treasurer of the church of St. Andrew at Cologne: he published little works not to be despised, by which he made his name known to posterity. Among them, in the Heidelberg library, written in his own hand, are held today:

Questions on the Sentences, 4 books. A notable dialectic, 1 book. Several books of commentaries on Aristotle, And certain other things.

He died under the emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord 1394, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the second indiction, buried at Heidelberg in the church of St. Peter. There are some who write that he was German; I grant them freedom of judgment. It is established, however, that he was called from the Paris school to Heidelberg for the beginning of the university.

John, monk of the monastery of Castell, in the diocese of Eichstatt, of the order of St. Benedict, German by nation, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular letters, excellent in intellect and eloquent in fluent speech, a distinguished theologian, philosopher, and rhetorician, wrote many and splendid volumes, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among them I have found only the great and very famous work, divided into two volumes, which he published with immense and commendable zeal:

On the Rule of St. Benedict, 2 books. A Breviary of the Bible, 1 book. Sermons on the season, 3 books. Sermons on the saints, 4 books. On the Passion of the Lord, 42 sermons, 5 books. Letters to various persons, 6 books. Besides these he published many other things, which have not yet come to my knowledge.

Conrad of Monte Puellarum, German by nation, canon of the church of Regensburg, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and most learned in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence: first absorbing the rudiments of the liberal arts in the Erfurt school, he then betook himself to the University of Paris, where, lecturing publicly to students on philosophy and sacred letters for eight years, he obtained the doctor's cap. He wrote for lord Lupold, bishop of Bamberg, a large and noble work, which he entitled, according to the Greeks:

Economics, 3 books. All of moral philoso[unclear] Monastics, to the duke of Austria, 4 books. And also Politics, 5 books. Various Questions, 6 books. And many other things.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Urban VI, in the year of the Lord 1390. Hen

The Abbot of Spanheim.

Henry Boyc, a Breton by nation, from the diocese of Leon, as he testifies at the beginning of his work on the Decretals, a man most learned in canon law and nobly trained in scholastic philosophy, outstanding in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, expansive and abundant in judgment, wrote in that faculty volumes not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the Decretals, 5 books. “To the venerable and [unclear] ...” On the Sixth Book of the Decretals, 1 book. On the Clementines, 1 book.

He is also said to have published commentaries on the Decrees and various other treatises on different subjects, which have by no means come into our hands.

Johannes Rusbrock, prior of the regular canons of Groenendaal in Brabant, in the diocese of Cambrai, a German by nation, a man, as they say, devout but little learned, wrote in his native tongue, for the edification of the simple, certain little works which after his death were translated into Latin by another. In some matters they are excellent, but in others they are said by doctors to be erroneous. Concerning these Johannes Gerson, chancellor of Paris, composed advisements. Of them the following are reported:

On the Adornment of Spiritual Marriage, 5 books. “Behold, the bridegroom comes; go out ...” On the Progress of Religious, 1 book. Exhortatory Letters, 1 book. And certain other works.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Johannes Schodehoven, a German by nation, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, prior of Mechelen, a man studious and learned in the divine scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people, wrote for the use of preachers of the word of God volumes not to be despised. Of these the following are extant:

A distinguished work on vices and virtues and every matter suitable for preaching, according to the order of the alphabet, in two volumes, which he entitled Polypodium, 2 books. “Many hide themselves ...” Various Sermons, 1 book.

He also published some other works, which have by no means come into our hands.

Michael Augrianus of Bologna, an Italian by nation, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man most learned in the divine scriptures and nobly trained in secular philosophy and canon law, whom Pope Urban VI first appointed vicar of the whole order, and who, finally elected general in the year of the Lord 1381, governed the order under obedience to Pope Urban for nine years. He wrote many excellent volumes, of which the following are reported:

To the Cardinal of Santa Maria in Trastevere, a distinguished and excellent work. On the Conception of Saint Mary, 1 book. On the Whole Psalter, 5 books. On the Sentences, 4 books. Questions on the Sentences, 1 book. Table of the Sentences, 1 book. On the Gospel of Matthew, 1 book. On the Gospel of Luke, 1 book. Table of the Moralia of Gregory, 1 book. Table of the Decretum, 1 book. Lenten Sermons, 1 book. He began a Dictionary, 3 books. On Valerius Maximus, 1 book. On the Ethics of Aristotle, 1 book. And certain other works.

Prevented by death, he did not complete this divine work of the new dictionary, but brought it only from A to C inclusive, in three volumes. He died in the last year of the emperor Wenceslaus, under Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord 1396, on the calends of December, in the eighth indiction, and was honorably buried before the high altar of his convent at Bologna. May he rest in the peace of Christ.

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

Philippus Ferrarien[sis?] Tholosanus, bishop of the church of Pax in Spain, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man learned in the divine scriptures and an outstanding declaimer of sermons, quick in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, formerly preaching in the kingdom of Sicily, converted many from iniquity and brought forth for God great fruits of his learning. He wrote elegant:

Sermons on the Season, 1 book. Sermons on the Saints, 1 book. And certain other works.

There are some who write that he was raised to the honor of the cardinalate because of his extraordinary learning and the uprightness of his life; about this I am not certain.

Walter Disse, an Englishman by nation, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, nuncio and legate of Pope Boniface IX in the kingdoms of England, Spain, Portugal, Navarre, Arago-

Abbot of Sponheim.

[unclear], and in the regions of Gascony, and in the other lands and kingdoms, preaching the Cross against the infidel schismatics, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, an outstanding declaimer of sermons, wrote little works not to be despised, by which he made his name known. Of these there are extant:

Against the Lollards, one book. Also On the Schism, one book. On Some Psalms, one book. Sermons de tempore, one book. Sermons on the Saints, one book. And certain others.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Gerard of Zutphen, German by nation, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant also of secular letters, subtle in intellect, distinguished in eloquence, and to be preferred no less for his manner of life than for his knowledge of the Scriptures, published certain little works pertaining to the instruction of devout brothers, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have seen only:

On Interior Reformation, one book, "A certain man descend[ed?]." On Spiritual [Ascension?], one book, "Blessed is the man whose..." Various sermons, one book.

John de [Hildinio?], of the order of the brethren of the Hospital of St. John of Jerusalem, a man learned in the divine writings, not ignorant of secular philosophy, an eminent doctor of sacred Scripture, an outstanding declaimer of sermons, sharp in intellect and composed in eloquence, published many excellent volumes and delivered several elegant lectures in the University of Paris. Of these the following are extant:

On the Gospel of Mark, one book, "He was made like a lion." On the Gospel of John, one book. On the Epistle to the Romans, one book. On the Epistle to the Corinthians, one book. On the Epistle to the Galatians, one book. On the Epistle to the Ephesians, one book. On the Epistle to the Philippians, one book. On the Epistle to the Colossians, one book. On the Epistles to the Thessalonians, one book.

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

On the Epistles to Timothy, two books. On the Epistle to Titus, one book. On the Epistle to Philemon, two books. On the Epistle to the Hebrews, one book. On the Annunciation of the Lord, one book, "Hail Mary, full of grace." Various sermons, one book, "Instruct your son, because as..." And many other things.

He is said also to have written commentaries and lectures on many books of the Bible, which have not yet at all come into our hands.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Philip of Monte [Calerio?], of the order of the Friars Minor of Saint Francis, a man practiced in the sacred Scriptures, a great and outstanding preacher of the word of God, wrote for the usefulness of those who serve in declamations little works not to be scorned; by nobly exercising his talent in them, he also destined his name for the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have found only the following:

Sermons de tempore, one book, "There will be signs in the sun and [moon]." Sermons on the Saints, one book. Lenten sermons, one book.

He is said besides to have composed various other treatises and to have explained some of the divine books, but none of them has reached me.

John, surnamed Grossus, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin of Mount Carmel, the nineteenth prior general - some have the twenty-first - a native of Toulouse, a studious and learned man, wrote in plain speech volumes not to be despised; by exercising his talent magnificently in them, he made his name known also to posterity. Of these I have seen only the excellent work which, containing the institution and progress of the Carmelite order, is entitled Viridarium, three books, "By what things [unclear]." His sermons, one book, and certain other things are also reported.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1400.

Nicholas de Gorra, of the order of the Friars of Saint Dominic, a man most studious in the holy Scriptures and nobly learned, outstanding in intellect, published in scholastic and plain discourse many volumes, the reading of which, for those who wish to be instructed in the holy Scriptures...

ABBOT OF SPONHEIM.

[unclear], it will not be to be rejected; of these I remember that few have come into our hands. Of the many, however, the following are reported:

On the Sentences, 4 books. On the Five Books of Moses, 5 books. On Isaiah the Prophet, 1 book. Likewise on Jeremiah, 1 book. On Ecclesiasticus, a large work, 1 book. On the Song of Songs, 1 book. “He will give a blessing.” On the Gospel of Matthew, 1 book. On the Gospel of Mark, 1 book. “He gave [him?] as a light to the nations.” On the Gospel of Luke, 1 book. On the Gospel of John, 1 book. Various Sermons, 1 book. And certain other things.

He is said, moreover, to have issued noteworthy commentaries and readings on almost the whole Bible, which have not come to the knowledge of my reading.

Jacobus of Teramo, a canon of Aprutium, archdeacon of Aversa, a very celebrated jurist, an excellent doctor of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, clear and well-composed in speech, whose authority among the professors of this faculty was great in his time, published in that discipline certain outstanding volumes, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have found only the dialogue On the Redemption of the Human Race, commonly called Belial, which the author entitled:

The Consolation of Sinners, 1 book. “And afterwards through the tree of knowledge.” He is said to have written On the Clementines, 1 book. And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Wenceslaus and of the new Pope Boniface, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Wilhelmus of Oppenbach, a German by nation, an eminent doctor learned in the sacred Scriptures, and nobly exercised in scholastic philosophy, sharp and vigorous in intellect, well fitted for disputing and untying questions of the Scriptures, wrote in the theological faculty little works not to be rejected, by which he made his name known in the Parisian school. Of these I have found:

On the Sentences, 2 books. Disputed Questions, 1 book.

Of Ecclesiastical Writers.

He is also said to have written sermons and certain other treatises, and to have worked out readings in the schools, which have not come to my knowledge.

Henricus of Langenstein, called “of Hesse,” a German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly instructed in secular philosophy, outstanding in intellect, abundant and expansive, since, after spending many years in lecturing on Genesis, scarcely reaching the fourth chapter of the book, he completed as many volumes. For he was ready in all things, copious in judging and writing, so much so that for him it was a matter of greater difficulty to keep away things worthy of remembrance that occurred to him of their own accord than to find new things to say. This man, as I found from a certain letter of his, I should believe to have been a canon of the church of Worms. He flourished first in the University of Paris, where he earned the laurel of the doctorate; then, for the adornment of the newly planted University of Vienna, he betook himself there, and both by teaching and by writing acquired great glory for his learning. Of his little works the following are reported:

On the Sentences, 4 books. A Prologue on Genesis, 5 books. On the Schism of Antichrist, 1 book. On the Instruction of the Priesthood, 1 book. On the Contemplative Soul, 1 book. On Contemplation, 1 book. Mirror of the Soul, 1 book. On the Canonical Hours, 1 book. Against the Astrologers, 1 book. On the Lord’s Prayer, 1 book. On the Hail Mary, 1 book. On the Creed of the Apostles, 1 book. On Contempt of the World, 1 book. Against Brother Telesphorus, 1 book. Against a Certain Wycliffite, 1 book. To the Canons Regular, 1 book. On the Property of Monks, 1 book. Sermons on the Season, 1 book. Sermons on the Saints, 1 book. On the Song of Songs, 1 book. Letters to Various Persons, 1 book. Various Questions, 1 book. 1 book. 1 book. book

The Abbot of Sponheim.

He also published many other things that have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Rupert the Bavarian Palatine, king of the Romans, and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord 1400.

Johannes de Bromyard, of the Order of the Friars Preachers of St. Dominic, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and learned through long practice, not ignorant also of secular letters, excellent in talent and an outstanding preacher, wrote certain distinguished volumes by which he secured the memory of his name among posterity. Among these the following are reported:

The Summa of Preachers, one book. “The life of preachers,” etc.

The Summa of Moral Law, one book. “What in the following work [unclear].”

Sermons on the Season, one book.

Sermons on the Saints, one book.

He is said to have written many other things besides, which have not come to my knowledge.

Johannes Gluel, German by nation, of the Order of the Friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, prior of Cologne, born in Aachen, an imperial city, a man excellently learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, of excellent and distinguished talent in delivering sermons to the people, wrote, among the other little works of his study, a volume not to be rejected by devotees of this religious order, on the origin and advancement of his order, which he entitled:

Mirror of the Carmelites, one book.

Sermons on the Season, one book.

Lenten Sermons, one book. “Store up for yourselves.”

Sermons on the Saints, one book.

He flourished in his convent at Cologne, writing and composing various little works, where at last, failing, he passed his day and was buried in peace.

Henricus Euta, or Oyta, German by nation, the unique ornament of the University of Vienna in Austria, [unclear] from the beginning, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly learned in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in talent, scholastic in speech, an outstanding preacher of sermons, wrote many distinguished volumes, of which very few have so far come into our hands. For I have read only:

On the Sentences, four books. “Concerning the prologue of the first [unclear].” “On [unclear].”

On Contracts, one book. “Love justice, you who [unclear].”

On the Conception of Saint Mary, one book. “A virgin shall arise from Israel.”

And certain sermons.

Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished in the University of Vienna, under Emperor Wenceslaus, together with Henricus de Hasia, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Henricus de Andernaco, German by nation, of the Order of the Friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and an outstanding interpreter of Aristotelian philosophy, excellent in talent and famous among all men of his time as a preacher of sermons, published little works of no slight authority, of which the following are reported:

A distinguished work On the Sentences, four books.

Sermons on the Season, one book.

Sermons on the Saints, one book.

Questions of Philosophy, one book.

And certain other things that have by no means come to the notice of our reading.

He flourished especially in the convent at Cologne, where he is also said to have been buried.

Blaius Andernarius, French by nation, of the Order of the Friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man learned in the holy Scriptures and nobly trained in the arena of scholastic discipline, clear in talent and an outstanding disputant, wrote several distinguished volumes, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Among these an illuminating and notable work excels:

On the Sentences, one book.

Questions and Collations, one book.

He is also said to have written some things in moral philosophy, but they have not come to me.

Bartholomaeus de Saliceto, the most celebrated jurist of all his time, subtle in talent and clear in eloquence, whose sayings are held in great authority among professors of civil law, published certain illuminating little works on the laws, by which he consecrated the memory of his name to immortality among posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the Code, one book.

On the Institutes, one book.

On the Use of Fiefs, one book.

And several other things.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Johannes, abbot of the monastery of St. Bavo, of the Order of the divine father Benedict, German by nation, an outstanding doctor and professor of the divine Scriptures, subtle in talent and compact in eloquence, and no less distinguished in religious way of life than in knowledge of letters, wrote

Abbot of Spanheim.

[He] wrote certain distinguished little works for the instruction of monks, of which the following are extant: On the Eating of Meat, book 1; Declarations on the Rule, book 1; Questions on the Sentences, book 1.

In addition, he is said to have written various and numerous treatises, but I do not recall that any of them have come into our hands, except that little book which he wrote on the eating of meat, in which he beautifully sets forth and soundly concludes that, for a healthy monk professed according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, the eating of meat is unlawful, and therefore altogether forbidden.

Richard Lavinham, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, an Englishman by nation, a man excellently learned in the Holy Scriptures, an outstanding expounder of secular philosophy, and also of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people, wrote several volumes as well, of which these are reported: Against the Lollards, book 1; On the Foundation of His Order, book 1; For the Book of Bridget, book 1; Various Sermons, book 1; On Logic also, book 1; and Various Questions, book 1.

He flourished at the University of Oxford, especially at the time when the heresy of John Wycliffe, that of the Lollards, began in Bohemia.

Johannes de Werdena, of the order, as they say, of the Friars Minor, a German by nation, a man studious and learned in the sacred writings, rich in reading of the ancients, and sufficiently learned in natural philosophy, excellent in talent, composed in speech with scholastic simplicity, and in his time a most celebrated deliverer of popular sermons, wrote, among the other monuments of his talent, little works very necessary for preachers of the word of God, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there are extant: Double Sermons on the Temporale, book 1, “Let us put on,” see; Double Sermons on the Saints, book 1.

But the other things which he composed have by no means come to our knowledge.

Jacobus, who is called Magnus, a native of Toledo, of the order of the hermit brothers of Saint Augustine, a man learned in the divine writings, distinguished in knowledge of natural philosophy, and abundant in reading of the ancients, is said to have issued various treatises and commentaries on the divine books, which have not yet come into our hands. I have found one outstanding and distinguished volume of his, on discourse in the inquiry of wisdom, entitled *So-

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

phologium*, 3 books, “Of the most illustrious prince.”

Concerning the others I have seen nothing. He flourished in the times of the emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1400.

Johannes Campsceñ, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, an Englishman by nation, long practiced in the Holy Scriptures and in continual reading of the ancients, rich in talent, an excellent deliverer of sermons, is said to have fashioned certain distinguished little works, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of their number, they report that there are extant very notable Sermons on the Temporale, book 1; Sermons on the Saints, book 1.

But of the other things which he composed I have not been able to find the titles of the works.

Thomas Gualensis, of the order of the Friars Preachers, an Englishman by nation, a man learned and very studious in the divine Scriptures, and nobly learned in secular letters, especially in scholastic philosophy, subtle in talent and clear in eloquence, also an outstanding deliverer of sermons and an acute disputant in scholastic lectures, wrote many distinguished little works on the Holy Scriptures, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity; of these, however, few have come into our hands. For I have found only the following: On the Whole Psalter, book 1, “Blessed is he who keeps”; On the Proverbs of Solomon, book 1, “In hidden places I shall prepare”; book 1; On Augustine’s City of God, 10 books, “The force of the river makes glad”; On the Song of Songs, book 1.

He flourished at the University of Oxford, where he is said to have composed many volumes, and especially various lectures on several books of the Bible.

Philippus, abbot of the monastery of Otterburg, in the diocese of Worms, of the Cistercian order, a German by nation, a man studious in the divine Scriptures, learned through long practice, and not ignorant of secular literature, published for the edification of readers volumes not to be despised; by soundly exercising his talent in them, he also left to posterity the memory of his name. Of their number the following are reported: a distinguished and notable work On the Song of Songs, book 1; Sermons on the Temporale, book 1; Sermons on the Saints, book 1; Letters to Various Persons, book 1.

If he published anything more, it has still by no means come to my knowledge.

Ni-

Abbot of Spanheim.

Nicolaus, a physician of outstanding learning, Italian by nation, Florentine by homeland, a man highly learned not only in medicine but also in the other letters of secular philosophy, distinguished in talent, polished in eloquence; how great his learning is among the physicians of this time is proved not by my words, but by their testimonies. He published certain notable little works in that faculty, among which an excellent work is reported:

Summa medicinae, one book.

And certain other things.

He died in the times of Rupert, king of the Romans, and of Pope John the twenty-third, in the year of the Lord 1412, in the fifth indiction.

Johannes de Duren, of the Order of Friars Minor of St Francis, German by nation, a man studious and nobly practiced in the Holy Scriptures, of great and distinguished reputation in delivering sermons to the people, is reported to have composed certain little works for the direction of simple priests as preachers, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these there survive:

Sermones de tempore, one book.

Sermones de sanctis, one book.

Quadragesimale, one book. “Sanctificate ieiunium.”

De septem peccatis mortalibus, one book. “Cum confessor idoneus.”

De occultis vitiis, one book. “Est via quae videtur ho-”

De confessione, one book.

He is also said to have written many other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

Tilmannus de Hachenberg, of the Order of Friars Minor, German by nation, from the diocese of Trier, a man studious in the divine Scriptures, learned through long practice, having a tongue polished by use in speaking, shone forth as great and most renowned in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote certain little works not to be despised by simple people, by which, profitably applying his talent, he left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these there survive:

Sermones de tempore, one book. “Erunt signa hic praedi-”

Sermones de sanctis, one book.

Sermones per quadragesimam, one book.

And certain other things.

He flourished in his convent at Koblenz, where he died and was buried.

Johannes de Ligniano, a very celebrated jurist, well instructed in the disciplines of the philosophers, outstanding in talent, distinguished in eloquence, is reported to have composed certain excellent little works in canon law,

On Ecclesiastical Writers

[unclear], applying himself to which, he both spent his time usefully and left to posterity the memory of his name. Of these, as Franciscus de Zabarellis testifies in the prologue on the Clementines, there are extant Comportationes on the Clementines, one book, and certain other works.

He flourished under Rupert the Bavarian, king of the Romans, and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1400.

Hugo of Schlettstadt, a German by nation, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and notably learned in the disciplines of the philosophers, subtle in intellect, and a distinguished disputant of scholastic questions, wrote, as they say, certain excellent volumes, by which he left to posterity the memory of his name. Of these there is extant a work of Questions on the Sentences, four books.

And certain other works.

He was, moreover, a follower and clear interpreter, in his determinations, of the holy father Bonaventure, of the Order of Minors, explaining those things which in that man’s distinctive philosophy might have seemed obscure and rather rare to the simple.

Paulus Venetus, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of St. Augustine, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and, in Aristotelian philosophy, second to none in Italy in his time, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, and an outstanding declaimer, composed many little works, especially in philosophy, by which he left to posterity the memory of his name. Of these are reported:

Against the Jews, one book. Summary on Natural Things, one book. Sermons on the Season, one book. Sermons on the Saints, one book. Sermons for Lent, one book. On the book of the Posterior Analytics, [two?] books. On the Physics, [two?] books. On the Metaphysics, [twelve?] books. On the Soul, [two?] books. Summary of Philosophy, one book. A Double Logic, [two?] books. On Generation and Corruption, [two?] books. On the book of Porphyry, one book. On the book of the Categories, one book. On Strode’s Consequences, one book. And many other works.

“Every doctrine,” etc. “Natural philosophy” “With you, most wise king” “So great a body of letters,” etc. “A conversation [unclear],” etc. “Considering,” etc. “Of human and divine things” “Greatest and strong,” etc. “As I was asking,” etc. “Jesus, God and man”

The Abbot of Spanheim.

He flourished under the emperor Wenceslaus, in the year of the Lord 1400. And, dying as a young man, he was buried in the sacristy of his order at Venice.

James of Cessolis, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man learned in divine Scripture and not ignorant of secular letters, excellent in talent, polished and well-composed in speech, second to none in his time in delivering sermons to the people, published certain distinguished volumes, by which he left to posterity a praiseworthy memory of his name. Of these there is extant a notable work, entitled On the Morals of Men and the Duties of Nobles and Commoners, treating the subject On the Game of Chess, in 4 books. “Among all kinds of [unclear].” Various Sermons, 1 book.

Other works, however, which he is said to have written have by no means come to our knowledge.

Thomas of Haselbach, German by nation, learned in sacred Scripture, not ignorant of secular philosophy, outstanding in talent, scholastic in speech, but excessively diffuse and prolix, and for that reason liable to the criticism of certain people. For when he was ordinary lecturer in sacred theology at the university of Vienna, lecturing on Isaiah the prophet for twenty-one years, he did not reach the end of the first chapter. He wrote some treatises on the divine Scriptures, of which the following many volumes are reported:

On Isaiah the Prophet, 1 book. On the Sentences, 4 books. On the Ten Commandments, 1 book. On the Five Senses of Man, 1 book. Sermons on the Season, 1 book. Sermons on the Saints, 1 book. And many others.

He flourished in the times of Rupert, king of the Romans, and of Pope Gregory XII, in the year of the Lord 1410.

Thomasinus, by homeland a Ferrarese, of the Order of Preachers of Saint Dominic, a man devoted to and learned in sacred Scripture, an outstanding preacher in rebuking the sins of peoples, is said to have composed certain excellent treatises for the instruction of simple priests, by which he transmitted knowledge of his name with praise to posterity. Of their number especially the following are reported:

Sermons on the Season, 1 book. Sermons on the Saints, 1 book. Sermons for Lent, 1 book. [unclear]

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

The rest, however, which he composed, have not come to our knowledge up to the present.

Thomas a Kempis, German by nation, of the Order of the Canons Regular of Saint Augustine, of the Mount of the divine martyr and virgin Agnes near Zwolle in the diocese of Utrecht, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, devout in life and conduct, and an especial lover of the blessed Mary ever virgin, wrote for the instruction of simple brethren treatises not to be despised, of which the following are reported:

On Contempt of the World, 4 books. “He who follows me, not [unclear].” “Behold how good and how pleasant,” 5 books. “He who has not renounced,” 6 books. “I beg you, dearest father,” 7 books. “Dearest, when you were in [unclear],” 8 books. “Written in Prophe[cy?],” 8 books. “Weep with me, all friends,” 9 books. “With the holy man you will be holy,” 10 books. “I am the flower of the field and the lily,” 11 books. “Your ways, O Lord, [unclear].” “Be comforted, be comforted,” 12 books. “The way of those men is right,” 13 books. “Hear, religious monk,” 14 books. “Permit the little children to come,” 15 books. “My son, from your youth,” 16 books. “The Lord rules me, and nothing,” 17 books. “Dearest brother, the book [unclear].”

He flourished in the times of Rupert, king of the Romans, and of Pope Gregory VI, in the year of the Lord 1410.

Nicholas, monk of the monastery of the Holy Cross in Austria, of the Cistercian Order, German by nation, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and rich in reading of the ancients, of excellent talent and clear eloquence, wrote certain useful treatises not to be despised, by which he transmitted the memory of his talent to posterity. Of these the following are reported: a work not to be rejected in praise of the most blessed Mother of God and Virgin Mary, useful to preachers, which he entitled:

Image of Saint Mary. “The name of the Virgin Mary.” Various Sermons, 3 books. 1 book.

The Abbot of Sponheim.

The remaining works, although many are reported that he composed, have by no means come down to us.

Bartholomaeus of Urbino, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of St. Augustine, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, a diligent investigator of the works of the holy fathers, wrote volumes not to be despised, of which the following are preserved: from the minor works of Saint Ambrose and Augustine he compiled into one work, with singular zeal, according to alphabetical order, to which he gave the title

The Thousand Sayings of Augustine, one book.

The Thousand Sayings of Ambrose, one book.

On Spiritual Warfare, one book.

And several other things.

He flourished in the times of Rupert, king of the Romans, and of Pope Gregory XII, in the year of the Lord 1410.

Franciscus de Platea, of the Order of Minors of St. Francis, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, notably instructed both in law and in secular philosophy, excellent in talent, an outstanding declaimer of sermons, is said to have composed by lamplight many distinguished minor works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with praise to posterity. Of their number the following are reported: an excellent and distinguished work which he entitled

On Restitutions, one book.

Whether Restitution Is [unclear] from Censures, one book.

Various Sermons, [unclear] books.

But the rest that he composed have not come to the knowledge of our reading.

Peter of Candia, Cretan by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor, first bishop of Novara, then archbishop of Milan, afterward cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, finally supreme pontiff, named Alexander V, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, magnificently instructed in scholastic philosophy, a very celebrated declaimer of sermons, who once presided over the public school in the University of Paris, by teaching and writing acquired great and immense praise. From his minor works there survive clear and useful commentaries:

On the Sentences, four books.

Various Sermons, one book.

And certain other things.

He died in the last year of Rupert, king of the Romans, and was buried in the convent of the Minors at Bologna, in the year of the Lord 1409, in the third indiction,

[unclear]

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

[unclear]

Franciscus de Bachone, a Catalan by homeland, of the Order of the Brothers of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, of the convent of Gerona, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, was so strong in teaching and disputing in the University of Paris that he was surnamed the Sublime Doctor. Among other monuments of his talent he wrote a great and distinguished work from the writings of the holy fathers, quite useful to declaimers of sermons to the people, which we may entitle

Repertory of Preachers, four books.

It is reported besides that he wrote certain other things also, but they have not come into our hands.

Michael Herbrant of Düren, of the Order of the Brothers of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, German by nation, lecturer in sacred theology and prior of the convent of Kreuznach in the diocese of Mainz, a learned man and so distinguished a declaimer that, summoned not only in the vicinity but also to remote places and cathedral churches, he preached while held in admiration by all. He enjoyed great intimacy and authority with Johann, the last count of Sponheim, and obtained from him many benefits for his convent. Among other things he wrote elegant

Sermons on the Season, one book.

Sermons on the Saints, one book.

Synodal Collations, one book.

And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of Rupert, king of the Romans, and Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1410.

Peter of Speyer, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of St. Augustine, German by nation, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and magnificently instructed in secular philosophy, outstanding in talent and clear in eloquence, of very celebrated reputation in declaiming sermons to the people, wrote certain distinguished minor works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Of their number are reported

Sermons on the Season, one book.

Sermons on the Saints, one book.

On the Books of the Ethics, two books.

But the other things that he composed have not yet come to the knowledge of our reading.

Reinardus of Fronthoven, German by nation, of the Order, as they report, of the Friars Preachers, a man zealous in the divine writings and skilled through long practice, and not ignorant of secular literature, wrote minor works not to be rejected by preachers of the word of God, by which he made his name known also to posterity. Of these I have seen only

Ser-

The Abbot of Spanheim.

Sermons on the Temporal Cycle, 1 book. Of the others I have seen nothing. Sermons on the Saints, 1 book. He flourished, as his associates say, in the convent at Koblenz, where he died.

John Capreolus, of the Order of Friars Preachers, by country a Toulousain, a man learned in sacred writings, excellently trained in the disciplines of Aristotelian philosophy, acute in intellect, sufficiently fit for disputation, a most zealous champion and defender of the sayings of St. Thomas Aquinas, wrote very distinguished memorials of his talent, by which he made his name known. Of these many volumes are extant: On the Sentences, 4 books. And various sermons, 1 book. And certain other works. He flourished under Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1415.

Henry of Coesfeld, by nation a German, of the Carthusian Order, prior of the house of St. Mary near Mount St. Gertrude in Holland, a man most learned in divine scriptures, devout in life and conduct, of great reputation, subtle in intellect, clearer in speech, and also a very celebrated declaimer of sermons, wrote many excellent volumes, the frequent reading of which is judged useful for devout brothers who love their salvation. Of these the following are reported: On Exodus Mystically, 1 book. On Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, 1 book. On the Three Substantial Vows, 1 book. Do Not Love the World. Against the Vice of Possession, 1 book. On the Annunciation of the Lord, 1 book. A Eulogy of Paul the Hermit, 1 book. The Mystical Circumcisorium, 1 book. On the Sacrament of the Altar, 1 book. Letters to Various Persons, 1 book. And several other works.

The work of William, bishop of Paris, On the Bodily and Incorporeal or Spiritual Universe, which surveys it with wonderful industry, he beautifully brought to a conclusion in a brief compendium. He died in the house of the Valley of Grace near Bruges, beneficially occupied in the act of visitation, in the times of Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 140[unclear], in the seventh indiction, on the Ides of July.

Henry [unclear]

283 On Ecclesiastical Writers.

[unclear]

Henry of Hachenburg, of the Order of Friars Preachers, by nation a German, a man magnificently exercised and well instructed in divine writings, of excellent talent and very celebrated reputation in delivering sermons to the people, wrote volumes not to be rejected for the guidance of simple priests. Of these there are extant: Sermons on the Temporal Cycle, 1 book. “I shall come and heal.” Sermons on the Saints, 2 books. He flourished, as his associates report, in the convent at Koblenz, where he composed various works.

[unclear] Jordanus, of the Order of the Friars of St. Augustine of the Hermitage, by nation a German, a devout man and an excellent expounder and interpreter of the divine scriptures, of most excellent talent in delivering sermons, wrote several elegant and devout treatises useful to the brothers, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these, however, few have come into our hands. The following are reported: On the Apocalypse of John, 1 book. An Apology for His Order, 1 book. On the Passion of the Lord: “Look and do according to...” Sermons on the Saints, 1 book. A Lenten Book: “Behold, he will give to his voice...” Various Questions, 2 books. And many other works. He flourished under King Rupert, in the year of the Lord 1410.

[unclear] Peter, bishop of Novigrad, by nation an Italian, from the town of Bruniquellus, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of St. Augustine, a man most learned in divine scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, outstanding in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, published several useful little works, by which, through his magnificently exercised talent, he commended his memory to posterity. Of these the following are reported: A certain notable work, in which he arranged all the histories of the New and Old Testament in alphabetical order and disposed them according to individual subjects. On the Sentences, 1 book. On the Proverbs of Solomon, 2 books. Also on Ecclesiastes, 2 books. On the Song of Songs, 2 books. And many other works. Moreover, he is said to have adorned almost the whole Bible with excellent commentaries. He flourished under Rupert, king of the Romans, in the year 1410.

Lau

The Abbot of Sponheim.

Laurentius Justinianus, a Venetian by nation, of the Celestine order, and learned, distinguished in character and life, although he could have had the very greatest riches and honors of this world, despising all things for the love of Christ, entered the aforesaid order. In it, shining with great religious devotion and abstinence, he published, for the edification of the simple, very devout little works, whose titles are given below:

The Tree of Life, 1 book. On Monastic Discipline, 1 book. On the Marriage of the Word and the Soul, 1 book. On the Agony of Christ, 1 book. On the Interior [Conflict?], 1 book. On the Lamentation of the Church, 1 book. On the Sacrament of the Altar, 1 book. On the Solitary Life, 1 book. On Contempt of the World, 1 book. On the Lord's Sermon at Supper, 1 book. On the Pastoral Office, 1 book. On Obedience also, 1 book. On the Degrees of Perfection, 1 book. Forty Sermons, 1 book.

He flourished in the time of Rupert, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1410. He is buried at Venice in the cathedral church, at whose tomb many miracles are divinely performed. Bernardus Justinianus, his nephew, wrote his life lucidly.

Augustinus of Rome, of the order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, prior general, a man most devoted to the divine scriptures and very learned, and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, outstanding in talent and renowned in eloquence, wrote many excellent volumes, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there are extant:

On the Sentences, 4 books. On all the Epistles of Paul, 14 books. On the Apocalypse of John, 1 book. On Free Will, 1 book. On Original Sin, 1 book. On Christ and the Church, 1 book. On the Charity of Christ toward the Elect, 1 book. On the Perfect Justice of the Church, 1 book. On the Power of the Pope, 1 book. On the Books of the Ethics, 8 books.

He is said to have written many other things besides, but they have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the time of the emperor Sigismund and Pope John XXIII, in the year of the Lord 1410.

Baldus of Perugia, once the hearer and disciple of Bartolus de Saxoferrato, the most celebrated jurist of all his time, and also nobly learned in secular philosophy, sharp in talent, profound in judgment, cautious and steadfast in counsel, wrote many distinguished little works in both laws, by which he obtained for his name everlasting memory among posterity.

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

Among their number the following are given:

On the Codex, 9 books. On the Old Digest, 14 books. On the New Digest, 12 books. On the Infortiatum, 14 books. On the Institutes, 4 books. On the Use of Fiefs, 1 book. On the Authentics, 1 book. On the Second Book of the Decretals, 1 book. Additions to the Speculum, 1 book. Many Consilia, 1 book. And several other things.

He died in the time of the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1423, in the first indiction, and was buried with honor at Pavia, in the convent of the Friars Minor of Saint Francis, in the month of July.

Angelus of Perugia, brother of the aforesaid Baldus and companion and associate in his studies, most learned in civil law, renowned in talent, most celebrated in fame and reputation among jurists, also composed many volumes in his faculty. By establishing monuments of excellent talent through them, he destined the memory of his name for the knowledge of many. Among their number the following most elegant commentaries are given:

On the Codex, 9 books. On the Old Digest, 24 books. On the New Digest, 12 books. On the Infortiatum, 14 books. On the Institutes, 4 books.

Indeed he is said to have worked through the whole body of civil law, and certain other things as well. He died in the time of the emperor Sigismund, in the same year as Baldus his brother, in the year of the Lord 1423, in the first indiction.

[Unclear], formerly a hearer of Perusinus, a man most skilled in both laws and not ignorant of Aristotelian philosophy, who, although he had been bound by the tie of a wife and occupied with family affairs, nevertheless was always engaged in the study of letters, published many little works in both laws, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. Among their number are given:

On the Decretals, 5 books. On the Sixth Book of the Decretals, 1 book. On the Clementines, 1 book. On the Rules of Law, 1 book. On the Old Digest, 24 books. On the New Digest, 1 book. Several Consilia, 1 book. And certain other things.

He flourished in the time of the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1410, the compater of Franciscus de Zabarellis.

Vincentius Gruner, a German by nation, a man learned in the divine scriptures and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, renowned in talent, scholastic in speech, published little works of reading not to be despised, by which he [unclear] his name with glory to the knowledge of later

The Abbot of Spanheim.

sent. Of these there survives a notable lecture, which he publicly wrote and read before the scholars at the new foundation of the Leipzig academy:

On the Office of the Mass, 3 books, “To the honor of the blessed ...” Disputed Questions, 1 book. And certain other works.

He flourished at the time of the transfer of the University of Prague to Leipzig, in the province of the margraviate of Meissen; Alexander V, pope, confirming it, endowed it with privileges in the year of the Lord 1410.

Johannes de Aurbach, a German by nationality, priest of the church of Bamberg, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, distinguished in talent, scholastic in speech, published little works of no slight authority, by which he preserved the memory of his name for posterity. Of these I have seen only the distinguished work:

On the Sacraments of the Church, 1 book, “To the praise of God, of souls ...”

Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished in the city of Bamberg and wrote various little works.

Dionysius de Burgo sancti sepulchri, of the order of the hermit brothers of the divine father Augustine, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and most learned in secular letters, subtle in talent and eloquent in an accomplished style, wrote little works not to be despised in each branch of literature, by which he left to posterity lasting monuments of his talent. Among them the following are reported:

Very beautiful and elegant commentaries: On Valerius Maximus, 1 book. On the Metamorphoses, 1 book. On the works of Virgil, 1 book. On the tragedies of Seneca, 1 book. On the Politics, 1 book. On the Rhetoric, 1 book. And certain other works.

Moreover he reduced all fables to a pleasing tropological sense.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1412.

Petrus de Aliaco, bishop of Cambrai and cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, formerly chancellor of the Paris academy, teacher of Johannes de Gerson, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular letters, especially in Aristotelian philosophy, excellent in talent and distinguished in eloquence, and also an outstanding declaimer of sermons, wrote many distinguished volumes, by which he left to posterity the memory of his name and talent. Of these I have found the following:

On the Sentences, 2 books, “What doctrine is this ...” On the Praise of Holy Scripture, 1 book, “Upon this rock I shall build ...” On the Beginning of Mark, 1 book, “What doctrine is this ...” On the [unclear] of the Church, 3 books, “Whether the church of Peter ...”

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

Mirror of Consideration, 3 books. Compendium of Contemplation, 3 books. On the Spiritual Ladder, 1 book. Briefly on the Psalter, 1 book. Meditations on Psalm 70, 1 book. On Laws and Sects, 1 book. On a General Council, 1 book. Exposition of Psalm 70, 1 book. Meditations on Psalm 42, 1 book. On the Song of Songs, 1 book. On the Seven Penitential Psalms, 1 book. On the Lord’s Prayer, 1 book. On the Same Anagogically, 1 book. On the Ave Maria, 1 book. On the Magnificat, 1 book. On the Canticle of Zacharias, 1 book. On the Canticle of Simeon, 1 book. On the Election of the Pope, 1 book. On Spiritual Exercise, 1 book. On the Twelve Honors of Saint Joseph, 1 book. On the Soul and Its Accidents, 1 book. Concord of Theology and Astronomy, 2 books. On the Sacraments of the Church, 1 book. Various Sermons, 1 book. Several Letters to Various Persons, 1 book. And certain other works.

He flourished at the time of the Council of Constance, at which he was also personally present, in the year of the Lord 1416.

Nicolaus Clemengis, archdeacon of Bayeux, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly instructed in secular letters, excellent in verse and prose, having obtained the mastership of sacred page in the Paris academy, gave great evidence of his learning. He wrote many distinguished volumes in both styles, by which he left the memory of his most brilliant talent. Among them the following are reported:

To the lord Petrus de Aliaco, bishop of Cambrai, the aforesaid cardinal, a notable work which he entitled:

On the Fruit of the Hermitage, 1 book. On the Corrupt State of the Church, 1 book. On New Feast Days, 1 book. On the Matter of the Schism, 1 book.

Letters

The Abbot of Sponheim.

Letters to various persons, one book. And many other things. He flourished in the times of the emperor Sigismund and of the Council of Constance, in the year of the Lord 1417.

John Dominici, cardinal of the title of Saint Sixtus, commonly called Ragusan, a Florentine by birth, of the Order of Friars Preachers, who was sent by Pope Gregory XII by provision to the Council of Constance, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people, wrote certain distinguished volumes by which he made his name known to posterity. Among them the following are reported:

On Ecclesiastes, one book. On the Song of Songs, one book. On the Gospel of Matthew, one book. On the Magnificat, one book. On the Epistle to the Romans, one book. Entitled Lucula noctis, one book. Itinerary of Devotion, one book. On the Love of Charity, one book. “If I speak with the tongues of men” Sermons on the season, one book. Sermons on the saints, one book. Sermons through Lent, one book. “Blessed is the man who has not gone away” And certain other things.

He died in the Council of Constance under the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1418, in the second indiction.

John, bishop of [Lombaria?], a German by nation, a native of Basel, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently trained in secular philosophy, outstanding in talent and renowned for eloquence, a very celebrated deliverer of sermons, produced little works of reading not to be despised, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with praise to the knowledge of posterity. Of their number the principal are reported:

On the Sentences, one book. Various sermons, one book. And certain other things.

Besides this, he is said to have delivered many speeches and conferences to the clergy, and also before the supreme pontiff and the assembly of cardinals, which I have not seen.

John Zacharias, a German by nation, a native of Erfurt, a man very studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, also an excellent interpreter of secular philosophy, subtle in talent, a most acute disputant, very suitable in delivering sermons both to the clergy and to the people, wrote certain distinguished little works by which he made his name known. Among them are reported:

On the Sentences, four books. On Genesis, one book. On Exodus, one book. On Leviticus, one book. On the epistles of Paul, fourteen books. Various sermons, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished under the emperor Sigismund, and in the Council of Constance was magnificently praised for disputing against the heretics, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Antonio de Butrio, an Italian by nation, a native of Bologna, easily the most celebrated jurist of all in his time, and excellently learned in other writings, both divine and human, renowned in talent and eloquence, and venerable no less for honorable conduct than for learning, published several little works in law, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Among their number the following are reported:

On the Decretals, five books. On the Clementines, one book. Repertory of Canon Law, one book. Repertory of Civil Law, one book. Most elegant Counsels, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Sigismund and of the general Council of Constance, in the year of the Lord 1417.

Gabriel of Spoleto, of the Order of Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, excellent in talent and an outstanding deliverer of sermons, wrote some commendable little works, by which he showed also to posterity the knowledge of his lively talent. But I have not deserved to see any of them up to now. Nevertheless, the principal works of his are reported:

Against the Heretics, one book. Against the Fraticelli, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of the Council of Constance and of the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1417.

Francesco Zabarella, a Paduan by nation, cardinal priest of the Roman Church, a man most learned in canon law, and nobly trained both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, subtle in talent and renowned for eloquence, wrote in law little works not to be scorned, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity.

The Abbot of Sponheim.

is made. Of their number the following are reported:

On the Decretals, one book. On the Clementines, one book. “That nothing new is [unclear].” On the canonical hours, one book. “About to repeat the decretal.” Various repetitions. And many other things.

He flourished at the Council of Constance under Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1418. There also he died, and was buried among the Friars Minor. In his praise Poggio delivered an oration.

Peter Maurocenus, a Venetian patrician, bishop-cardinal of the sacrosanct Roman Church, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and in canon law, and not ignorant of secular letters, is known to have fashioned, by his excellent talent, many excellent little works, in which the liveliness of his intellect shines forth. But I have not deserved to see any of them up to the present. There is reported as his notable volume:

On the Sixth Book of the Decretals, one book. And various determinations.

He flourished in person at the Council of Constance, under Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1413.

Nicholas of Dinkelsbuhl, German by birth, ornament and rector of the University of Vienna in Austria, most learned in the holy Scriptures, very erudite in secular philosophy, distinguished in talent, scholastic in discourse, outstanding in life and conduct, wrote many excellent volumes, by which he transmits his name to posterity with glory. Of their number the following are reported:

On the Sentences, four books. Questions on the Sentences, one book. On the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, one book. “It is written in Matthew 22.” On the Ten Commandments, one book. “If you ask the Father for anything.” On the Lord’s Prayer. “In the Gospel which is read.” On the eight beatitudes, one book. “Next it must be said.” On the three parts of penance, one book. “There are two commandments of charity.” Sermons on the season, one book. “It should be noted that, as is said.” one book. “Consequently it must be said.” one book. “There are two commandments of charity.” one book. Ser- one book. “Consequently it must be said.” one book. “It should be noted that, as is said.” one book. On sins of the tongue. one book. “Which are the commandments of charity.” one book. And on mortal sins. one book. “Which are the commandments of charity.” one book. And on all the capital vices. one book. “Which are the constant commandments.” one book. And on every mortal sin. one book. “Which are many times commandments.” one book. And on the four virtues. one book. “Which are many commandments.” one book. And on all good things. one book. “Which are very many commandment-.” one book. And on pathetic blessedness. one book. “Which are dangers and peniten-.” one book. And on grace and merit. one book. “Which are exhortations and.” one book. And on fidelity and the word-. one book. “Which are teachings and [unclear].” one book. And on penance and indulgence. one book. “Which are commandments and confe-.” one book. And on charity and justice. one book. “Which are examples and admoni-.” one book. And on mortal sin and di-. one book. “Which are sermons and prayers.” one book. And on spiritual sin and in-. one book. “Which are virtues and vices.” one book. And on confession and penan-. one book. “Which are sacraments and all [unclear].” one book. And on purification and salvo-. one book. “Which are virtues and defects.” one book. And on indulgence and grace. one book. “Which are many times commandment-.” one book. And on blessedness and virtue. one book. “Which are many exhortatio-.” one book. And on merit and grace. one book. “Which are teachings and [unclear].” one book. And on penance and indulgen-. one book. “Which are dangers and pene-.” one book. And on charities and justice. one book. “Which are examples and admoni-.” one book. And on mortal sins and di-. one book. “Which are examples and admo-.” one book. And on spiritual sin and in-. one book. “Which are virtues and defec-.” one book. And on confession and penance. one book. “Which are sacraments and all-.” one book. And on purification and salvo-. one book. “Which are virtues and defectio-.” one book. And on indulgence and grace.

On Ecclesiastical Writers

Sermons on the saints, one book. Moral sermons, one book. And many other works.

He was personally prominent at the Council of Constance, having been sent by the University of Vienna, under Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Peter of Rosenheim, a monk of the monastery of Melk in Austria, of the Order of St. Benedict, German by nation, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and magnificently instructed in secular letters, an outstanding philosopher and poet, ready and distinguished in talent, produced both in verse and in prose little works not to be cast aside, in which he properly exercised his talent. Among these there is extant a metrical work which he wrote, at the urging and request of Nicholas [Dinkelsbuhl?], to Lord Branda, cardinal of St. Clement, apostolic legate in Austria, on the chapters of the whole Bible, which he entitled

The Rosy Memorial of Divine Things, one book. The star-ruling [one], heaven, earth...

A Notable History of the Times, one book.

Various Sermons, one book.

He flourished in the time of the Council of Constance, in the year of the Lord 1420, and composed many and various works.

Raphael Fulgosius, from Piacenza by nation, a man most learned in both laws and well instructed in the precepts of secular philosophy, excellent in talent, cautious and steadfast in counsel, produced certain distinguished volumes in civil law, by which he displayed the force and liveliness of his talent even to posterity. Among these the following are reported:

On the Code, nine books. On the Old Digest, twenty-four books.

On the New Digest, twelve books. Many Legal Opinions, one book.

And certain other works.

He flourished in the time of the Council of Constance and of Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1416.

John of Palomar, archdeacon of the church of Barcelona, an eminent doctor of the Decrees, and nobly learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, subtle in talent, scholastic in speech, distinguished in life and conduct, produced little works of reading not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these there is extant a distinguished treatise to John, abbot of the monastery of the Scots of the Order of St. Benedict at Vienna:

On Abstinence from Meat, one book. The sons will rise in judgment...

Sermons and Questions.

The rest that he composed have by no means come to the knowledge of my reading.

The Abbot of Spanheim

He flourished at the university of Vienna in Austria, and composed many works in the time of Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Raphael Cumanus, eminent professor of civil law and a very celebrated interpreter, excellent in talent and outstanding in counsel, whose authority among jurists is by no means slight, wrote in that faculty certain distinguished little works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Among these the following are reported:

On the Code, nine books. On the Old Digest, twenty-four books.

Also Legal Opinions, one book. And several other works.

He flourished under Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1416.

John of Teneramunda, a man zealous and very learned in the divine Scriptures, devout in life and conduct, distinguished in talent, ordered in speech, produced very useful little works for the edification of religious brothers, by which he instructed not only those then present, but also those who would come after him, in the love of God. And they are these:

On the Knowledge of God, one book. On the Nature and Fall of Man, one book.

On the Restoration of the Fallen, one book. On the Love of God, one book.

On the Joy of Man, one book. On the Sacrament of the Altar, one book.

On the Christian Faith, one book. On the Honor of God, one book.

On the Conception of Saint Mary, one book.

He also elegantly composed many other works, which have not come to my knowledge.

Gasparinus, a very celebrated grammarian, from Bergamo by native place, born in the little village of Barzizza, a man most learned in secular letters, a most outstanding philosopher and rhetorician, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, who called back from the dead the elegance of Latin speech, half-dead as it was: he wrote many distinguished little works in that faculty, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Among these there are extant:

On Orthography, one book.

Letters to Various Persons, one book. I rejoice very greatly and [am glad]...

Various Orations, one book.

On the Letters of Cicero, one book.

On the same author’s On Duties, one book.

On the same author’s On the Orator, one book.

On the same author’s On Old Age, one book.

And certain other works.

He flourished in the time of the Council of Constance and of Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1430.

298 On Ecclesiastical Writers

Antonius of Genoa, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of St. Augustine, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, and a professor and very celebrated interpreter of canon law, outstanding in ability and distinguished in eloquence, wrote certain small works of reading not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name with praise to posterity. But I have not had the privilege of seeing any of them, except that which is entitled: Compendium of Moral Figures, one book. The rest have not come to me. “To religious men [in Christ?]...”

He flourished in person at the general Council of Constance, under Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1418.

Johannes de Mola, by homeland a Bolognese, a very celebrated doctor of both laws, excellent in ability and distinguished in eloquence, whose learning and eloquence in his time splendidly illuminated all Italy, is said to have published many distinguished volumes in both laws, whose authority is extolled with the highest praises among the professors of this faculty. Among these the following are reported first:

On the Three Books of the Decretals, one book.

On the Sixth Book of the Decretals, one book.

On the ff. Infortiatum, fourteen books.

On the ff. Novum: “Before we come to...”

And certain others.

He died at Bologna in the times of Emperor Sigismund and Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1435, indiction 14.

Antonius of Parma, prior general of the Camaldolese Order, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular literature, excellent in ability, composed in speech, sufficiently fit in delivering sermons to the people, wrote for the direction of preachers of the word of God several distinguished small works, by which he made his name known. Of these the chief are reported:

Sermons on the Season, one book. “When he had drawn near...”

Sermons on the Saints, one book.

Sermons through Lent, one book.

And certain others.

He was present in person at the Council of Constance, under Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Leonardo Aretino, an eminent philosopher, orator, and historian, a man in every respect most learned, skilled in Greek and Latin speech,

The Abbot of Sponheim.

[Leonardus Aretinus?], first secretary to Innocent VII, Gregory XII, Alexander V, and John XXIII, Roman pontiffs, down to the Council of Constance, and then summoned by the Florentine senate, was appointed general chancellor; in that office he remained until the end of his life with great fidelity and authority. Among other things he wrote an outstanding work of Dialogues, 1 book; A History of His Own Time; On the Good Deeds of the Florentines, 2 books; On the Praises of Florence; A History of the Goths, 4 books; A History of the Punic War, 2 books; The Life of Aristotle, 1 book; On the Life of Cicero, 1 book; A Volume of Letters, 1 book.

He also composed some other works most elegantly, which have not come to my knowledge. Moreover he translated many things from Greek into Latin: namely, the treatise of the blessed priest Basil On the Instruction of Pupils; also, from Plutarch, the lives of Tiberius and Gracchus among the Greeks, and of Paulus Aemilius, Cato the Younger, and Sertorius among the Romans. He likewise translated Xenophon’s little book On the Tyrant, Plato’s Gorgias and Phaedo, and certain letters, Aristotle’s Economics, and the books of the Ethics and Politics. And other things which have not come to me.

He flourished in person at the Council of Constance under the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420. He died, however, under Frederick III as emperor and Eugene IV as pope, in the year of the Lord 1443, in the sixth indiction, on the seventh Ides of March, in about the seventy-fourth year of his age.

Poggio the Florentine, a philosopher and eloquent orator, perfectly trained in Greek and Latin speech, and for many years a most eloquent writer of apostolic letters, is said to have composed some little works of excellent talent, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Lorenzo Valla was this Poggio’s most bitter rival, and wrote various things against him. He himself published: On the Situation of the Region of India, 1 book; Against Lorenzo Valla, 2 books; Letters to Various Persons, 1 book; Various Orations, 1 book; and many other things.

He rendered Dionysius Siculus and many other Greek authors into Latin. Moreover, at the Council of Constance he delivered very many funeral orations. The filthy work which he entitled Facetiae I have judged rightly to be excluded from this catalogue of illustrious men, since the reading of it offends the devout, harms the unwary, and infects the carnal.

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

He flourished in person at the Council of Constance under the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Lorenzo Valla, a Roman patrician, by far the foremost of the grammarians of this age, a most outstanding philosopher, orator, and theologian, subtle in intellect, sharp, and vehement, who, preferring Latin eloquence to Greek, composed many works for its adornment, and, being most skilled in Greek and Latin speech, published little works not to be despised in reading, by which he transmitted his name with praise to the knowledge of posterity. Among these the following are reported: Elegances, 6 books; On the Reciprocity of sui and suus, 1 book; A Book of Many Letters, 1 book; also On Quintilian, 12 books; Dialectic, 1 book; Panegyric On the True Good, [unclear] books; On Free Will, 1 book; Apologue against Poggio, [unclear] book; Against Antonio da Rho, 1 book; and many other things.

“When often with me the elders,” 1 book. “You alone, Johannes,” 1 book. “When I was undertaking, Paul,” 1 book. “I would very much wish, Garzia,” 1 book. “I hear that Poggio another,” 1 book.

He translated into Latin Homer, Thucydides, and several others.

He flourished in person at the Council of Constance under the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1429. Concerning him someone says as follows: What did that most biting censor of the Latin language, Lorenzo Valla, beget for himself by his dreadful and exacting reproof? What praise, I ask, did he obtain after death other than that, according to his merits, that fine epigram about him is read and proclaimed everywhere?

Now after Valla, dead, sought the shades, Pluto does not dare to speak Latin words. Jupiter would have deemed him worthy of heaven’s honor, But he himself fears him as censor of his tongue.

What he thought about the Donation of Constantine, by which Constantine endowed the Roman church, his book beautifully shows; would that so great a man had never published it.

Giovanni Tortelli, by nation an Aretine, a very close friend of Lorenzo Valla, to whom Valla wrote the six books of the Elegances of the Latin Language; subdeacon and chamberlain of the Roman pontiff, and afterward companion of Pope Nicholas and an intimate associate of his studies,

The Abbot of Sponheim.

a count, perfectly trained in Greek and Latin letters, a very celebrated philosopher, rhetorician, and theologian. Among other little works of his talent he wrote a large and distinguished volume, which he entitled Commentaries on Grammar, one book.

Also On Dialectic, one book.

He published various letters, one book.

And many other things.

He translated the Life of Athanasius of Alexandria into Latin for Pope Eugenius, and rendered the historian Appian word for word. And other things.

He flourished under the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Hermann Petra of Stutdorp, of the Carthusian order, a German by nation, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, devout in life and conduct, vicar and rector of the house of nuns of his order, of Saint Anne near Bruges in Flanders, where for twenty-nine years he was distinguished by much religion and learning, wrote certain devout little works of his talent. Of these the following are reported: a notable work divided into six volumes over the cycle of the year, containing

Sermons on the Season, one book.

Sermons on the Saints, one book.

Fifty sermons On the Lord’s Prayer, one book.

On the Governance of Nuns, one book.

And very many other things.

He died under the emperor Sigismund and Pope Martin V, in the year of the Lord 1428, on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, in the sixth indiction.

[Guarinus Veronensis?], perfectly trained in Greek and Latin eloquence, the most celebrated philosopher and rhetorician of all in his time, once at Venice a pupil of Manuel Chrysoloras of Constantinople, who brought Greek letters back into Italy, wrote many distinguished volumes, by which he left the memory of himself to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On Cicero’s Orator, one book. “How much of Cicero’s ora-” [unclear] “In explaining this au-” [unclear]

On the Poet Lucan, one book.

On Quintilian, one book.

In Praise of Eloquence, one book. “How much admiration” [unclear]

Many orations.

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

And he published very many other things, which have not yet come into our hands.

He flourished under the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Henry of Hesse the Younger, of the Carthusian order, prior of the house of the monks of Mary, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, published many very elegant volumes, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity; and he publicly lectured on many of them in the universities before his entry into religion. Of these the following are reported:

On the Sentences, four books.

On Genesis, one book.

On Exodus, one book.

On the Proverbs of Solomon, one book.

On the Apocalypse of John, one book.

A Dialogue between a Bishop and a Priest, one book.

Useful Sermons, one book.

And certain other things.

He died under the emperor Sigismund and Pope Martin V, in the year of the Lord 1428, in the sixth indiction.

John Gerson, a Frenchman by nation, chancellor of Paris, formerly a disciple of Peter of Ailly, cardinal of Cambrai, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, sure and firm in judgment, cautious in counsel, and a very distinguished interpreter of doubtful matters, outstanding in life and conduct, by far the foremost of the theologians of his time, wrote in verse and prose many most excellent little works, through which his name will always possess immortality among posterity; the reading of them is no less useful than pleasant to devout and religious men. Of these there is extant:

On the Praise of Scribes, one book. “To search the Scriptures”

On the Harmony of the Evangelists, one book. “That the Gospel was brought”

On Ecclesiastical Power, one book. “Ecclesiastical power de-” [unclear]

On the Removability of the Bridegroom, one book. “But the days will come when”

On the Manner of Conducting Oneself in Schism, one book. “For the removal of certain” [unclear]

On Ecclesiastical Unity, one book. “Ecclesiastical unity” [unclear]

On Ecclesiastical Estates, one book. “The peace which all”

On the Manner of Living of the Faithful, one book. “The first rule which”

On Ecclesiastical Defects, one book. “Perhaps it is said to me, Ec-” [unclear]
