On Ecclesiastical Writers.

On nocturnal pollution, one book. “It was doubted by me.” On diurnal pollution, one book. “I wrote some things earlier.” On the chastity of ecclesiastics, one book. “There are eunuchs who made themselves.” On abstinence from meats, one book. “Great and wondrous is.” On the temperance of prelates, one book. “Already in one earlier reading.” On the life of clerics, one book. “Repent, believe.” On humility, one book. “From God it came forth, to God.” One book. “A certain noble man.” On nobility, one book. “King of kings, kindly Jesus.” On the consideration of a prince, one book. “Soldiers in the desert.” A dialogue of two soldiers, one book. “Whatever things have been written.” On the consolation of theology, one book. “A thing [unclear], O Monica.” An apologetic dialogue, one book. “They have been accustomed [to seek] the source.” Josephina, in verse, one book. “Conceived of a virgin.” A centiloquy on concepts, one book. “I baptized you with water.” One book. “He has put down the mighty from.” A centiloquy on impulses, eight books. “Repent, believe.” On mystical theology, one book. “Treating in the readings.” On the same, practical, one book. “To you it has been given to know.” An elucidation of the same, one book. “Grace to you, peace.” On the perfection of religion, one book. “The meditation of my heart.” On the meditation of the heart, one book. “In simplicity of heart.” On simplicity of heart, one book. On direction of the heart, one book. “I will confess to you in uprightness.” On the illumination of the heart, one book. “The kingdom of heaven is like.” Also on the eye, one book. “The disciples rejoiced.” Against faintheartedness, one book. “He who is fainthearted.” On the various temptations of the devil, one book. “To us under the hand of God.” On discretion in exercise, one book. “God wills that there be reason.” On the passions of the soul, one book. “Passion, fervor.” On the perfection of the heart, two books. “You shall love the Lord your God.” On the mountain of contemplation, one book. “Some perhaps will wonder.” On spiritual beggary, one book. “All my poverty, my weakness.” On the value of prayer, one book. “One must always pray.” On the Song of Songs, one book. “We have sung to you, and.” On the Magnificat, twelve [readings?]. “Treating the song of Mary.” A poem on the same, one book. “My soul magnifies.” On the angelic hymn, one book. “Glory to God in the highest.” On the Song of Songs, one book. “I love you, sacred order, dear [unclear].”

Abbot of Spanheim.

On the Marriage of Wisdom, 4 books. “I sought a bride for myself.” On the Twofold Logic, 2 books. “And John was clothed.” To the Rectors of Boys, 1 book. “Allow the little children to come.” Sermons in the Council of Constance, 1 book. “Walk while you have the light [unclear].” Sermons to the Clergy, 1 book. [unclear] Sermons to the People, 1 book. Dialogue on Any Subject, 1 book. Several Letters to Various Persons, 1 book. He also published many other smaller works, indeed, but very useful, of which certain knowledge has not come down to us.

He was personally prominent in the Council of Constance, in which, laboring gloriously for the extirpation of heresies, at last, after it was dissolved, he was deprived of home, country, relatives, friends, dignities, and his own possessions for the defense of the truth, and was sought by many plots. Hence, compelled by necessity, he fled to the city of Lyons, and there after a few years he died, under Emperor Sigismund and Pope Martin V, in the year of the Lord 1429, in the seventh indiction, in the sixty-sixth year of his age, on the fourth day before the Ides of July, and was buried there with honor among the Celestines.

Vincent Ferrer of Valencia, of the Order of Friars Preachers, to whom some letters of John Gerson are extant, a man most learned in the divine scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, subtle in talent and distinguished in eloquence, devout in morals and conduct, and the most celebrated preacher of sermons of all in his time, shining with miracles while alive and after death, wrote elegant works:

Sermons on the Season, 1 book. “Blessed is he who comes in...” Sermons on the Saints, 1 book. “He is rich toward all who...” Sermons throughout Lent, 1 book. Certain Letters.

He was personally prominent in the Council of Constance, in the year of the Lord 1418. After his death, because of his frequent miracles, he was canonized by Pope Callistus III, in the year of the Lord 1455, in the third indiction. His feast is in April [unclear].

Boniface Ferrer of Valencia, a Catalan by birth, twenty-fifth prior of the Carthusian Order, brother of the aforesaid Blessed Vincent the Preacher, a man learned in the divine scriptures and an outstanding doctor of canon law, not unlike his holy brother in life and conduct, governed the Grande Chartreuse vigorously by word and example. Among other things he wrote a noteworthy treatise on why few in the Carthusian Order have been canonized and why they do not publicly perform miracles:

To Boniface of the Same Order, 1 book. On the Approbation of the Order, 1 book. Certain Letters. And many other things.

He was prominent in the times of Emperor Sigismund and Pope Martin V, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Lupus of Oliveto, a Spaniard by birth, prior general of the Order of Hermit Monks of Saint Jerome, a man devoted to and learned in the divine scriptures, and an outstanding restorer of his order, wrote several excellent little works by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these are reported:

From the Sayings of Saint Jerome, The Rule of His Order, 1 book. Sermons on the Saints, 1 book. And certain other works.

This rule, newly compiled in thirty-three chapters, Martin V confirmed.

He was prominent at the time of the Council of Constance, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Dominic of San Gimignano, a most excellent jurist, and nobly learned both in the divine writers and in the other secular disciplines, subtle in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote certain excellent volumes on canon law, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there is extant a notable and very celebrated work, divided into two volumes:

On the Sixth Book of the Decretals, 2 books. “Because the first gloss at the end...” And various declarations.

He also wrote a Repertory in law, and commentaries on the second and third books of the Decretals. Counsels in law by the same author.

He flourished at the same time as Paulus de Castro and John of Imola.

The rest, however, which he is said to have composed, have not come to my knowledge.

Paul of Saint Mary, a Jew by birth, a Christian by faith, first bishop of Cartagena and afterward bishop of Burgos in Spain, archchancellor of the king of Castile and Leon, a man most devoted to and very learned in the divine scriptures, and a master of sacred theology, having been converted to the Catholic faith in his mature age, advanced so far in life and doctrine that among all the doctors of Spain he had no equal in his time. He wrote to his son Alfonso de-

THE ABBOT OF SPANHEIM.

the dean of Compostela, doctor of laws, on the Postils of Nicholas of Lyra:

Notable Additions, 1 book. “What do you want for yourself, as one living”

Scrutiny of the Scriptures, 2 books. “Search the Scriptures”

And certain other things.

He flourished, and completed this Scrutiny of his, under Emperor Sigismund and Pope Eugene IV, in the year of the Lord 1454, in the twelfth indiction, in the eighty-first year of his age.

Petrus Paulus Vergerius, by country a Justinopolitan, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and very learned in secular letters, a philosopher and very celebrated rhetorician, perfectly instructed in Greek and Latin speech, once a hearer of Chrysoloras, the Byzantine philosopher teaching Greek letters at Venice, wrote certain distinguished little works of excellent talent, by which he left the memory of himself to posterity. Among these there is extant a notable work, containing, concerning the deeds of the lords of Carrara:

A very beautiful History, 1 book.

On Noble Manners, 1 book.

In Praise of Saint Jerome, 1 book.

And many other things.

He flourished at the Council of Constance, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Maphaeus Vegius, by country a man of Lodi, datary of Pope Martin V, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and outstandingly learned, and very learned in secular letters, a very celebrated orator and poet, and no less distinguished in conduct than in knowledge; through whose care and expense the remains of Saint Monica, mother of Saint Augustine, were translated from Ostia Tiberina to Rome and were laid in a new chapel built at great cost by him, in which he himself also was buried: he wrote, both in meter and in prose, certain distinguished volumes, among which there is extant a very celebrated work, necessary for all religious persons, composed from divine and human literature, addressed to certain sisters, which he entitled:

On Perseverance, 7 books. “Since grave matters often, as happens”

On the Penitential Psalms, 1 book.

In Praise of Saint Monica, 1 book.

The Thirteenth Book of the Aeneid, in heroic verse, 1 book.

Many Epigrams, 1 book.

On Military Affairs,

A Dialogue, which is called Philaletes,

Many Letters.

And very many other things.

ON ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Sigismund and Pope Martin V, in the year of the Lord 1430.

Johannes Placth, a German by nation, ornament and pillar of the Heidelberg school, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures, and nobly instructed in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in talent, scholastic in speech, distinguished in life and conduct insofar as the secular estate permits, an outstanding teacher in delivering sermons to the people: among other things he wrote a great and notable volume, which he lectured on regularly and publicly in the aforesaid University of Heidelberg:

On the first [unclear] of the Decretals, 1 book. “Venerable fathers”

Against the Bohemians, 1 book. “As the wise man says”

Questions on the Sentences, 1 book.

Several Sermons.

Various Questions.

And certain other things.

He flourished under Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1439.

Johannes Dieppurg, called de Franckfordia, a German by nation, a doctor of Heidelberg, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, a keen disputant and an outstanding expounder of sermons, formerly chaplain and secretary of Ludwig, duke of Bavaria and count palatine of the Rhine, and often an envoy in many difficult cases: he wrote little works of reading not to be scorned, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Among these the following are reported:

Against the Hussites, 1 book. “When recently in the year of the Lord”

Against the Feymeros, 1 book. “The law of the Lord outwardly [unclear]”

On Contracts, 1 book. “As in the forum of the soul where in”

On Predestination, 1 book. “Glory to God in the highest”

Many Sermons, 1 book.

An Oration before the King of England, 1 book.

An Oration before the Duke of Savoy, 1 book.

An Oration before the King of France, 1 book.

Various Questions, 1 book.

Several Letters,

Diverse Orations.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Sigismund and Pope Eugene IV, in the year of the Lord 1430.

The Abbot of Sponheim.

Raymundus Sebeide, a Spaniard by nation, a man zealous and learned in the divine scriptures, and also exceptionally well taught in secular letters, a distinguished doctor of arts and medicine, who by teaching and writing in the university of Toulouse gave great proof of his erudition, is said to have written many excellent little works. Of these I have seen only a large volume, which he had read publicly in the aforesaid university; at its beginning he promises many glorious things, and some applaud themselves concerning the truth of them as though experienced, because he had noted beforehand:

Of Creatures, or On Man, one book.

Disputed Questions, one book.

To the praise and glory [unclear]

The rest are unknown to me.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Sigismund and Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1450.

Franciscus Barbarus, a Venetian by birth, a disciple in Greek letters of Chrysoloras, the Byzantine philosopher, a man most learned in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine scriptures, a clear philosopher and a supreme orator in both languages, while still a young man wrote certain little works not unworthy of reading, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among them there is extant a work which he entitled:

On Marriage, one book.

Letters to Various Persons, sixteen books.

And certain other things.

From Plutarch he translated into Latin, for his brother Zacharias, the life of Aristides and of Cato, and of many illustrious men. Likewise also other things.

He died in the times of Emperor Frederick III and Pope Nicholas V, in the year of the Lord 1454, in the second indiction.

Thomas Walden, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, English by nation, and prior general of the English province, a man most learned in the divine writings and nobly taught in Aristotelian philosophy, acute in intellect and quite fit for disputation, distinguished no less in conduct than in knowledge, also an excellent preacher of sermons, and formerly confessor and secretary of Henry V, king of the English, wrote, among the other monuments of his talent, a distinguished work divided into three great volumes against the infamous Wycliffites and Hussite heretics, which Pope Martin V, after examination, confirmed by apostolic authority. This work is entitled:

The Doctrinal of the Church, one book.

Let God arise and let [his enemies] be scattered, three

On Ecclesiastical Writers

Also on the Sentences, 4 books. On the Ethics, 10 books. On the Physics, 8 books. On the book On the Heaven and the World, 4 books. On Generation and Corruption, 2 books. On the Meteorology, 4 books. On the books On the Soul, 4 books.

He says besides that he wrote many other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He died at Rouen, honorably buried in his own convent, under the emperor Sigismund, in the last year of Pope Martin V, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1430, in the eighth indiction, on the third day of the month of November.

Paulus de Castro, a jurist, the most celebrated of all men of his time, a man of great learning and eloquence, who for many years taught civil law gloriously at Siena, Florence, and Padua, having been hired at a public salary, composed many little works on the laws, known and dear to the professors of this faculty; by these he left to posterity the memory of his most famous name. Among them the following are reported:

On the Code, 9 books. On the Old Digest, 24 books. On the New Digest, [unclear] books. On the Infortiatum, 14 books. On the Institutes, 4 books. Most elegant Opinions, 1 book. And several other things.

He died in the times of the emperor Sigismund and Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1437, in the fifteenth indiction.

Ambrosius Florentinus, general abbot of the Camaldolese order, once a pupil of Chrysoloras, the Byzantine philosopher, when he was teaching Greek literature at Venice, a man most learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular studies, a most lucid philosopher, rhetorician, and theologian, left to posterity many distinguished monuments of his talent. He was the nuncio and envoy of Pope Eugenius to the Council of Basel, where he delivered a solemn oration on his behalf before the fathers. He wrote a distinguished volume:

Letters to Various Persons, 1 book. Various Orations. And several other things.

He also translated into Latin from Greek the four books of Blessed Dionysius the Areopagite, in a more elegant and easier style; also the original Life of Blessed John Chrysostom, addressed to the emperor Sigismund; likewise Basil On Virginity, addressed to Cardinal Gabriel, afterward Pope Eugenius IV; likewise Laertius On the Life of the Philosophers, addressed to Cosmas de’ Medici. But he also rendered the three books of Saint John Chrysostom to Stagirius, the afflicted monk, in lucid and adorned speech. And several other things still unknown to us.

He also translated Ephrem the Syrian. He himself wrote On the Sacraments; On [unclear] the Holy Spirit.

He flourished in the times of the Councils of Constance and Basel, both of which he adorned by his presence, in the year of the Lord 1430.

Caietanus, by country a Vicentine, a canon of Padua, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, notably instructed in secular letters, a distinguished philosopher and physician, a most celebrated theologian, who publicly taught sacred scholastic letters in the school of Padua, acquired great praise for his learning. He wrote, in both branches of literature, as they report, several little works, by which he left to posterity the memory of his care. Among them these are reported:

On the Physics, 8 books. On the books On the Soul, 4 books. On the book On the Heaven and the World, 4 books. And several other things.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Sigismund and Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1450.

Henricus Gulpen, abbot of the monastery of St. Giles in Nuremberg, of the order of the holy father Benedict, a German by nation, a distinguished jurist, exceptionally learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular philosophy, and no less venerable for his religious way of life than for his knowledge of the Scriptures, whose readiness of talent and prudence in counsel Johannes Nider, having experienced them, commends in his little work On the Ants, wrote elegantly on the seven distinctions:

On Penance, 1 book. On Consecration, 1 book. On the Passion of the Lord, 1 book. And certain other things.

He was personally present at the Council of Constance, when he was still a secular master of arts studying law, in the year of the Lord 1417.

Jacobus Forliviensis, a philosopher and physician of very celebrated reputation, who is considered by many to have far surpassed all professors of philosophy and medicine of his time, distinguished not only for learning but also for experience in curing human illnesses, wrote for those toiling in his faculty very useful little works, by which he made his name known to posterity. The chief of these are reported: On

On Ecclesiastical Writers

On the extension of the degrees of forms, one book. On the first [book of] Avicenna's Canon, one book. On the aphorisms of the same, one book. On the Techne also, one book. And certain other things. He flourished in the times of Sigismund, the most Christian emperor, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1430.

Rudolphus of Bruxella, a village of Swabia, German by nation, of the diocese of Speyer, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and notably learned also in secular philosophy, which they call Aristotelian, an eminent professor of sacred theology, who in the Heidelberg school acquired great praises for his learning: in that faculty he wrote works not to be despised, by which he made his name known to posterity, namely:

Questions on the Sentences, one book. Very useful sermons, one book. Various questions, one book. Several orations to the fathers, one book. Although holy mother And many other things. He flourished in the Heidelberg school at the time of the Council of Basel and thereafter, in the year of the Lord 1430.

Hugo of Siena, Italian by nation, a man very learned in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a distinguished philosopher and very celebrated physician, excellent in talent and outstanding in eloquence, wrote volumes in medicine not to be lightly esteemed by students, by which he left to posterity the memory of his name. Among these the following are reported:

On the first [book] of Avicenna, one book. On the Aphorisms of Hippocrates, one book. On the Techne of Galen, one book. And many other things. He flourished in the times of the Council of Basel and of Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1450.

Henricus de Gauda, German by nation, magnificently learned in the holy Scriptures, subtle in talent and a very acute disputant of scholastic questions, in the Heidelberg school, both by reading, by teaching, and also by composing, easily held first place in his time. He wrote certain excellent works of his talent, of which only a few have so far come to my knowledge.

On the book of the Sentences, one book. A fountain of gardens, a well On celebration, one book. Pray

The Abbot of Sponheim

Various orations. Disputed questions. And certain other things. He flourished in the times of the Council of Basel and of Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1435.

Santes de Arduinis, born from the city of Pesaro, a man most learned in philosophy and medicine, and most experienced in healing human bodies, held in great esteem among the Venetians in his time, published certain excellent works of this faculty, by which he destined the memory of his most celebrated name for the knowledge of posterity. Among these there exists a notable work on all natural and artificial poisons, one book. On smelling also, one book. On procreation, one book. And certain other things. He flourished under Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Nicolaus de Susato, German by nation, a very celebrated doctor of sacred theology, and most learned both in secular philosophy and in the divine Scriptures, held in esteem by Ludovicus, duke of Bavaria and count palatine of the Rhine, and in the Council of Constance joined with the other cardinals from the German nation for electing the supreme pontiff, as is found in the acts of the same council: he wrote several excellent works of his talent, by which he left to posterity the memory of his name. Among these are reported:

Questions on the Sentences, one book. Many sermons, one book. Various questions. And many other things. He flourished in the Council of Constance under Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1417.

Johannes de Marliano, a very celebrated philosopher and physician, excellent in talent, distinguished in experience of this art, and not among the lowest of the physicians of his age, published certain excellent and lucid works both in philosophy and in medicine, the reading and study of which are said to be of no little use to students of these subjects, namely:

On reaction etc., one book. On antiperistasis, one book. And many other things. He flourished in the times of Sigismund, the most Christian emperor, in the year of the Lord 1430.

On Ecclesiastical Writers

[unclear] Johannes Gritsch, a German by nation, from Basel as his native city, of the Order of Friars Minor, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, sufficiently instructed both in canon law and in secular philosophy, outstanding in ability and distinguished in eloquence, of very celebrated reputation in delivering sermons to the people, wrote works not to be despised for preachers of the word of God, by which he commended the memory of his name to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

Sermons for the Temporal Cycle, one book. Sermons on the Saints, one book. Sermons for Lent, one book. “When you fast,” etc., [unclear] On the Passion of the Lord, one book. And certain others.

He flourished, as his own people say, in the time of Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1430.

[unclear] Johannes Nider, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a German by nation, a man devoted to and learned in the divine writings, sufficiently learned in scholastic philosophy, of excellent and distinguished ability in delivering sermons to the people, an inquisitor of heretical depravity and a very keen investigator of the little women whom the common people call witches, wrote in plain speech several volumes, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the Contracts of Merchants, one book. “Since the office of merchants” On Moral Leprosy, one book. “Once, when we read in Le-” The Law of the Decalogue, for consecrated [unclear] On Ants Morally Treated, five books. “Often traversing those things which” On the Consolation of a Fearful Conscience, one book. “Among the disciplines I found” Mirror of Perfection, one book. Sermons for the Temporal Cycle, one book. “Behold your king,” etc. “Three” Sermons on the Saints. “Come after me,” etc. Lenten Sermons, one book. “Be converted to,” etc. And many other things.

He flourished in the time of Emperor Sigismund, at the Councils of Constance and Basel, in the year of the Lord 1430.

[unclear] Nicolaus Siculus, abbot of [Monacen?], of the Order of Saint Benedict, sprung from the city of Catania, called de Tudeschis, first auditor of the causes of the lord Pope in the Rota, afterward archbishop of Palermo, and finally cardinal of the holy Roman Church, the most celebrated jurist of all, subtle and acute in intellect, ready and firm in counsel, clear and composed in speech, who deservedly is called the lamp of the law, wrote many distinguished volumes, by which he made his name known to posterity; of these the following are reported:

On the Decretum, unfinished, one book. On the Decretals, five books. “Since every reason of the supreme” On the Clementines, one book. For the Council of Basel, one book. “Since the truth of words” Judicial Process, one book. “The peace-making king of all” One Hundred and Four Opinions, one book. “The contingency of the fact is such” Various Disputations, one book. And many other things.

He flourished in person at the Council of Basel, in the year of the Lord 1435. And on behalf of the authority of that council, before the princes at Frankfurt, he publicly read the aforementioned treatise and delivered an elegant oration there.

The Abbot of Sponheim

Ludovicus Pontanus of Rome, an Italian by nation, a very brilliant jurist, and no less devoted to the holy Scriptures than to secular philosophy, excellent in ability, concise and weighty in judgment, published volumes not to be despised for those wishing to make progress in the legal faculty, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of their number I have seen only the work entitled:

Notable Singulars, one book. “The word is understood entirely”

Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished in the time of the most excellent Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1430.

Johannes Noblet, of the Order of the Brothers of the Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin of Mount Carmel, a Frenchman by nation, of the Paris convent and school, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular disciplines, since before entering religion he had been, by art, practice, and profession, a salutary physician of sick bodies, wrote several distinguished little works, of which the following are reported:

On the Sentences, four books. On the Canonical Epistles, seven books. “Noble in the gates is her husband” Centiloquy of Riddles, one book. Various Sermons, one book. And many other things.

In addition, on many books of the Bible he wrote marvelous and elegant commentaries [the text breaks off].

[unclear] are said to have been written, which have by no means come to our knowledge.

Johannes de Ragusio, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, outstanding in talent and distinguished in eloquence, of very celebrated reputation in delivering sermons to the people, produced certain excellent little works of his ability, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have read a well-constructed work addressed to the fathers of the Council of Basel: Against the Hussites, one book, “Most reverend, venerable [fathers?] ...” Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished in person at the Council of Basel, where he publicly delivered the said treatise against the heretics before the fathers, under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1458.

B

Londus Flavius of Forlì, secretary of Pope Eugene IV, a man skilled in every discipline of the liberal arts, a very celebrated philosopher and rhetorician, and an eminent historiographer, excellent in talent, eloquent in speech, and second to none in grace of expression, wrote many distinguished volumes, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Among these the following are reported:

Three Decades, so entitled.

On the Deeds of the Romans, three books, “Of the Roman empire ...”

On Rome Triumphant, ten books.

On Rome Restored, five books.

On Italy Illustrated, eight books.

Letters to Various Persons, one book.

Various Orations, one book.

And several other works.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Sigismund, under Pope Eugene IV, in the year of the Lord 1435. He left five sons from a legitimate marriage, cultivators of the liberal arts.

H

Heimericus de Campo, a German by nation, vice-chancellor of the University of Cologne, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and second to none in his time in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in talent and an outstanding disputant of difficult questions, wrote many excellent little works; nevertheless, few of these have so far come into our hands. He was personally present at the Council of Basel, sent by the University of Cologne, where, at the urging of Master Nicholas of Cusa, later cardinal, he produced Compendium of Questions, one book. Afterward, on several occasions [unclear].

The Abbot of Sponheim.

On the Sentences, four books, “As Augustine says in the book ...”

On Being and Essence, one book, “Being and not-being are opposed ...”

Compendium of Divine Things, four books, “In this little work under ...”

Various Questions, one book.

Many Sermons, one book.

On the Authority of the Council, one book.

And several other works.

He flourished at the Council of Basel, where he wrote and disputed much, in the year of the Lord 1438, under Emperor Albert.

Georgius Trapezuntius, apostolic secretary, a man most learned in every respect, a very celebrated philosopher, rhetorician, and poet, who, having been put by Pope Eugene in charge of the public school at Rome, taught rhetoric and poetry for many years and left after him many disciples most skilled in every science, wrote certain excellent volumes, by which he made his name known to posterity. Among these are extant:

A very beautiful Rhetoric, one book.

A singular Dialectic, one book.

On the Orations of Cicero, one book.

Various orations and letters.

And certain other works.

He flourished at Rome in the times of Pope Eugene IV, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1435.

Florianus de S. Petro, an Italian by nation, a native of Bologna, easily the most learned of all men of his time in civil law, and not ignorant of either the divine Scriptures or secular philosophy, sharp in talent, distinguished in eloquence, a subtle disputant and cautious counsellor, wrote in that faculty certain very excellent little works, by which he commended the memory of his very celebrated name to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the Code, nine books.

On the Old Digest, twenty-four books.

On the New Digest, twelve books.

On the Infortiatum, fourteen books.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Sigismund and Pope Eugene IV, in the year of the Lord 1435.

Nicolaus Lackman, a German by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor of St. Francis, minister of Saxony, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of Aristotelian philosophy, outstanding in talent and fit for disputation, of excellent reputation in delivering sermons to the people, wrote not without [unclear].

On Ecclesiastical Writers

[unclear] little works for reading, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these, the following are said to be the more important:

On the Sentences, 4 books. Various Questions, 1 book. Sermons on the Temporale, 1 book. Sermons on the Saints, 1 book. And many other works.

He flourished in the time of the Council of Basel, under Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1440.

John of Schoonhoven, a German by nation, of the order of the Canons Regular of St Augustine, from the monastery in Brabant, in the diocese of Cambrai, which is commonly called Groenendaal and in Latin Viridis Vallis, in which John Ruusbroec formerly held the office of prior, was a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, cautious in intellect, composed in speech, and no less distinguished in conduct than in knowledge. He wrote to Simon, his nephew:

A Spiritual Exhortation, 1 book. “Great joy to me” On the Course of a Monk, 1 book. “That to you, dearest” [unclear] On the Progress of a Monk, 1 book. “Fight the good fight” A Defense of John Ruusbroec, 1 book. “When a certain doctor” [unclear] Various Sermons, 1 book. Letters to Various Persons, 1 book. And many other works.

He flourished at the time of the Council of Constance, under Emperor Sigismund and Pope Martin V, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Peter de Colle, of the order of the Friars Minor of St Francis, a German by nation, was a man learned in the divine Scriptures, excellently instructed in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, and eloquent and lucid in delivering sermons to the people. He published several volumes for the edification of readers, by which he transmitted the memory of his distinguished name to posterity. Among these there survives a well-arranged work, which he recited before the fathers at the Council of Basel:

On the Authority of a Council, 1 book. “The Church fought many” [unclear] Questions on the Sentences, 1 book. Various Sermons, 1 book. And many other works.

He flourished at the time of the same Council of Basel, at the beginning of the reign of Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1440.

The Abbot of Sponheim

Hermann, a monk in Campo, of the Cistercian order in the diocese of Münster, a German by nation and a Westphalian by homeland, was a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and excellently instructed both in canon law and in Aristotelian philosophy, ready in intellect and clear in speech. He wrote several little works of his practiced talent, by which he labored considerably in defense of the Council of Basel. Among these I found a little work that he entitled On Definitive Voices:

In a General Council, 1 book. “Now after very often repeated” [unclear] On the Power of the Pope and of a Council, 1 book. “Blessed Athanasius” Also On Schism, 1 book. On Neutrality, 1 book. Of the rest which he composed, although many are reported, nothing has come down to me.

He flourished at the time of the Council of Basel, in the year of the Lord 1440.

John Gauer, a German by nation, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, lector of sacred Scripture, of the convent of Mainz, was a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently capable in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote little works of his practiced talent not to be despised, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these there survive:

On the Sentences, 4 books. “To the praise of almighty God” Also On Exodus, 1 book. “The law for the common utility” A Harmony of the Evangelists, 1 book. “Because God sent his Son” Sermons on the Saints, 1 book. A Triple Lenten Work, 3 books. “When you fast, know” [unclear] And many other works.

He flourished in the time of the Council of Basel, under Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1440.

Bernardino, of the order of the Friars Minor, an Italian by nation and from Siena by homeland, was a man learned in the divine Scriptures, the most celebrated preacher of all his time, most holy in life and conduct, inasmuch as both living and dead he shone with countless miracles. He wrote certain little works for the edification of the faithful, by which he also showed the power of his talent to posterity. Of these there survive:

On the Apocalypse of John, 1 book. “Blessed [unclear] threefold” On the Eternal Gospel, 1 book. “For I did not come to dissolve the law” On the Christian Religion, 1 book. “Now abide faith, hope” On con-

320 On Ecclesiastical Writers

On the conception of St. Mary, one book, “The depths were not yet,” and On the Passion of the Lord, one book. Sermons for the season, one book. Sermons on the saints, one book. And certain other works.

He died at Aquila, a city of Abruzzo, in the reign of the emperor Frederick III, under Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1443, in the sixth indiction, in the sixty-fifth year of his age. And because of frequent miracles he was entered by Pope Nicholas V in the catalogue of the saints, in the year of the Lord 1450, seven years after his death. His feast is celebrated on the twentieth day of the month of May.

Antonius Guainerius, an Italian by nation, from Pavia by homeland, a most celebrated doctor of the art of medicine, and nobly learned in the precepts of the philosophers, excellent in ability and notably distinguished by skill in his profession, wrote in that field of learning certain lucid little works, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On disease of the stomach, one book. On fever also, one book. On diseases of the groin, one book. On pleurisy, one book. On the womb, one book. On fluxes, one book. On arthritis in the joints, one book. On the sufferings of stone, one book. On the third book of Avicenna, one book. And many other works.

He flourished at the time of the Council of Basel, in the year of the Lord 1440.

Gerardus Stredam, a German by nation, of the Carthusian order, prior of the house of All the Apostles near Liege, a man most devoted to the divine Scriptures and excellently learned through long practice, also venerable in religion, prudence, and authority, wrote for the edification of simple brothers certain little works, of which the following are reported: To the abbot of Saint Adrian of Geraardsbergen,

On pastoral care, one book. On the Ten Commandments, one book. On the Seven Sacraments, one book. Mirror of religious, one book. Dialogue on the virtues, one book. Dialogue on the vices, one book. Sermons for the season, one book. Sermons on the saints, one book. And certain other works.

He died at the beginning of the reign of the emperor Frederick III, under Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1445, in the sixth indiction.

Matthaeus Palmerius, an Italian by nation, a Florentine by homeland, a historian, philosopher, and most eloquent orator, who at the Council of Florence, which Pope Eugenius IV held against the synod of Basel, was counted among the distinguished men, wrote a book full of error concerning the angels; and, stubbornly defending it, he was condemned as a heretic and burned at the city of Corna. Carefully reviewing the Chronicle of Eusebius of Caesarea, he corrected it and, completing it down to the year of the Lord 1448, entitled it to Petrus Cosmas de’ Medici, one book, “Innate in our minds.” Letters to various persons, one book. Various orations also. And certain other works.

He flourished in the times of the Council of Basel and of Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1440.

321 The Abbot of Sponheim

Johannes Ernesti, a German by nation, once the ornament and rector of the school of Heidelberg, learned in the holy Scriptures and rich in his reading of the ancients, subtle in ability, eloquent with singular grace of speech, an outstanding disputant of questions, wrote, as they report, certain distinguished little works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with glory to posterity. Of their number the following are reported:

Questions on the Sentences, one book. A question in disputation, one book. Many sermons, one book. An oration on the Nativity of the Lord, one book, “Although of speaking concerning the greatest...” On fasting, to the university, one book, “Most sacred desires...” Many and various orations, one book. And many other works.

He flourished at the time of the Council of Basel, at the beginning of the reign of the emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1440.

Bartholomaeus, of the Carthusian order, prior of the house of Bethlehem in the town of Roermond in Guelders, a German by nation, an acute, devout, and celebrated interpreter of sacred letters, wrote for the edification of his brothers certain distinguished little works, by which he magnificently exercised his ability and left to posterity the memory of his name. Of their number the following are reported:

Exercise of devotion, one book. Sum of vices, one book. On abstinence from meats, one book. On the proclamations of the brothers, one book. On an oath, one book. And certain other works. On rash judgments, one book.

On Ecclesiastical Writers

He died under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1446, in the ninth indiction, on the fourth day before the Ides of July.

Henry of Vuerlis, a German by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor, minister of the province of Cologne, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, excellent in talent and scholastic eloquence, an acute disputant and an outstanding preacher of sermons, composed certain lucid volumes, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these there is extant the notable work:

On the Sentences, four books. On Ecclesiastical Power, one book. Various Sermons also, one book. And many other things.

He flourished in the times of the Council of Basel and of Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1440.

Andreas of Traiectum, a German by nation, a monk of our monastery of Spanheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, which is situated within the bounds of the diocese of Mainz, between the Rhine and the Hercynian forest which, called Saonus, extends westward toward Trier, a man certainly studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant also of secular letters, outstanding in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote, both in verse and in prose, not contemptible little works, of which the following are held:

Soliloquies of a Man to God, one book. “When once the divine [unclear]...” On the Progress of Virtues, one book. “Having gone out perhaps [unclear]...” On the Use of [unclear], one book. “Your fraternity’s [unclear]...” Letters to Various Persons, one book. “Reverend father, recently from...” Various Conferences, one book. “Although among all who wrongly...” Poems and rhythms. And certain other brief works.

He flourished in the aforesaid monastery of Spanheim, before the introduction of the very recent Bursfeld reform, in the year of the Lord 1445.

Antoninus, of the Order of Friars Preacher, archbishop of Florence, an Italian by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, excellent in talent and distinguished in eloquence, famous and of celebrated reputation in preaching sermons to the people, and no less venerable in life and conduct than in learning, wrote many splendid volumes, by which he labored magnificently for the edification of the Church militant. Of these there is extant a great and very celebrated work, divided into four not small volumes, which he entitled Sum[unclear].

The Abbot of Spanheim

Summa of Cases of Conscience, four books. A Vast and Notable Chronicle, three books. Manual for Confessors, one book. On Ecclesiastical Censure, one book. Sermons on the Season, one book. Sermons on the Saints, one book. And certain other works.

“How greatly magnified are...” “I shall speak propositions from [unclear]...” “Those searching have failed in [their search?]...”

He died, after many labors in sacred study, not without a reputation for holiness, under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1459, in the seventh indiction, on the sixth day before the Nones of May, and was buried at Saint Mark’s, a convent of his order. He was inserted into the number of the saints by Pope Adrian VI; his feast is kept on the second day of May.

Leonard of Utino, of the Order of Friars Preacher, a man indeed studious and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, of excellent talent and outstanding reputation in preaching sermons to the people, wrote for the use of preachers certain splendid little works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following are reported:

Sermons on the Season, one book. Sermons on the Saints, one book. “Interpreter of divine things...” On Laws through Lent, one book. And certain other works.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1445.

John of Capistrano, a town in Abruzzo not far from the city of L’Aquila, of the Order of Friars Minor, formerly a disciple of Saint Bernardino of Siena, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently taught in canon law, excellent in talent and distinguished in eloquence, and devout also in life and religious conduct, a very celebrated preacher of the divine word, who by word and example converted many from iniquity, wrote certain little works of no small usefulness, of which few have come down to me:

On Covetousness, three books. “Do not lay up treasures for yourselves...” Against the Hussites, one book. Various Sermons, one book. Some Letters. And certain other works.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1450, and not without a reputation for holiness.

324 On Ecclesiastical Writers [unclear]

Nicholas of Cusa, bishop of Brixen and cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church of the title of St. Peter ad Vincula, a German by nationality, from the diocese of Trier: a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, easily the foremost of the theologians in his time, and outstandingly learned in secular letters; a very celebrated philosopher, rhetorician, and mathematician; subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech; skilled in three languages, Hebrew, Greek, and Latin; most upright in life and conduct, and singularly devout; a sincere and fervent lover of the salvation of souls. When he was sent as legate into Germany, he did and established many things useful for the reformation of the Church, and especially of our order. He wrote many excellent volumes, of which the following are extant:

On the Vision of God, 1 book. On the Peace of Faith, 1 book. Restoration of the Calendar, 1 book. On Mathematical Complements, 1 book. Sifting of the Alcoran, 3 books. On the Hunt for Wisdom, 1 book. On the Game of the Globe, Mystically, 2 books. Compendium, 1 book. Trialogue on Possest, 1 book. On Mathematical Perfection, 1 book. Against the Bohemians, 1 book. On the Beryl, 1 book. On the Gift of the Father of Lights, 1 book. On Seeking God, 1 book. On Genesis, 1 book. On the Summit of Theory, 4 books. On Learned Ignorance, 3 books. On Conjectures, 2 books. On the Filiation of God, 1 book. On Genesis, 1 book. The Layman, on Wisdom, 4 books. On the Squaring of the Circle, 1 book. On Fortune, 1 book. Directory for the Speculator, 1 book. Sermons for the Whole Year, 1 book. Letters to Various Persons, 1 book. And many other works.

I shall now disclose what to you It was from these who among Take, most holy father To the praise of the almighty So great is the power of the highest My purpose is to [unclear] Since I see you at the seat Receive a brief compendium Since to us [unclear] The noble mind is anxious Nicholas, by the mercy Whoever has read those things which in Also already before [unclear] Through your desire that you can I see you with a certain deep He will admire, and rightly Now, such as it is, having been given At last he compelled me Often more delightfully [unclear] A certain poor man comes together You know us three, etc. [unclear]

The Abbot of Sponheim

Near Cusa, the village of his birth, on the banks of the Moselle opposite Ürzig, he built a very famous hospital in honor of St. Nicholas the bishop; he richly endowed it with estates and revenues, and adorned it with many books in every branch of knowledge, Greek, Latin, and others.

He died under Emperor Frederick III in the year of the Lord 1464, in the twelfth indiction, on the eleventh day of the month of August, in the sixty-fifth year of his age. He was buried at Rome; his heart was sent to the aforesaid hospital and is buried there in the middle of the choir beneath marble.

Johannes Rode, abbot of the monastery of St. Matthias the Apostle outside the walls of Trier, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a German by nationality, from Trier by homeland: a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, outstandingly learned in canon law, devout in morals and conduct, a very celebrated restorer of regular observance, from whose labor and foundation the most recent Bursfelde reform of our order in Germany began. He once devoted himself to letters in the school of Heidelberg, where, becoming a bachelor of sacred theology and a very learned licentiate of canon law, he seemed already in mind and body to despise the world. Then, having been made a canon of the church of Metz, dean of St. Simeon, and official of the court of Trier, he despised all things for love of Christ and, to everyone’s amazement, entered the Carthusian order outside Trier. After some years he undertook the office of prior, although unwilling and refusing it. But Otto, archbishop of Trier, seeing that this man was learned, experienced, and zealous, had him brought out of the charterhouse by authority of the supreme pontiff and appointed him abbot in the aforesaid monastery; through him he reformed many monasteries in his diocese. He himself also, by authority of the Council of Basel, magnificently extended the reform. He wrote, moreover, for the reformation of monks:

Useful Constitutions, 1 book. Since the divine office which On the Quality of an Abbot, 1 book. Since from on high proceeds every And certain other works.

He died under Emperor Albert and Pope Eugene IV, in the year of the Lord 1439, in the twentieth year of his abbacy, in the second indiction, on the first day of the month of December. He was buried in the said monastery of St. Matthias the Apostle at Trier, before the altar of the protomartyr Stephen, in the right apse of the choir, beneath a stone inscribed with his name.

Varinus of Verona, once a pupil of Chrysoloras the Byzantine philosopher, a man in secular writings [unclear] of all in his time

326 On Ecclesiastical Writers

[unclear], by far most learned, and not ignorant of divine letters, most skilled in Greek and Latin speech; by whose efforts the studies of the liberal arts, which seemed weakened and now almost extinct, were stirred up and recalled into the light. He taught first at Venice, afterwards at Ferrara, and in both places had very celebrated pupils. He wrote to Prince Leonello the work entitled:

On the Difference between a Flatterer and a Friend, one book. Also a brief Grammar, one book. A Comparison of Scipio and Gaius, one book. Letters to Various Persons, one book. Several Orations, one book. Many poems. And not a few other things.

By order of Pope Nicholas V he translated into Latin Strabo’s Geography, a work no less useful than pleasant. From Plutarch he made Latin versions of the lives of many illustrious men. But he also translated Plutarch himself On the Education of Children, with many other works, most elegantly; these are partly extant.

He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Pius II, in the year of the Lord 1460, in the eighth indiction, on the day before the Nones of December; buried at Ferrara in the convent of the Carmelites, honorably given a marble tomb.

Henry Kalteisen, archbishop of the churches of Nidaros and Caesarea, of the Order of Friars Preachers, German by nation, from Koblenz by homeland, where he also entered the order; first made lector of the sacred palace, preacher of the Holy Cross, and inquisitor of heretical depravity; and afterwards, as we have said, consecrated by apostolic authority as chief bishop of two provinces, he became known as renowned throughout the whole world for his learning and preaching. Since he was a very celebrated doctor of sacred theology, he wrote, among other things, notable works:

Sermons on the Season, one book. Sermons through Lent, one book. On the Magnificat, one book. Various Questions, one book. Conferences to the Clergy. And several other things.

He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1465, in the thirteenth indiction, on the sixth day before the Nones of October; buried in his own convent at Koblenz.

Jo-

The Abbot of Sponheim

Johannes Bertachinus of Fermo, a very celebrated legal scholar, and singularly devoted to that faculty, outstanding in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote certain small works in law, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Among them there is a most famous work, divided into three large volumes, which he compiled very diligently and in fine order with much labor, and entitled:

Repertory of Both Laws, five books. “Princes are wont [unclear] immortal...” Various Questions.

He published besides several other things, which have not come to the knowledge of our reading.

Pope Pius II, Tuscan by nation, Sienese by homeland, previously called Aeneas Silvius, sat in the supreme pontificate after Callixtus III for six years. A man learned in every respect, an outstanding philosopher, orator, and poet, he left many monuments of his talent to posterity. He, poor, served a certain prelate in the Council of Basel for a time. Then, received into the chancery as a scribe, he was created first bishop of Trieste, afterwards of Siena, thereafter cardinal, and finally was elected pope by the votes of all. Concerning his writings, the following are reported, composed with great powers of eloquence:

On the Miseries of Courtiers, one book. “Foolish are those who to kings...” On the Education of Children, one book. “All who to virtue...” Solution of Questions, one book. “Recently there was present at the imperial...” “The city of Siena, whence to you...” Against the Taborites, one book. “Although among the Bohemians...” To Nicholas of Cusa, one book. “It came to me this very...” one book. “About to write some things to you...” On the Faith, to the Turk, one book. “Of the prophet Ezekiel...” On the Expedition against the Turks, one book. “[Heraldus?] of Alphonsus...” To the Bishop of Krakow, one book. “That all things which are perishable...” On the Origin and History of the Bohemians, one book. “It would be well, illustrious man...” Precepts of Rhetoric, one book. “Me, suffering from gout, recently...” Europe, to Cardinal Antonio, one book. Di- On the Foreknowledge of God, one book. “But he was in the city

528 On Ecclesiastical Writers

Dialogue against the Turks, one book. On grammar, one book. An unfinished work of histories, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. On the disaster of Constantinople, [unclear], one book. On the disaster of the universal Church, one book. An oration in the Mantuan assembly, one book. An oration to Pope Calixtus, one book. An oration before the assembly of cardinals, one book. On the deeds done by himself, one book. Various orations. Many epigrams, and certain other most elegant little works, which I have not seen, he is said to have written; by them he made his name known to posterity. He died under Emperor Frederick III, at Ancona, as is said, in the year of the Lord 1464, in the twelfth indiction, on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of September, likewise in the sixty-fourth year of his age; he was buried at Rome in the church of St. Peter, beside the altar of St. Andrew.

L Lanfrancus de Oriano, a very celebrated jurist and not ignorant of secular literature, outstanding in talent and renowned for eloquence, wrote in his profession certain volumes not to be despised. By them he transmitted the memory of his talent to posterity, and proved himself in study in many and splendid ways. Of their number the following are extant:

Repetitions, Quoniam contra, De proba., one book. Quoniam contra haec decret... Commentary on the Clementine Saepe, De ver. sig., one book. Ista Clementina in se con... On c. Dispendiosam, De iudi., one book. Non est necesse diuide... Repetition on c. Raynucius, De testa., one book. In textu ubi Raynucius... On the law Admonendi, De iureiu., one book. Haec lex diuiditur in du... On the interpretation of statutes, one book. Pro euidentiori intelle... On law Centurio, De vul. & pu. substi., one book. Famosa est ista lex ha... Repetition on the rubric De cau. pos. & pro., one book. He also published many other works which have not come to notice.

H Henricus Gorrickem, a German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, renowned in talent, scholastic in speech, and an acute disputant, who in the university of Cologne was considered distinguished in his time by lecturing and composing, wrote little works of no contemptible reading, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. Of these there are extant:

103

The Abbot of Sponheim

Conclusions on the Sentences, four books. Cupientes aliquid de p... On superstitions, one book. In lectione... Against the Hussites also, one book. On the celebration of feasts, one book. A summary of St. Thomas, one book. Sermons and conferences, one book. He also published questions, determinations, and moreover various lectures, diverse books, and treatises, which have by no means come to the notice of our reading. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Pius II, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1460.

Johannes Kanneman, of the Order of Friars Minor, a German by nation, a man learned in the holy Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in talent, renowned for eloquence, was outstanding in delivering sermons to the people. Thinking wrongly about ecclesiastical power, when he was sought by the minister of Saxony for prison, he escaped by flight and fled to the Observantines; thereafter he amended his error along with his life. Johannes de Hagen, the Carthusian, a very learned man, had already reproved him and recalled him to the paths of equity. He wrote:

A defense of himself, one book. Multi famosi viri... Egredimini filiae Sion... On the Passion of the Lord, one book. Various sermons, one book. Certain questions, one book. And many other works. He flourished in the times of Emperor Frederick III and Pope Pius II, in the year of the Lord 1460.

Jacobus Jüterbuck, a German by nation, of the Order of Carthusians, vicar of the house of Mount St. Saviour near Erfurt, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, renowned in talent, clear in speech, a cautious interpreter of doubtful matters, and also devout in life and conduct, wrote many varied little works, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the jubilee year, one book. On the causes of many sufferings, one book. On the morals of Christians, one book. On the threefold state of human beings, one book. Consolation for the evils of this age, one book. On the manner of observing an interdict, one book. Ad amputandum errores...

On Ecclesiastical Writers

Apologetic for religious, one book. On the cautions of the various states, one book. On the knowledge of secrets, one book. On truth to be spoken or kept silent, one book. On thoughts, one book. On contracts, one book. On the evils of this age, one book. On the obedience of monks, one book. On the art of dying, one book. On the stability of monks, one book. On the restraint of thoughts, one book. A soliloquy of man to the soul, one book. On the art of curing vices, one book. On the seven mortal sins, one book. On the same mental sins, one book. On the power of demons, one book. On the dignity of prelates, one book. On the observance of the commandments, one book. On the Sabbath, one book. On the state of a more secure life, one book. On the direction of intention, one book. On the progress of the spiritual life, one book. On indulgences, one book. Various sermons, one book. Walking, Jesus, beside And many other works.

He died in the times of Emperor Frederick III and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1466, in the fourteenth indiction.

Nicolaus Dorbellus, of the order of the Friars Minor of Saint Francis, of the province of Tours, a man most learned in the divine scriptures and second to none in scholastic philosophy, distinguished in talent and sufficiently fit for disputing and unraveling questions of the scriptures, wrote certain distinguished volumes, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity; and in the school at Poitiers, both by disputing and by teaching, he earned great praise for his learning. Among his works the following are reported: a distinguished and very celebrated work, and almost divine, pleasant for its singular usefulness,

The Abbot of Sponheim

On the Sentences, four books. On the little summaries of Peter of Spain, seven books. On mathematical science, one book. On Aristotle's Physics, eight books. On On the Heavens and the World, two books. On On Generation and Corruption, two books. On On Generation and Corruption, three books. On the books of the Meteorology, five books. On the books On the Soul, six books. On the books of the Metaphysics, ten books. On the books of the Ethics, twelve books. And certain other works.

He was a profound interpreter and very keen defender of the sayings of John Scotus; expounding philosophy from his writings, and dividing this very work into three parts, mathematical, theological, and ethical, he named it the Compendium.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Frederick III and Pope Callixtus III, in the year of the Lord 1455.

Petrus de Unzola, a citizen of Bologna, a very celebrated jurist and well instructed in the disciplines of the liberal arts, outstanding in talent, is said also to have written some other works, but they have not come to my knowledge.

Henricus de Herph, of the order of the Friars Minor of Saint Francis, German by nation, of the province of Cologne, a man zealous in the divine scriptures, not ignorant of pontifical law, outstanding in talent and clear in speech, of very celebrated reputation in delivering sermons to the people, to be revered no less for his religious life than for his knowledge of the scriptures, wrote works of not negligible authority, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of their number the following are reported: A large volume. [unclear] On the precepts of the Decalogue, one book. Sermons for the season, one book. Sermons on the saints, one book. Sermons through Advent, two books. Because, as the Wise Man bears witness As the Philosopher says The first part having been completed Nature, here begins the book On generation, here begins On first things, begins the book Of honorable goods The second part having been completed Through the treatise, compendiously, one book. I find another law in Behold, your king comes Rabbi, where do you dwell? Who will be able to think On

On Ecclesiastical Writers

On the three parts of penance, one book, “No one can [serve] two lords”; and certain other things.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Pius II, in the year of the Lord 1460.

Johannes de Turrecremata, of the Order of Preachers, bishop of Sabina, and cardinal priest of the most holy Roman Church, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and an outstanding declaimer of sermons, quick in intellect and clear in speech, wrote many little works of his talent, by which he made his name known. Of these the following are reported. To Arsenius, a monk of the monastery of Saint Benedict, which he himself held in commendam, he composed a great work, and one not to be rejected:

On the Rule of Saint Benedict, one book, “Since, with the help of our Lord”; On the whole Psalter, one book, “To the most blessed father and cle…”; Questions on the Sunday Gospels, one book, “To the holy and most revered…”; Questions on the Gospel readings for the saints, one book; On holy water, one book, “The reverend father recently enjoined me…”; Sermons on the season, one book, “Divine Scripture teaches us…”; Sermons on the saints, one book; and very many other things.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and the supreme pontiffs Pius and Paul, in the year of the Lord 1460.

Johannes of Mechelen, a German by nation, a man trained by long study in the divine Scriptures, not moderately learned in scholastic philosophy, excellent in intellect, distinguished in knowledge, publicly taught theology for many years in the school of Cologne and acquired great praise for his learning. He wrote certain distinguished little works of his talent, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

A notable work on the Sentences, one book; On the Psalter, one book; Various questions, one book; Sermons and collationes, one book; and very many other things.

He flourished in the time of Emperor Frederick III and Pope Pius II, in the year of the Lord 146[unclear].

Dionysius Rykel, otherwise de Leuwis, a German by nation, of the Carthusian order, of the house of Bethlehem at Roermond, a man most devoted to the divine Scriptures and skilled through continual exercise; The Abbot of Sponheim skilled also, not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, distinguished in life and conduct, singularly devout, so much so that he was even considered worthy of divine revelations, to whom there are extant several letters of Nicholas of Cusa, a most learned cardinal, wrote so many and such great works that, in number of little works, apart from Augustine, he had no equal among the Latins. He devoted himself to contemplation and prayer with such fervor that one would think he could never have written anything. Again, he was so diligent in writing and reading that one would suppose he could nowhere have been able to pray or contemplate. He slept very little, and his abstinence from food and drink was admirable; after the example of blessed Jerome, he judged it sweet to meditate day and night on the law of the Lord, always either writing something useful or reading, so that sacred reading frequently took its turn.

Of his little works he himself made the following review, in a certain index:

On the Sentences, four books. The Abbot of Spanheim 357

He died under Frederick, the third emperor, and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1471, in the fourth indiction, on the twelfth day of the month of March. He was buried, not without a great reputation for sanctity, in the common cemetery of the brothers of the aforesaid house of Roermond. Finally, he reduced the books of John Cassian to an easier style for the sake of the simpler brothers; the preface of this work begins thus: “Declaration,” etc.

And these very many and very distinguished works of so great a man were printed for the public use of the Church about twelve years ago at Cologne by various printers, at the instance of the Cologne Charterhouse.

Bessarion, Greek by nation, cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, commonly called the Nicaean, and patriarch of Constantinople, a man most learned in every respect, a philosopher and orator second to none in either language, wrote certain very distinguished volumes of his genius, by which he transmitted his name to posterity with immense glory. Of these, the following are reported: against Mark, bishop of Ephesus, who held erroneous views on the Holy Spirit in the manner of the Greeks at the Council of Florence, he wrote an eminent and very distinguished work, which he entitled Confutation, one book. In that work, “Thus when I wish to remain,” one book. In praise of Plato’s philosophy, five books. Praises of his fatherland, two books. To the Greek emperor, of consolation, three books. Several orations and letters. And certain other things. Against the calumniator of Plato, four books. Whether nature and art act by design, one treatise. On the Eucharist, one book. He translated from Aristotle the fourteen books of the Metaphysics.

He also founded at Venice a notable library, very richly furnished with many books both Greek and Latin, over which Marcus Antonius Sabellicus, a most learned man, was placed at no small stipend; of him we shall speak later.

At length, full of days, he died while on an embassy to France, under Fre-

under Frederick, emperor the third, and Sixtus, pope the fourth, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1473, in the sixth indiction.

Johannes Hagen, otherwise de Indagine, a German by nation, of the Carthusian order, of the house of Saint Salvator near Erfurt, prior in Eisenach and in Stettin, a man most devoted to study in the divine Scriptures and very learned, and an excellent doctor in canon law, distinguished in talent, ready and provident in counsel, wrote in plain style many distinguished volumes to princes, bishops, and other prelates of churches, having been questioned on various and diverse matters; of these I recall that few have come into our hands. For, as I have learned from the writings of a certain devout father of the same order, he published more than three hundred treatises, among all of which the notable work that he entitled:

340 On Ecclesiastical Writers

John, abbot of the monastery of Niuicella, devoted to and learned in the sacred Scriptures, nobly trained in canon law, subtle in intellect, distinguished in eloquence, wrote many different little works of his own, by which he transmitted the memory of his most celebrated name to posterity with glory. Of these the following are extant: an illustrious and distinguished work entitled The Concordance of the Bible of the Canons, one book: “In the beginning God created.”

Sermons on the Temporale, one book: “Look, lift up [your] head.”

Sermons on the Saints, one book: “Having left the nets, [unclear] Peter.”

Letters, Various Questions.

The rest which he composed have not come to the notice of our reading.

Jacob of Gruytrode, a German by nation, of the order of the Carthusians, prior of the house of All the Apostles near Liège, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, devout in the conduct of his life, excellent in intellect, sweet in eloquence, wrote certain distinguished devout little works, the reading of which is not deemed unprofitable for religious persons, lovers of their own salvation. Of these the following are reported:

On True Virtues, three books.

On the Seven Mortal Sins, one book.

On the Four Last Things, one book.

On the Life of the Lord Jesus, one book.

On Preparation before Mass, one book.

On the Definition of the Name Monk, one book.

Meditations on the Passion of the Lord, one book.

A Lectionary for the Table, one book.

Mirror of Prelates, one book: “Eat, friends, [unclear].”

Mirror of Priests, one book.

Mirror of Secular Men, one book.

Mirror of Old Age, one book.

Colloquy of Jesus and the Monk, one book.

Colloquy of Jesus and the Prelate, one book.

Colloquy of Jesus and the Old Man, one book: “Do not be indignant, I pray.”

Colloquy of Jesus and the Hermit, one book.

Colloquy of Jesus and the Disciple, one book.

Contemplation of Saint Mary, one book.

Little Crown of Saint Mary: “You have wounded my heart, [unclear].”

Abbot of Spanheim

Dialogue of Mary and the Sinner, one book.

On the Name of Jesus and Mary, one book.

Sermons on the Temporale, one book.

Sermons on the Saints, one book.

Letters to Various Persons, one book.

He died most devoutly under Emperor Frederick and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1472, in the fifth indiction, on the day before the Ides of February.

A man devoted to and learned in the sacred Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, ready and circumspect in counsel, and distinguished by experience in many matters, wrote certain distinguished volumes, by which he transmitted his name to posterity with glory. Of these there is extant the very elegant work On the Deeds of the Supreme Pontiffs, one book.

And certain other things.

He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1477, in the ninth indiction.

William Forleon, a Breton by nation, of the order of the Friars Minor of Saint Francis, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently trained in secular philosophy, distinguished in intellect, scholastic in eloquence, who in the Parisian school, by teaching, by disputing, and also by writing, won great praise for his learning, published certain distinguished little works on the Scriptures. Of these there is extant the very celebrated work On the Sentences, one book; Various Questions, one book.

A hearer and disciple of his was once that most learned man, and easily the foremost of the theologians of our age, Master Stephen called Brulefer, a Frenchman by nation, of the same order, who taught theology in the Paris convent; afterwards betaking himself to the observance of the order at Mainz in Germany, he there began to lecture on the Sentences, which he now continues with praise in the convent at Metz. This William flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1470.

[unclear] Albert—

Albertus de Eyb, a German by nation, canon of the church of Bamberg and chamberlain of Pope Pius II, a man zealous and learned in secular letters, not unacquainted with the divine Scriptures, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, an outstanding rhetorician and poet, wrote little works not unworthy of reading. Of these the following are extant: to lord Johann, duke of Bavaria, bishop of Munster and later primate of Magdeburg, a distinguished work entitled:

The Poetic Pearl, one book. “You have very often desired…” On the Married State also, one book. Letters to Various Persons, one book. And many other things.

He flourished under Frederick III, emperor, and Pope Pius II, in the year of the Lord 1460.

[unclear]

Rodericus, bishop of Zamora, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not unacquainted with secular letters, excellent in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, wrote little works of no contemptible authority for their talent, by which he commended the memory of his name to posterity. Of these I have so far seen only one volume, which he entitled:

Mirror of Human Life, one book. “Above all human…” The rest I have not seen.

He flourished in the times of Frederick III, emperor, and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Ambrosius Coriolanus, of the order of the hermit friars of St. Augustine, prior general, a Roman by homeland, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and distinguished in knowledge of secular letters, excellent in intellect and eloquent in speech, learned and eloquent, wrote certain notable little works by which he commended his name to immortality. Of these, however, few have come to my knowledge by reading; I have set them below:

On the Rule of Saint Augustine, one book. “From every learned parent…” A Commendation of the Same Rule, one book. “After blessed Augustine…” On the Second Rule, one book. “Keen in intellect, foremost in life…” On the Praises of the Same, one book. “Very often, when in…” Various Orations, one book. “Most blessed father, they have been accustomed…” He also wrote many other things.

He flourished under Frederick III, emperor, and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1470.

The Abbot of Sponheim

Benedictus Stendel, from the town of Halle in Saxony, a German by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, excellent in intellect and clear in speech, who for many years gloriously taught theology in the school of Erfurt and shone forth distinguished as much in life as in doctrine, wrote certain little works not unworthy of reading. From these he lectured ordinarily in the said university on the following:

On Genesis, one book. On Exodus, one book. On Leviticus, one book. On Numbers, one book. On Deuteronomy, one book. Various Sermons, one book. Diverse Collations, one book. And certain other things in logic, philosophy, and the other studies and scholastic exercises.

He flourished under Frederick III, emperor, and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Sifridus, titular bishop of Cyrene, of the order of Friars Preachers, a German by nation, vicar in pontifical matters of Theoderic, archbishop of Mainz, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not unacquainted with secular letters, skilled in the Hebrew and Latin languages, subtle in intellect and clear in speech, a keen disputant and outstanding preacher of the divine word, ready in counsel, distinguished in life, wrote certain little works worthy of reading, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these the following are extant: to the aforesaid Archbishop Theoderic,

On the Usury of the Jews, one book. “It is inquired in the forum of conscience…” On Rents and Redemption, one book. “It was asked first whether…” Sermons and Collations, one book. Various Questions, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished under Frederick III, emperor, and under Pius and Paul, Roman pontiffs, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Godescalcus of Meschede, a German by nation, a Westphalian by homeland, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently instructed in secular philosophy, keen in intellect, distinguished in life, a profound doctor of sacred theology, who for many years gloriously taught that science in the school of Erfurt, and great [unclear] of his learning

On Ecclesiastical Writers

... won praise for his [unclear] from everyone; in the same university he wrote and lectured on certain excellent little works, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these there are reported:

Questions on the Sentences, 4 books. Sermons for collation, 1 book. Various disputed questions, 1 book. And many other things.

This man’s brother, Theodericus Grefmunt of Meschede, doctor of arts and medicine, a man most learned in every respect, still survives and resides at Mainz; he himself, among other things, elegantly composed a treatise On the Regimen of Health in Time of Pestilence. He has a son called by his own name Theodericus, scarcely completing three lustra of age, whose admirable talent, and singular learning as well as eloquence, far surpasses many of advanced age, even doctors; there is extant with me his notable book On the Seven Liberal Arts. For he has written both to me and to others almost countless letters, most ornate in whatever subject, and various speeches displaying Ciceronian fluency, to such a degree that, like another Adeodatus, once the son of the most holy Augustine, by his talent, readiness in writing and arguing, and subtlety, he is an object of admiration and astonishment to many, even learned men.

Godescalcus, moreover, the brother of his father, flourished under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1470. And he died before this decade.
